Is the Artipoppe Zeitgeist Baby Carrier Worth the Steep Price Tag? One Mom's Candid Opinion
by
Kelsey Haywood Lucas
| December 28, 2023
Latest update:
See more
Kelsey Haywood Lucas
A mom of two shares her honest thoughts after testing out the pricey baby carrier.
When I was pregnant for the first time, I added the iconic
Artipoppe Zeitgeist baby carrier
to my registry on a whim: It was expensive, yes, but stunning; the most stylish
baby carrier
I had ever seen and precisely what my babywearing dreams were made of. Four years and two children later, I’m still in love with
the Artipoppe Zeitgeist’s style
— but it’s the carrier’s cozy comfort and unexpected durability that has made it a beloved, trusted accessory throughout my motherhood journey (of which babywearing has been a hugely important part).
If you’re not yet acquainted,
Artipoppe
is a luxury babywearing brand that’s known for its great style and quality — and for being a favorite among fashion-forward celebrities like Hailey Beiber, Hilary Duff, Kylie Jenner, Kelly Rowland, and more. (Seriously, a lot more.
Take a look
.)
Artipoppe makes three primary products: a baby wrap, a ring sling, and the
Zeitgeist baby carrier
— its most popular product, and the one I own. I used this carrier with my daughter (now 4) from birth through toddlerhood. Today, I’m about 16 months into using it with my son (and we’re still going strong!). In this review, I’ll share my honest opinion on the Zeitgeist’s features and answer the one question that everyone always asks: Is the Zeitgeist worth the price tag?
Baby carrier loved by celebs
Artipoppe Zeitgeist Baby Carrier
$370+
See More
Available from Artipoppe
What is the Artipoppe Zeitgeist baby carrier?
The Zeitgeist baby carrier is an adjustable, buckled carrier with cross-back straps that can be worn in three ergonomic positions: front carry facing in, front carry facing out, and back carry. It’s incredibly comfortable to wear and feels more like a soft baby wrap than, say, a bulky piece of hiking gear. It’s versatile and long-lasting (it’ll hold a child from the newborn stage to the toddler years), and it’s made of sustainably sourced materials.
To my knowledge, there’s no baby carrier brand that offers a higher quality carrier in such an extensive, beautiful range of styles. The cost of the Zeitgeist reflects this — it’s one of the most expensive options on the market. While nobody needs a carrier that costs upwards of $370 (more on pricing below), it’s a lovely option for parents who want to invest in something that’s going to look stunning, complement their unique sense of style, and meet the highest standards for sustainability and luxury materials. (And this won’t be everyone! If you’re seeking similar vibes at a lower price point, skip down to the bottom of this post for suggestions on the best Artipoppe alternatives.)
The base-level price of the Zeitgeist starts at $370 for certain prints in fabrics, like linen and cotton. (These are a great option; I own the
Leopard Classic in cotton
, which is what my personal comments in this review are based on, and I wholeheartedly recommend this fabric.) The next level — consisting of specialty prints or fabrics like organic hemp, organic cashmere, organic velvet or denim — ranges between $390 and $790.
And then for the true luxury seeker, there are even some designs made with a $3,750 blend of vicuña and cashmere that’s available in several prints. (Vicuña wool is known for being one of the finest and most expensive fabrics in the world; the animals can only be shorn once every three years, and after each shearing they are tagged and released back into the wild in certain areas of South America.)
Key features of the Artipoppe Zeitgeist baby carrier:
Weight capacity:
7 to 45 pounds
Carry positions:
Three ergonomic options; front carry facing in, front carry facing out, and back carry
Comfort features for caregiver:
Cross-back shoulder straps for even weight distribution; padded shoulder straps for optimal neck and shoulder support
Comfort features for baby:
Padded leg openings; facing-out insert; adjustable neck cushion
Safety:
Acknowledged “hip-healthy” by the International Hip Dysplasia Institute; complies with the American ASTM F2236 and European CEN/TR 16512-2015 safety standards for baby carriers
Care instructions:
Varies by material and fabric; the cotton version reviewed here is machine washable
My honest experience — the pros
If I had to succinctly describe my experience with the Artipoppe Zeitgeist, I’d tell you that this carrier is like the perfect pair of jeans: so comfortable and cute that you’ll find yourself wearing it daily, when running errands or hanging around the house — but you can also dress it up for a special occasion. It’s comfortable, it works with every outfit, and it feels easy and effortless. But let’s dive into the details a bit more…
Kelsey Haywood Lucas
The Artipoppe Zeitgeist offers the best of both babywearing worlds.
The Zeitgeist combines the best of both babywearing worlds: It has the light, cozy, natural feel of a baby wrap (those intimate, cocoon-like vibes are so nice — especially for newborns and naps!). But it also boasts the support, stability and convenience of something with buckles (it can clip on or off in seconds with zero hassle, and it can be worn all day without needing to readjust).
It grows with your baby—from newborn to toddler.
Thanks to a few thoughtful details and four sizing positions, the Zeitgeist is comfortable for babies of all ages — from snoozy newborns to squirmy toddlers (or, more specifically, from 7 pounds to 45 pounds). One of my favorite features is the adjustable neck cushion, which can be put up when your baby needs more support around the head (great for smaller babies or napping), and then quickly strapped down when the baby wants a better view or more range of motion.
The Artipoppe Zeitgeist is shockingly durable and easy to clean.
Confession: I’ve had my Zeitgeist for more than four years, and it frequently gets thrown on my muddy, sandy, sticky car floor. Still, I’ve only needed to spot clean it a few times. Yes, I’ve been lucky to not have any major spills or diaper disasters happen while wearing it; but the fabric is so durable and breathable that dust, dirt, and spills seem to wipe right off. (It also probably helps that
my carrier
is a deep chocolate color.) My babies have played with it and pulled on it for years, and not a single stitch has unraveled; it’s in the exact same condition as it was when I unboxed it. And in the case that the carrier were to need a major clean, I love knowing it’s safe to toss into the washing machine.
This carrier feels like an extension of your outfit — not a piece of baby gear.
Many carriers are defined by a bulky silhouette, utilitarian straps and buckles, and a big, brand-name tag stuck front and center — but you’ll find none of that with an Artipoppe carrier. The Zeitgeist is actually a beautiful complement to any outfit: The
simpler styles
will blend seamlessly with whatever you’re wearing, while the bolder designs (like this
swan print
or
this fringed edition
) function as a fashion focal point — kind of like wearing a coat or bag that ‘makes’ an outfit.
Kelsey Haywood Lucas
The Artipoppe Zeitgeist is breastfeeding-friendly.
For moms who wish to breastfeed while baby-wearing, the Artipoppe Zeitgeist is a great option: It provides enough roominess and flexibility, and the straps can be loosened for additional space if necessary.
…And the cons of the Artipoppe Zeitgeist
The price tag is high.
The Artipoppe Zeitgeist is one of the most expensive carriers on the market, ranging from $370 to $3,750, which unfortunately makes it inaccessible for many.
Some fabrics may be trickier to clean.
While my cotton carrier can be thrown in the washing machine, several of the other fabrics (like cashmere and vicuña) can only be washed by hand.
There’s no chest strap to tighten when wearing in back-carry position.
While I personally haven’t found the lack of a chest strap to be a problem in back-carry position, I’ve heard from some moms who say they really need the extra support of a chest strap when back-carrying very squirmy or active toddlers.
The single size may not fit all bodies.
The carrier is available in one size, and some online reviews have pointed out that the Zeitgeist might not be a fit for larger body types.
Tips and tricks for using the Artipoppe
I could tell you all about how easy it is to put on the Zeitgeist — but Artipoppe made
a series of quick videos to show you the different carry options
, and they’re extremely helpful.
A few more things I want to point out…
Once you adjust and tighten your straps, you can roll them up and tie them off with small, elastic loops that are positioned on the straps. This means you won’t have any strap excess hanging down.
To wear the baby in a forward-facing position, be sure to attach the facing-out insert to the inside of the carrier (included standard with all carriers, and available to purchase separately in the case of loss). This insert narrows the body panel so the baby’s arms can wrap around it, and it provides extra support to the baby’s chest — ensuring a comfortable, ergonomic position.
The carrier comes equipped with black safety buttons and elastic safety loops — you’ll see how to use those in the
demonstration videos
.
For cooler climes and winter months, there’s a cozy
winter insert
that offers additional warmth (sold separately from the carrier).
So…is it worth it?
Everyone always wants to know if the Artipoppe is “worth it” — and while my personal answer would be an emphatic absolutely, it depends on your own personal priorities.
Do you plan on babywearing often? When you see someone wearing the Artipoppe, does your head turn or  do you stop scrolling? Do you care if your carrier looks like an elevated, intentional accessory vs. a piece of babywearing gear? Is the sourcing and sustainability of your carrier important to you?
If you answered “yes” to any or all of these questions, it’s likely that you’ll love the Artipoppe Zeitgeist. (I certainly do.)
When I look back on the past four (going on five!) years of motherhood, the Zeitgeist played a starring role in so many happy, beautiful memories: sunset walks on the beach, strolls around the zoo, and cuddles literally everywhere we went. (Can I just say how wonderful it feels to be able to spontaneously kiss the top of your baby’s head while you’re out grocery shopping?)
The Zeitgeist helped me get through the more difficult moments, too. As a first-time mom, I vividly remember strapping my newborn to my chest and pacing around our house for hours in the early evening — it was the only way I could make it through the
“witching hour
,” when close contact was the only thing that soothed those nightly bouts of fussiness. And when my second baby’s frequent cries and sensitivity turned to
colic
, I quickly realized that the only way to keep him happy and comfortable was to strap him in the Zeitgeist and keep him close to my heart for hours on end.
I could have done these things in any carrier, of course (as long as it was safe and comfortable). But the Zeitgeist wasn’t just a piece of baby gear; it was a beautiful, stylish carrier that felt like a joy to wear. It felt very much like me at a time when maintaining my sense of selfhood was particularly important.
My advice? If style and aesthetics are important to you, and you plan to babywear often, find a carrier that you’ll fall in love with. If the Artipoppe Zeitgeist feels like a big splurge, consider asking friends and family to contribute to a group fund — or just take a few other extraneous items off your newborn shopping list (there are so many things we really don’t need, while a carrier is something you could use for hours every day). Prioritizing what’s important to you is a hugely important lesson when it comes to so many things in motherhood—starting with your baby gear.
Dupes to consider
Is the Artipoppe carrier amazing? Yes. Are there also other, equally amazing carriers out there — with different features, at lower price points? Also yes! The ideal carrier for one parent will be very different than the ideal carrier for another — whether that’s because of features, budget, or both. That’s why I’ve curated a range of top-notch alternatives if you’re looking for a different carrier with similar vibes.
Wildbird Aerial Carrier
($268): Based on appearance alone, the Wildbird Aerial Carrier is the closest style I’ve seen to the Artipoppe Zeitgeist. Love that there are no big, branded tags on this one.
ErgoBaby Omni Dream
($199): This carrier is one of many options from trusted brand ErgoBaby and has many similarities to the Zeitgeist: a minimal design, extreme softness (it’s cotton, which is key for comfort and breathability), plenty of versatility and carry positions, and a range of stylish patterns.
Beco Gemini
($80): A simple, cross-back design and reasonable price point make this carrier a solid option for those who want Artipoppe vibes on a budget. Made with 100% cotton and available in a wide range of colors and prints, it’s soft and breathable — and there’s a style for everyone.

Wintertime means brisk stroller walks in fresh snow, ski trips, and other outdoor activities — but
dressing baby for the weather
can be less than delightful. After all, your little one can’t exactly tell you if they’re warm enough and, if not properly bundled, are prone to getting
hypothermia
or frostbite. If you live in a cold or snowy climate, a baby snowsuit is a must-have (as are
baby hats
and
mittens
!).
But picking out just one is no easy feat, especially since the market is flooded with options. Luckily, What to Expect staff and community members have plenty of baby snowsuit recommendations based on what kept their own little ones warm during previous winters.
How I Chose the Best Baby Snowsuits
To find the best baby snowsuits, I spoke to
Daniel Ganjian, M.D.
, a pediatrician at
Providence Saint John's Health Center
in Santa Monica, California, to learn what keeps babies safe and comfortable during chilly temperatures. Using Dr. Ganjian’s feedback, I created an initial list of over 20 baby snowsuits that were made of:
Lightweight fabrics, so as not to restrict baby’s movement
Waterproof materials to keep baby dry and warm
I then narrowed down the list using recommendations from What to Expect staff and community members, prioritizing baby snowsuits that parents praised for:
Growing with their child, thanks to features like adjustable straps, sleeves, and hems
Being easy to put on and take off
Low-maintenance care (nearly all of my picks can be tossed in the wash!)
The result: 10 parent-approved snowsuits — from lightweight fleece to heavy-duty down — that will keep your little one warm when the weather gets frightful.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

A Doctor's Note on Baby Snowsuit Safety
Per the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), infants and
children should not wear large coats or snowsuits while riding in their car seats
. This means you will have to change your baby into their snowsuit once you reach your destination.
Additionally, Dr. Ganjian suggests avoiding overly thick snowsuits that add extra weight and restrict your baby’s movements, especially if you expect your baby will fall asleep while wearing it. (Say, for example, if you take them for a walk in the winter.) “The latest safe sleep guidelines
recommend children not be in weighted swaddles or blankets
— a snowsuit would fall into this category,” Dr. Ganjian says.
FAQs
When should baby start wearing a snowsuit?
Your baby should start wearing a snowsuit when they are first exposed to cold weather. The specific age may vary, depending on where you live. But if temperatures are near or below freezing, or there is snow or cold wind, a snowsuit is a good idea.
How should I dress my baby in the winter?
According to
the AAP’s Winter Safety Tips
, you should dress your child for cold weather like so:
Start with close-fitting layers on the bottom like tights, leggings or long-sleeved bodysuits.
Next, add pants and a warmer top, like a sweater or thermal-knit shirt, along with a jacket.
Finally, add a
hat
,
mittens
, socks,
booties
and, of course, a snowsuit.
When is the weather too cold to bring baby outside?
The AAP recommends avoiding wind chills below -15 degrees with your baby. Keep in mind, though, that if it feels cold to you, it may feel even colder to your baby. Little bodies can’t retain heat as well as adults, explains Dr. Ganjian, who adds it might be best to stay inside and be safe.
Why isn’t it safe for my baby to wear a snowsuit or winter coat in their car seat?
“The added bulk of a snowsuit can create a gap between the baby and the car seat harness,” Dr. Ganjian says. “This can lead to improper restraint in case of a crash, increasing the risk of injury.”
Snowsuits can also limit movement, which is important for baby to be comfortably and safely positioned in the car, he says. Dr. Ganjian recommends dressing in layers that are easy to peel on and off. “This allows for a snug fit with the car seat harness while providing adequate warmth,” he says.

A new What to Expect analysis reveals that baby product recalls hit a 10-year high in 2025. Here's how to spot the red flags on your favorite shopping sites.
Back to Top
In This Article
Sleep items and toys account for half of the recalls
Stricter laws and enforcement have prompted more recalls
Products sold online have added to the recalls
What you can do as a parent to avoid unsafe products
Methodology
Key takeaways
Baby and children's products now make up a third of U.S. product recalls.
Sleep items and toys make up most of the recalls in this category.
Online marketplaces often sell dangerous children's products to parents.
You're browsing for a new bassinet and find a 5-star dupe for a fraction of the name-brand price. It looks identical, the reviews are glowing, and it's at your door in two days. But that too-good-to-be-true deal is exactly what's fueling a record-breaking surge in product recalls. In 2025, baby gear recalls hit a 10-year high, a new What to Expect analysis of data from the Consumer Product & Safety Commission (CPSC) shows.
Last year, the CPSC recalled 145 different baby and children's products — more than twice as many as it did in 2015. Recalls of baby and children's products also account for more of the recalls happening — 23% of the recalls in 2015 versus 34% in 2025. In other words, even though the total number of recalls has gone up, baby and children's products still account for a bigger share of the pie.
Design by Brittany Fung
Sleep items and toys account for half of the recalls
The vast majority of the recalls analyzed fall into just a few categories. Sleep products — including cribs, bassinets, playards, pajamas, robes, crib bumpers, mattresses, and inclined sleepers — account for a quarter of recalls (25%). Toys make up another quarter (25%).
The next biggest categories include bikes, ride-on toys, and helmets (15%); apparel (10%); and infant gear, such as strollers, carriers, and bath seats (10%). Other items — including other children's furniture, decor, and feeding products — make up the remaining 15%.
As a parent, these recalls can sound concerning. Are baby and children's products getting less safe? Not quite — here's what you need to know if you're shopping for your baby or child.
Design by Brittany Fung
Stricter laws and enforcement have prompted more recalls
The jump in recalls is happening in part because stricter safety standards have gone into effect, experts tell What to Expect. Until fairly recently, the existing rules around infant sleep products focused on cribs and bassinets and failed to address other products marketed as making babies sleep better.
"Essentially anybody can bring anything to market if it doesn't violate existing standards," says
Benjamin Hoffman, M.D.
, the immediate past chair of the
American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Injury, Violence and Poison Prevention
. "The burden of proof is to demonstrate harm as opposed to the requirement to demonstrate absence of harm prior to coming to market."
Stricter standards for infant sleep products finally came after more than 100 infants died in
inclined sleepers
from 2009 to 2019.
Trusted Source
American Academy of Pediatrics
Sudden Unexpected Infant Death in Inclined Sleepers: 2009-2023
See All Sources
[1]
In 2021, Congress passed the Safe Sleep for Babies Act, effectively banning inclined sleepers along with crib bumpers.
Trusted Source
Congress.gov
Safe Sleep for Babies Act of 2021
See All Sources
[2]
This change prompted a number of recalls, says Lisa Trofe, executive director of the
Baby Safety Alliance
.
In fact, recalls of children's sleep products went from a relatively low number (six to 15 per year from 2015 to 2022) to new highs. In 2025, the CPSC recalled 38 different children's sleep items, the most in the entire 10-year period that What to Expect examined.
Other legislation — like
Reese's Law
, which introduced new safety requirements for button cell batteries — also went into effect during this time.
Trusted Source
Consumer Product & Safety Commission
Button Cell and Coin Battery Business Guidance
See All Sources
[3]
You can clearly see the impact that these new rules and regulations had on baby and children's products: The share of recalls that specifically mention a standards violation jumped from 21% in 2015 to 73% in 2025.
"The CPSC has strengthened its enforcement approach," CPSC Acting Chairman Peter A. Feldman tells What to Expect. "We are operating more efficiently, using better data and tools, and acting more quickly when hazards are identified. That means we are intervening earlier — often stopping unsafe products before they can cause widespread harm."
Products from online sellers have also proliferated, adding to the recalls
Laws aren't the only things that have changed in the past decade: "The retail environment has changed very drastically over the last 10, 15, years," Trofe says. Nowadays, more parents shop online to get baby-ready.
And while shopping online is certainly convenient, it can also connect parents with unsafe products. Popular online marketplaces like Amazon and Walmart allow for what's called third-party sellers, which are independent merchants that sell products through these platforms. These products can come from different countries that may not have the same safety regulations that exist in the U.S.
“We are seeing more consumer products entering the U.S. market, particularly from China, which increases the risk that unsafe products will reach consumers," Feldman confirms to What to Expect.
Both Amazon and Walmart tell What to Expect that they require all products sold on their sites to comply with applicable laws and brand policies, and that they use verification processes to check this. However, experts tell What to Expect that some dangerous products can — and do — fall through the cracks.
Anybody can bring anything to market if it doesn't violate existing standards. The burden of proof is to demonstrate harm.
Benjamin Hoffman, M.D.
"Many e-commerce platforms really do everything in their power to ensure that those [unsafe] products are delisted or taken down or not made visible in the first place," Trofe says. "But there are ways for those unscrupulous sellers to get around those types of things."
You might see some of these when you're browsing online: dupes of popular products, sometimes with lots of five-star reviews, but sold for much lower prices than similar products from brands you know and recognize. These cheaper options can look really appealing, especially for something like a toy that seems low-stakes — but they may pose a choking hazard or contain unsafe levels of lead.
What to Expect’s analysis revealed CPSC recall listings full of imported third-party products with gibberish brand names like
Uuoeebb Infant Walkers
, which pose a deadly fall hazard, and
YCXXKJ Baby Bath Seats
, which could tip and cause a child to drown. Even though they don't make headlines like recalls of bigger brands, thousands of these products make their way into families' homes on a regular basis.
Even as bigger platforms like Amazon and Walmart have gotten more savvy with third-party listings, dangerous products can still pop up and stay online for hours or days — or sometimes even longer — before getting taken down. "We're playing whack-a-mole with this stuff," Dr. Hoffman says. "New third parties enter marketplaces all the time."
What you can do as a parent to avoid unsafe products
While these findings may feel overwhelming, there are some simple rules of thumb that can help you choose safe products. Here's how experts say you can avoid potentially dangerous buys.
Buy your car seat and crib new.
These are the only two essentials you'll need, Dr. Hoffman says, and getting these items new helps ensure they meet the latest safety standards. If you can't afford a new car seat or crib, contact your local coalition of
Safe Kids Worldwide
. This organization can connect you with donated or discounted products that will keep your baby safe, Trofe shares.
Check product labels.
Car seats should have a label stating that the product complies with Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 213. For your crib or playard, look for a manufacturer label showing a date of June 2011 or later.
Consider looking for a
Baby Safety Alliance verified seal
when shopping for other baby products. "That means the product has been tested to the most up-to-date and stringent safety standards that exist in the United States, and goes beyond the mandatory CPSC rules," Trofe explains.
Exercise caution with used gear.
Secondhand marketplaces can keep recalled products in circulation, passing from family to family. The CPSC has even recalled some products like the
Fisher-Price Rock 'n Play sleeper
multiple times because so many still circulate on the resale market.
Trusted Source
Consumer Product & Safety Commission
Fisher-Price Reannounces Recall of 4.7 Million Rock 'n Play Sleepers; At Least Eight Deaths Occurred After Recall
See All Sources
[4]
Double-check whether
secondhand or older products
have had a recall by searching the product name on the
CPSC website
.
If it's too good to be true, think twice.
When you're shopping online, exercise some healthy skepticism. Look closely at who's selling the product and what's in the description, Trofe advises. "Buy from the brand directly if there's a question, and understand if the company name is not a trusted one," she says. Skip unusually good deals for
knockoff products
, she adds. If there's a name-brand stroller that sells for $600, and there's something that looks very similar that's only $100, that should be a red flag.
Register your products.
You know those paper registration cards that come with pretty much every baby item you buy? It's a good idea to fill those out (either by hand or online) so the manufacturer knows how to contact you in the event of a recall, Trofe and Dr. Hoffman say.
Report any injuries.
You can help keep babies and children safe by reporting any dangerous products (including close calls) you encounter to
saferproducts.gov
.
Methodology
Recall data were obtained from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) recall database, which contains recall announcements for consumer products regulated by the agency. The dataset includes all recalls issued between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2025. A keyword search was conducted to identify potentially relevant recalls. All recalls identified through the keyword search were then manually reviewed to determine whether the recalled product was specifically intended for babies or children. After manual review and refinement, the final dataset includes 914 recalls involving baby and children’s products between 2015 and 2025. Annual totals of child-related recalls were compared with the total number of CPSC recalls issued each year to calculate the share of recalls involving baby and children's products.

My 3-year-old would probably live outside if she could. Her love for the great outdoors means I always have an arsenal of skin-protecting tools at the ready — yes, even in the winter! By our door, I keep a basket stocked with essentials: a hat, a few pairs of
sunglasses
and, of course, baby sunscreen.
I've been buying and testing baby-safe sunscreen since she was 6 months old — the age both the
American Academy of Dermatology
(AAD) and
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) say it's safe for little ones to start wearing SPF. My credit card company may have been alarmed by the sheer amount I spent on sunscreen that first year. But thanks to all that trial and error, I’ve found the best baby sunscreens to protect sensitive skin—ones that kids will actually wear without a meltdown.
And because sharing is caring, I’m passing on my discoveries! Here’s everything you need to know about choosing baby sunscreen, plus my top picks for the best ones you can buy today.
How I Chose the Best Baby Sunscreen
It’s not hard to find a baby-safe sunscreen; almost all of them have “baby” somewhere on the packaging. The challenge is choosing the best sunscreen for your baby, because each one is different.
To learn what parents should look for in a baby-safe sunscreen, I spoke to
Bernard Cohen, M.D.
, Director of the Johns Hopkins University Pediatric Dermatology and Cutaneous Laser Center;
Ife J. Rodney, M.D.,
a dermatologist and founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics; and
Marissa J. Perman, M.D.
, a pediatric dermatologist at the University of Philadelphia. I also consulted recommendations from the AAP and AAD, along with the Environmental Working Group (EWG)’s
Guide to Sunscreens
, which analyzed more than 2,200 sunscreens and found that only 25 percent deliver safe and effective protection. Based on the non-profit organization’s findings, Rodney says, “It’s a good idea to focus on sunscreens that contain zinc oxide and titanium dioxide because they reflect the harmful rays away from the skin.”
Per this guidance, all of the baby sunscreens I selected are:
Broad spectrum formula
to protect against both UVA and UVB rays
Mineral sunscreens (also known as physical sunscreen), which include titanium dioxide or non-nano zinc oxide for optimal protection and stay on the surface of the skin
Rated a 3 or lower based by theEWG; the rating system goes from 0 to 10, with lower numbers having less hazardous ingredients. A few products are also designated as EWG Verified, which means they meet the non-profit’s strictest criteria for efficacy.
Aligned with the
U.S. Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) guidelines to meet safety standards
Free of synthetic fragrances and harsh chemicals, such as homosalate, oxybenzone and octinoxate — ingredients that the
FDA
is investigating to see if they are absorbed through the skin
Reef-safe
A minimum
sun protection factor
(SPF) of 30, which filters out 97% of UVB rays
Even with this guidance in mind, however, I was still left with dozens of options. To further narrow down the list, I spoke to five What to Expect staff members who have seven kids between them and have tried all of the sunscreens on this list. I also relied on my own experience as well as recommendations from What to Expect community members, specifically those whose children are prone to eczema or have sensitive skin.
Of course, I kept the overall application experience top of mind, too. (Lathering yourself in SPF is tough enough, let alone a wiggling infant.) That’s why I carefully considered elements such as the ease of application, whether sunscreens left a white cast, and the packaging's ease of use.
These recommendations, paired with our experts’ insight, resulted in the following list of 10 baby-safe sunscreens that are easy to apply, smell good and don't leave baby’s skin feeling sticky.
Korin Miller
contributed to this article.

Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

Why We Love It
A favorite of WTE parents and editors alike is
Thinkbaby SPF 50+ sunscreen
uses zinc oxide as its active ingredient and is free of oxybenzone, parabens and phthalates. Unlike some mineral sunscreens which can be thick and hard to spread, Thinkbaby’s sunscreen goes on creamy and blocks 98 percent of UVB rays. It's also extra water-resistant because it lasts up to 80 minutes, so you can head to the pool with baby and know that she's protected. Another nice perk? It absorbs quickly, so your little one won't feel sticky or have a chalky residue on her skin after you apply.
Olivia DeLong, What to Expect's senior health editor, uses Thinkbaby for both herself and her daughter. "I did a lot of research during pregnancy and actually started using it then and loved it," she says. “It goes on super easily, and I always felt like my daughter was protected and I wasn't using anything with lots of chemicals or junk in it." She also notes that the lotion is great for covering her daughter's body, while she uses the stick format for her face, ears and neck.
I also tried Thinkbaby sunscreen
(along with several other options) and found this one truly lives up to the hype. I appreciate that the formula is thick for easier application, but still goes on smoothly. It's also hypoallergenic which is great for children, like my daughter who has sensitive skin but requires regular sunscreen application.
One minor downside is that it isn't readily available in drugstores, so you don't want to be caught without it on vacation. But given that it's often on sale, you can stock up at the start of summer and make it through the season burn-free.

Fragrances are common in sunscreen, but they can irritate baby’s delicate skin.
Alba Botanica’s Mineral Sunscreen
is totally unscented, so there’s no need to worry about a reaction due to synthetic or strong smells. In fact, many WTE community members give this brand a thumbs up for its transparency around ingredients.
This sunscreen comes in the form of a creamy lotion with a titanium dioxide and zinc oxide base that rubs in easily. It feels surprisingly lightweight, but provides up to 80 minutes of SPF 30 protection in the water before you need to slather it on again. The
EWG
has no concerns about efficacy with this product, so you can use it with confidence until the expiration date.
Alba Botanica’s formula includes protective and moisturizing ingredients like niacinamide, squalene and vitamin E. It’s also gluten-free, in case that’s a concern for your little one, and non-comedogenic, so it won’t clog baby’s poress.  I like to use it on my face after I’ve slathered up my little one and have never had sunscreen-induced breakouts with it.
Admittedly, it is a bit pricey, but a little truly goes a long way when it comes to this sunscreen. Plus, the cruelty-free formula is reef-safe, too.

When baby is dressed from head to toe in sun-protective clothing, a few quick swipes of a sunscreen stick might be all you need to protect her exposed skin. "Sticks are especially nice for the face, as they are easier to control keeping out of the eyes," Dr. Perman says. What makes this
Mustela Mineral Baby Sunscreen Stick
stand out is that it goes on surprisingly smooth — thanks to the addition of organic ingredients like shea butter, avocado oil and jojoba — whereas other mineral sunscreen sticks can be thick and hard to spread.
After getting sunscreen in my daughter’s eyes one too many times, I made the switch to the Mustela stick for her face—and let me tell you, it was a game-changer. From that moment on, most of our sunscreen applications were tear-free.
I love how smoothly the stick glides on — no need to press hard, which is a win when dealing with a squirmy toddler. Plus, the tint makes it easy to see where it’s applied, without requiring extra rubbing (because we all know that rubbing + wiggly child = sunscreen in the eyes and tears for hours).
This sunscreen stick is
EWG Verified
, which is the organization’s highest mark of approval.
The organic formula is also hypoallergenic and approved by the National Eczema Association, making it a great choice for sensitive skin. And bonus — it’s water-resistant for up to 80 minutes!

What To Look For in Baby Sunscreen
In addition to ingredients, formulas and SPF levels, there are a few other things to keep in mind when shopping for a baby sunscreen.
Application type:
Baby sunscreens typically come in stick and lotion form, and the best type for you comes down to personal preference. You might even want to have both on hand, as stick sunscreen is easy to apply to the face to avoid baby's eyes and mouth, while cream is better for covering larger parts of baby's body. As for aerosol sunscreen sprays? Even though they might seem convenient for quickly applying SPF on a wiggly kid, Dr. Perman cautions against them. “I worry they are not applied with the appropriate thickness,” she says, particularly if you're on a windy beach, when the spray may blow away before it makes it onto baby. Plus, it's possible your baby could accidentally breathe in the chemicals from the spray. For these reasons, we kept aerosol sprays off of our list and included only lotion and stick options.
Water resistance:
No
sunscreen is waterproof
, but you can buy water-resistant sunscreen which stays effective for 40 minutes in the water (some extra-resistant brands last up to 80 minutes). Even if your child won't be spending tons of time in the water, the AAD still recommends
using a water-resistant sunscreen
for optimal protection. For this reason, you'll find that almost all of our picks are water-resistant up to at least 40 minutes.
FAQ
Can babies under 6 months wear sunscreen?
Yes, you can apply sunscreen to babies younger than 6 months old, but you'll want to use it in minimal quantities. As mentioned previously, the AAP recommends that you only use sunscreen on small areas of their body, like your little one's face or the tops of their hands and feet. In general,
keep babies under 6 months out of the sun
and use protective lightweight clothing to cover their skin, including long sleeve shirts, pants and hats. Additionally, you want to avoid putting sunscreen on parts of her body that baby often puts in her mouth.
After 6 months of age, you can apply sunscreen to all exposed areas of your child's body. You'll still want to keep baby in the shade when possible, however, to avoid sunburn.
Is mineral sunscreen better for babies?
Mineral sunscreen, also known as physical sunscreen, is the preferred choice for baby sunscreen. Unlike chemical sunscreen, mineral sunscreens stay on the surface of the skin and aren't absorbed into the body, explains Marissa J. Perman, M.D., a pediatric dermatologist at the University of Philadelphia. They're also usually free from chemicals like oxybenzone and octinoxate.
Mineral sunscreen is
especially effective on sensitive parts of the body
, such as nose, cheeks, tops of the ears and shoulders, the AAP notes, because it acts as a better barrier against the sun.
Another plus, especially for parents, is that mineral sunscreen  starts working immediately since it doesn't need to be absorbed by the skin. If you're using a chemical sunscreen, however, you'll want to apply it 15 to 30 minutes before going in the sun.
How to apply baby sunscreen
If baby is under 6 months, keep sunscreen use minimal. Apply a thin layer to small exposed areas like her face when shade and protective clothing are not available.
For babies over 6 months of age, you can apply sunscreen all over her body, making sure to cover any areas that are exposed to the sun.
As for
reapplying baby's sunblock
, you should do so every two hours that you're outside, plus immediately after getting wet or towel drying, according to the AAP.

The first time I spotted red, raised bumps on my baby’s bottom, I panicked and grabbed the first cream I could get my hands on at the drugstore. Now, four kids later, I’ve learned that the best diaper rash creams shine in different scenarios — whether you’re dealing with a sudden flare-up, a severe case, or preventing irritation from even occurring in the first place.
Diaper rash
is one of those rites of passage most parents don’t exactly look forward to. It’s a common skin irritation typically caused by a mix of moisture, friction, and irritants due to enzymes in poop and pee. Other times, the ingredients in your diaper or bath products can be the culprit. And for whatever reason, some babies are just more rash-prone than others due to their sensitive skin (my youngest falls in this camp!).
Needless to say, I’ve built up quite the arsenal of rash treatments. I’ve found that the best diaper rash creams are amazingly effective at
soothing skin almost instantly
. My go-to — and What to Expect’s overall pick — is
Triple Paste’s 3X Max Ointment
. It once cleared up my daughter’s raw, intense rash overnight. But there are plenty of other standouts I’ve turned to over the years, such as affordable alternatives or those with a lighter consistency, because every baby is different. Remember: What works for my family may not work as well for yours.
That's why I went ahead and compared the top formulas with input from pediatricians and insider tips from fellow moms in the What to Expect community. Rest assured that all of the recommendations below come backed by those of us who have also grappled with the stress and intimidation of stubborn diaper rash.
How We Chose the Best Diaper Rash Creams
I first referenced guidelines from leading experts, including the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) and the
American Academy of Dermatology Association
(AAD).
I then consulted three pediatricians:
Gina Posner
, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at MemorialCare Medical Group in Fountain Valley, California, and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board;
Anjuli S. Gans
, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia; and
Julia Reading
, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician at Providence Medical Institute in San Pedro, California, to get additional insights into diaper rash creams.
As a mom of four myself, I leaned heavily on my own experience with diaper rash creams. I've tested nearly all of the most popular diaper rash creams on the market, taking careful note of how long they took to be effective, how easy they were to apply, and whether they caused any additional irritation. In line with my findings and expert feedback and guidance, I made sure that all of the products on this list:
Contain either
zinc oxide
,
petrolatum
, or
beeswax
, three ingredients that leading experts recommend to effectively heal diaper rash. (More on that below.)
Are free of added fragrance, which the AAP says can make diaper rash worse.
Avoid ingredients that have been flagged as unsafe for children under age 2
I also spoke to four moms on the What to Expect team who have four children between them and have tried several of the products on the list. Because every family’s experience is unique, I double-checked my findings against what parents in the What to Expect Community shared were the most effective and why. These brands received positive reviews for:
Effectiveness:
Most importantly, a diaper rash cream needs to work. All of the products featured below had rave reviews from parents, who called out the formula’s ability to quickly heal their child’s diaper rash.
Ease of application:
Although effectiveness is the biggest consideration, some products are easier to apply than others. With diaper rash cream, it’s especially nice if the formula isn’t too difficult to spread.
Accessibility:
Diaper rash can appear suddenly, and the last thing you want is to wait days for baby to get relief. All of the products on this list are easy to purchase at major online retailers such as Amazon and Target or at drugstore chains.

A Doctor’s Note on Diaper Rash Creams
Diaper rash can be caused by different things, but the two main culprits are irritants and fungi. “Barrier creams — especially those containing zinc oxide and/or petrolatum — are the first-line treatment for routine diaper rash caused by moisture, friction, and irritants,” Gans says. “These creams act as physical shields, protecting the skin while it heals and preventing worsening of inflammation.”
Size:
Diaper rash creams range in size from small tubes to large tubs. Although some products may initially appear more expensive, it’s helpful to check the price per ounce (often listed in a smaller font on a retailer website) in addition to the listing price.
Type:
Skin care products that target diaper rash are most commonly creams, ointments, or pastes. Ointments and creams are great for soothing and protecting, and pastes usually contain zinc, an ingredient that’s a little better for soothing but can also help prevent diaper rash from occurring in the first place.
Ingredients:
The AAP and the AAD, along with the doctors I spoke with, recommend choosing a diaper rash cream that contains zinc oxide, beeswax, and/or petrolatum as the active ingredient. If the rash is mild, a petroleum-based product may be sufficient. But if your baby has a moderate to severe rash, zinc oxide-based products will provide a bit more protection from further irritation. It may also help to experiment and try different creams to see which works best for your baby’s bum and type of diaper rash.
Zinc oxide.
“Zinc oxide is considered a first-line treatment for diaper dermatitis because it serves as an effective physical barrier, protecting the skin from moisture, irritants, and friction—all key contributors to diaper rash,” explains Gans, who adds a 40% concentration of zinc oxide is especially effective in moderate to severe diaper rash. “While the widespread use of barrier ointments like zinc oxide is based on longstanding clinical experience, there is support for its benefits: Zinc oxide has been shown to have mild anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and astringent properties that help calm inflamed skin and promote healing,” she explains.
Petrolatum.
This is one of the most effective and widely-recommended barrier agents in pediatric dermatology, according to Gans. “It acts as an occlusive moisturizer—meaning it forms a physical barrier over the skin that prevents transepidermal water loss and protects against irritants like urine and stool,” she explains. “It is hypoallergenic, fragrance-free, and well tolerated in infants, making it a first-line choice for preventing and treating mild diaper dermatitis.”
Beeswax.
“Beeswax is thought to act similarly to petrolatum as an occlusive barrier that locks in moisture,” says Reading. Beeswax may also be anti-inflammatory, she adds. “While less commonly studied in pediatric-specific literature, beeswax has mild emollient and protective properties and may contribute to barrier function in combination formulations,” Gans says. “However, because it is more likely to be found in boutique or natural diaper balms, it’s important to note that some formulations may contain fragrances or other additives that could irritate sensitive infant skin.”
When to use antifungal (yeast) vs barrier creams for irritation types
But when diaper rash sticks around for several days, it’s possible that baby has developed a fungal or yeast infection, Gans says. These are the biggest signs of a yeast-related rash:
Bright red, beefy plaques in the diaper area
Satellite lesions, which are small red or darker skin-colored bumps or pustules just outside the main rash
Involvement of the skin folds, which are typically spared in non-yeast rashes
Skin that looks shiny and bright red or darker skin-colored in these areas. “Yeast likes areas with high moisture,” Gans explains.
If you suspect baby has a yeast-related rash, a topical antifungal medication like nystatin may be needed. “Once the antifungal is applied, a barrier cream can be layered on top to protect the skin further,” she says. “Treatment typically continues until the rash resolves and for up to two weeks.” If the rash gets worse or doesn’t improve within seven to 10 days, Gans says it’s time to follow up with your pediatrician.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the best cream for diaper rash?
First, consider the type of rash your baby has. If the rash is mild, a petroleum-based product may be sufficient. But if your baby has a moderate to severe rash, zinc oxide-based products will provide a bit more protection from further irritation. It may also help to experiment and try different creams to see which works best for your baby’s bum and type of diaper rash.
If the product you’re using doesn’t seem to be helping, make an appointment with your pediatrician. Some babies, especially those who are taking antibiotics, can develop a fungal infection in the diaper rash area that may require different treatment.
What heals diaper rash the fastest?
Although every baby is different, zinc oxide-based products tend to heal diaper rash the fastest.
In addition, the following strategies can help manage diaper rash:
Keep baby’s skin dry.
Moisture is your enemy, so make sure to dry your baby's skin well at every diaper change (before applying cream).
Change your baby often.
Because moisture from dirty diapers can cause skin to chafe, frequently changing your baby’s diaper can help prevent rash.
Clean baby’s skin during diaper changes. The AAP recommends a wipe that is free of alcohol and fragrance, or cleansing baby’s skin with water and gentle cleanser. Allow baby’s skin to air-dry before coating it with cream.
Can you use diaper rash cream on newborns?
Most diaper rash creams are officially recommended for babies 6 months and older. If, however, your newborn has a diaper rash and preventative strategies aren’t helping, Dr. Posner says applying diaper rash cream on the area is likely fine. Always check with your pediatrician to be safe.
What's good for severe diaper rash?
Thicker creams and pastes are best for soothing existing or severe rashes. I personally turn to formulas that have 40% zinc oxide.
When should you call the doctor about your baby’s diaper rash?
Sometimes diaper rash doesn’t respond to home treatment. The AAD recommends reaching out to your child’s doctor if her rash doesn’t go away or worsens, or if your little one develops any signs of infection. That can include a fever, pus draining from the rash, blisters or if your baby is especially difficult to console.
“If the skin is super red, cracking, fluffing off or the cream’s not working, definitely talk to your pediatrician,” says Dr. Posner.
Luckily, though, home treatments can resolve diaper rash most of the time. Read on for our top picks for the best diaper rash creams.
Where should you apply diaper rash cream?
You can apply diaper rash cream liberally on your baby’s bottom — in fact, the AAP says that there’s generally no such thing as too much diaper cream. (The exception is if you’re prescribed an antifungal cream for your baby’s diaper rash. In that case, you should apply it according to the pharmacist’s instructions.)
“A lot of parents don’t put enough diaper rash cream on,” says Dr. Posner. “You really need a thick layer, like icing on a cupcake.”
Unless it’s soiled, it’s also not necessary to wipe diaper cream off at every change. You can just wait and remove it at the end of the day, the AAD says. But make sure the area has dried a little before putting a new diaper on your baby. (Remember: moisture breeds bacteria.) After wiping, you can fan the area or wait a minute or two before closing the diaper and getting your baby dressed.

I Chose the Nuna Travel System Over the Doona — Here’s Why I’d Do It Again
by
Elizabeth Buxton
| June 4, 2025
Latest update:
See
 more
Nuna / Elizabeth Buxton
It folds with one hand, skips the car seat base and was the MVP of my baby’s first flight.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
What Is It
: Nuna TRVL lx + PIPA urbn Travel System
Why I Love It
: This sleek, compact system folds with one hand, installs without a base, reclines fully for naps and makes travel with a baby feel effortless.
How Much Is It
: $900
Where to Buy It
: Available at
Nordstrom
As a shopping editor and first-time mom to my 8-month-old daughter Lou, I’ve tested a lot of baby gear. The
Nuna TRVL lx + PIPA urbn travel system
is one of the few that’s earned a permanent spot in our trunk. I started using it a few months after Lou was born, and it quickly became my go-to for errands, car trips and longer travel, including her first flight.
I already had a full-size stroller (the UPPAbaby Vista V3) for neighborhood walks but needed something lighter and easier to fold for quick transitions. Like most new parents, I was tempted by the Doona. Nearly all of my friends had it and recommended it. But after spending time in the
What to Expect community
, where parents consistently praised the Nuna system, I changed my mind. The one-handed fold, sleek design and baseless car seat install came up again and again. After comparing both, I chose the Nuna. No regrets.
What Is the Nuna TRVL lx + PIPA urbn Travel System?
A premium travel system that combines the Nuna TRVL lx stroller and PIPA urbn infant car seat. Built for families who need portability and smart design, it features a true one-handed fold, no-base installation using rigid LATCH and a clean, modern look.
Nuna TRVL lx + PIPA urbn Travel System at a Glance
Stroller Weight
: 17 lbs (including canopy and arm bar)
Car Seat Weight
: 7 lbs (without canopy and insert)
Stroller Dimensions
: 32 x 21 x 45.5 inches (Open); 27 x 14.25 x 21 inches (Folded)
Car Seat Dimensions
: 25 L x 17.5 x 22 inches
Parts Included
: TRVL lx stroller; PIPA urbn infant car seat; Canopy and arm bar (stroller); Canopy and insert (car seat)
Stroller Weight Limit:
Suitable for children up to 50 lbs;
Car Seat Weight Limit
: For infants 4–22 lbs and less than 29" tall
Warranty
: 2-year limited warranty (stroller); 1-year limited warranty (car seat)
Photo:
Nuna
Light, Easy-to-Fold and All-Around Amazing
Nuna TRVL lx PIPA urbn Travel System
$900
See More
See More
Set-Up and Use
Elizabeth Buxton
Setup took under five minutes and didn’t require a manual or tutorial. The fold is intuitive, and I figured out the one-handed close immediately. I now use it for errands, restaurants and travel. It handled Lou’s first trip (security lines, gate-checks and car transfers included) without any major meltdowns.
Why I Love It
The system's one-handed fold is a lifesaver when juggling a baby and bags. Its compact design fits easily into tight spaces, and the no-base-needed car seat installation is perfect for quick transitions in and out of vehicles. The stroller's full-recline feature allows for comfortable on-the-go naps, and the overall design is both functional and stylish.
Elizabeth Buxton
The TRVL lx is also made for travel; it's the “carry-on” to my Vista’s “checked bag.” It’s compact, intuitive and looks better than most strollers in its class. Compared to the Doona, it lasts longer, offers more flexibility and doesn’t feel like a one-note solution. Several friends with the Doona have told me they wish they’d seen this system first. (I even influenced one of my mom friends to upgrade from her Doona to the Nuna!)
Pros
A truly impressive one-handed fold
: I can collapse it while holding Lou and a diaper bag. It also stands vertically when folded, which is great for tight spaces like restaurants.
Ultra-lightweight frame
: At just over 13 pounds, it’s easy to lift into a trunk or overhead bin.
No base needed
: The PIPA urbn installs with built-in rigid LATCH (ideal for Ubers, taxis, and rental cars).
Smart design details
: The magnetic buckle, leatherette handlebar and fully reclining seat (which converts to a bassinet-style lounger) are well-executed and genuinely useful.
Elizabeth Buxton
Cons
Not built for rough terrain
: It’s not the smoothest ride for bumpy sidewalks or off-road strolling, but that’s not what it’s meant for
Lower car seat weight limit
: The PIPA urbn maxes out at 22 pounds and 29 inches, so you may need to upgrade to a convertible seat earlier than with some other infant options.
Is It Worth It?
Elizabeth Buxton
At $900, this isn’t an impulse purchase. But if you’re building a registry, it’s an ideal pick for a group gift. I use it constantly — because it helps me move quickly and confidently with a baby, whether I’m at the airport, in a cab or trying to avoid a parking lot meltdown (me, not Lou). I’ve already convinced a friend to buy it after seeing how smoothly it worked during a trip, and I’d recommend it to any parent looking for a sleek, efficient travel system that delivers on every promise.

The One Disney World Splurge That Was Worth Every Penny
by
Jessica Booth
| April 22, 2026

Zoe / Jessica Booth
Navigating crowds, protecting kids from the sun, and finding space for a mountain of snacks — here’s why this stroller is essential for your Disney itinerary.

All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
While planning our family’s first trip to Disney World, I was very optimistic, packing our days with Lightening Lanes and character dining reservations. My daughters, who were 3- and 5-years-old at the time, seemed to be the perfect age to soak in all of the magic the parks had to offer, and I figured their high-energy, incredibly active personalities would be able to handle the long days with little issue.
As you can probably imagine, the trip didn’t go quite as smoothly as I’d imagined. Between the early mornings, extreme humidity, and overall excitement, my 3-year-old crashed early most days — and 5-year-old was hanging by a thread. The thing that kept us from falling apart:
Zoe Twin V2 stroller
. Throughout the four days, the Zoe stroller became our fifth family member, serving as our home base, carry-all, and ideal nap spot.
Jessica Booth
The Disney-approved dream ride
In my pre-trip research, every mom deemed the Zoe Twin V2 a Disney World-friendly stroller. First, it meets the
park’s stroller requirements
(no larger than 31 inches wide and 52 inches long, in case you’re curious.)
Jessica Booth
Aside from that important detail, the Zoe Twin V2 is just a great travel stroller; easy to tote around even when you have other luggage. Folding it is an absolute breeze and opening it is just as easy, which makes airplane gate check less stressful. The handlebar makes it easy to carry with one hand, and at 19 pounds, it doesn’t feel too heavy or bulky.
Naptime hero
Even though my kids seem to run on never-ending batteries, I knew we wouldn’t be able to get through the day if they didn’t have a comfy place to relax. The Zoe’s seats are roomy, with an adjustable recline that can go back far enough for them to lay nearly flat, even while wearing giant fluffy Mickey Mouse ears. The extra large canopies also provided plenty of protection, which was key when temps were pushing 90 degrees and clouds were MIA.
We added a stroller fan, and my daughters were able to comfortably snooze while my husband and I enjoyed an iced Joffrey’s coffee (Pro tip: sit by the Liberty Square Riverboat if you need a cool-down break in Magic Kingdom.) And since you can adjust the canopies and seats individually, my 5-year-old was able to comfortably sit up and look around even when my 3-year-old was the only one sleeping.
Smooth ride
Another priority for me in a Disney-friendly stroller was finding one that was easy to navigate, and the Zoe Twin V2 nailed it. Even when it’s laden with two older toddlers and one too many souvenirs, we had no issue navigating through the crowds or going up and down curbs. Padded shoulder straps kept my kids from complaining and the adjustable footrests kept their legs sturdy too.
Souvenir central
Jessica Booth
The Zoe Twin’s storage basket offers a surprising amount of room, and I was able to stuff it full with an admittedly excessive amount of souvenirs, snacks, and extra clothes. Combine that with the
parent organizer
we used and we didn’t have to carry one thing as we walked around – a game changer when it’s so hot you feel like you’re walking on the surface of the sun.
Is the Zoe Twin V2 worth the splurge?
The
Zoe Twin V2
was an upgrade from a double stroller we already had, and I can confidently say it was 100% worth it. It kept my kids comfortable, allowed for multiple naps so we could avoid overtired meltdowns, and was easy for us to push through the crowds. In short, it made our trip feel just as magical as we wanted it to be. We loved it so much, it’s been with us on every trip since, because we literally couldn’t imagine being without it.

The first time I noticed crusty yellow scales covering my newborn daughter’s otherwise perfectly adorable scalp, my heart did a flip. I immediately dialed my pediatrician’s office to figure out what was wrong. Thankfully, the diagnosis was pretty straightforward: it was a case of cradle cap. Totally harmless, totally painless, and totally treatable with one of the best cradle cap shampoos.
Also known as
seborrheic dermatitis
, cradle cap is basically baby dandruff. It usually appears in the first few weeks of their life as red, flaky patches on the scalp. (It can also be found in baby skin folds and in the diaper area, although that’s less common.) While it looks uncomfortably dry and itchy, it isn’t. In fact, the worst part might be how much it bothers you.
Luckily, localized cases of cradle cap are simple to treat. New parents may be afraid of washing their baby’s scalp if cradle cap presents, but don’t be frightened: The
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) advises washing your baby’s hair every other day to gently remove and loosen up new flakes. That means you’ll need to have a great cradle cap shampoo on hand. Below, you can check out a few parent and pediatrician favorites.
How We Tested and Selected the Best Shampoos for Cradle Cap
As a mom of two young daughters who both dealt with cradle cap for months, I took my personal experience into account. I tried several different cradle cap shampoos and treatments to get rid of the flakes with my daughters and kept those in mind when compiling this list.
I also combed through dozens of conversations in the What to Expect Community, looking for insights into which cradle cap shampoos worked best for them. I also swapped stories with my mom friends who’ve survived stubborn flakes, asking them what they used and loved (or would skip altogether).
Most importantly, I spoke with three experts in the medical field who have experience dealing with cradle cap both professionally and personally with their own kids. This includes
Gabriella Dauer
, M.D., FAAP, pediatrician at
Dauer Pediatrics
in South Florida;
Dina Elbeltagy
, M.D., dermatologist and medical writer; and
Sanober Pezad Doctor, M.D
., an integrative and holistic dermatologist whose specialities include pediatric dermatology. They weighed in on what’s normal, as well as what ingredients are safe and which to avoid. For example, Dr. Pezad recommends mild formulas made with organic ingredients.
Based on their input, I also expanded my search to include popular cradle cap treatments like gels, masks, conditioners, sprays, and serums.
I conducted my own research to learn more about cradle cap and the best ingredients for treatment using resources such as the AAP and the

(AAD).
From there, I finalized my list of the best shampoos for cradle cap by keeping the following criteria in mind:
Pediatrician-approved ingredients:
Options with antifungals like ketoconazole or pyrithione zinc, as recommended by Dr. Dauer.
Gentle formulas:
Shampoos that are safe for baby skin and eyes, and that promise to be tear-free.
Irritant-free:
I tried to avoid artificial fragrances, dyes, or harsh preservatives whenever possible. I also skipped shampoos with salicylic acid, tar, or selenium sulfide, which can be too strong for delicate newborn skin.
Soothing extras:
I kept a close eye out for moisturizing additions like oat extract, shea butter, glycerin, and natural oils that nourish baby’s scalp, as per Dr. Elbeltagy's advice.

A Doctor's Note on Cradle Cap
“Cradle cap is a typical newborn scalp condition that is very common and involves a mix of oil production, dead skin cells, and yeast building up on the newborn scalp,” explains
Gabriella Dauer
, M.D., FAAP, pediatrician at
Dauer Pediatrics
in South Florida.
Most babies will experience mild or moderate cases of cradle cap; it’s rarely serious. “In more severe cases, a crusty mass may cover most of the scalp and even extend onto the face, neck, and behind the ears,” adds
Dina Elbeltagy
, M.D., dermatologist and medical writer. If that’s what you’re seeing, you’ll definitely want to check in with your pediatrician.
In some instances, your pediatrician may recommend a low-dose hydrocortisone cream or medicated shampoo that contains an antifungal ingredient like zinc to get rid of the patches faster, but just note that these products can sometimes be irritating to delicate newborn skin. The
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) recommends starting off with a mild shampoo — like those mentioned in this roundup — to treat cradle cap at home first.
It's also important to note that cradle cap doesn’t indicate an allergy, poor hygiene, or an infection. Rather, experts believe it’s likely triggered by maternal hormones that cross the placenta before birth, increasing inflammation and oil production.
Freelance writer
Zara Hanawalt
originally contributed to this article.
Shampoos FAQs
How often should I wash my baby’s scalp and hair with shampoo, especially if they have cradle cap?
You don’t need to wash your baby’s hair every day, even if they have cradle cap. Dr. Dauer recommends washing their hair twice weekly at a very young age. “They’re not really getting dirty or out playing to accumulate dirt and sweat at that very young age,” she says. “Your doctor can help determine the frequency with which to use a medicated shampoo with ketoconazole, but shampoos with pyrithione are safe to use daily.”
“While there isn’t a higher limit, I often recommend parents to freely wash their child’s scalp as often as required, especially with a mild baby shampoo. Every second or third day is ideal and plain water works just as fine if washing the scalp daily,” echoes Dr. Pezad.
What triggers cradle cap?
“No one knows for sure the exact cause of cradle cap,” says Dr. Pezad. “There are several theories that suggest possible etiologies such as mother's hormonal changes during pregnancy which stimulate the infant's oil glands.” Experts believe that sebum (the body’s natural oils) and yeast (which lives on your skin) play a role as well, but it’s unclear exactly how they interact to cause seborrheic dermatitis aka cradle cap.
How likely is cradle cap to come back after treatment?
Even if you’ve managed to get rid of cradle cap completely with shampoo, it can still come back. “Since cradle cap is a form of dandruff, it can come and go for a while, even after treatment,” Dr. Elbeltagy says. She recommends regular gentle shampooing and brushing to prevent it from recurring. If it’s very persistent, you should speak with your pediatrician.
What’s the best remedy for cradle cap?
Contrary to many parents’ first instincts, washing a cradle cap-afflicted scalp is one of the most effective ways to address the issue. “Wash the scalp every second or third day with a mild
baby shampoo
,” advises Dr. Pezad. “Thereafter use a soft toothed comb to brush off the accumulated scales in severe cases.” Massage baby’s scalp gently with your fingers, a brush or comb while shampooing to help loosen the scales. Put baby or mineral oil on the scalp before bathing to help with super stubborn scales. In more severe cases, your doctor might prescribe a cortisone lotion to use after bathing to help reduce inflammation.

There's a reason pacifiers are a universal symbol for babies: By offering something to suck on other than the breast or bottle, pacifiers can help soothe a fussy infant who isn't hungry, tired or in need of a clean diaper. And if your baby is born premature, pacifiers may still be a helpful tool, experts say.
"Pacifiers can help premature babies in a number of ways," says
Anjuli Gans
, M.D., a pediatrician at CHOP Karabots Pediatric Care Center. There are calming benefits, for one. "Premature babies in the NICU are often in a loud, busy environment," she notes. "Some research has shown that pacifiers help regulate their heart rate and oxygen levels, which can help buffer the stress of that environment."
Premature babies also often have to develop their sucking and swallowing reflexes, Dr. Gans adds, noting that pacifiers can help strengthen the muscles involved in this.
What’s more, pacifiers offered during sleep have also been linked to a lower risk of
sudden infant death syndrome
(SIDS).
Here’s what you need to know about choosing a pacifier for your little one, along with the
best pacifiers
for preemies.
How We Chose the Best Pacifiers for Preemies
We spoke to Dr. Grans and
Daniel Ganjian
, M.D., a pediatrician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, to learn about pacifier safety and what features to look for when shopping. Per their recommendations, as well as guidance from the
American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
and
Consumer Product Safety Commission
(CPSC), all pacifiers on this list:
Are molded from one solid piece of plastic
Measure at least 3.8 centimeters across to ensure they won’t be a choking hazard
Don’t come with any attachments, which could be dangerous
We utilized reviews from What to Expect’s community of caregivers to learn which preemie-sized pacifiers parents felt were most comforting for their babies. Per their feedback, we made sure that every pacifier on the list satisfied the following criteria:
Available in a small enough size for a preemie baby to comfortably use
Easy to clean, e.g. dishwasher-safe
Made of safe, durable materials
Other Preemie Pacifier Features To Consider
When shopping for preemie pacifiers, keep these features in mind:
Nipple shape:
Some pacifier brands have an orthodontic nipple, which is intended to better support baby's oral development. Other brands may have designed the nipple to look more like the “real thing” to feel natural in a breastfed baby's mouth. Many parents find that they need to experiment with a few different brands to learn which one their baby prefers.
Size
: Not all pacifiers are the same, so start small. Look for pacifiers that are labeled for babies 0+ or 0 to 6 months, and keep an eye out for specific preemie sizing if the brand offers that.
Easy to clean:
Look for pacifiers that can be sterilized easily. Dishwasher-friendly options, which you should be able to drop in the same cleaning rack you use to wash bottle parts, are especially convenient.

Preemie Pacis FAQs
Do preemies need special pacifiers?
In short, it will depend on your baby. "Some may and some may not," Dr. Gans says. "Depending on a baby's size, oral anatomy — do they have a high arched palate or a
tongue-tie
? — or other medical conditions, they may do better with different shapes or sizes of pacifiers." If you’re unsure, ask your pediatrician what features your child might need.
Ultimately, though, you’re looking for a pacifier small enough for your preemie’s mouth, says Dr. Ganjian. When shopping, that means looking for a pacifier labeled 0+ or 0 to 6 months.
"As long as the pacifier is small enough and baby is comfortable, then go for it," Dr. Ganjian says. "Try a few different ones. They may hate one pacifier, but love another."
Can preemies sleep with a pacifier?
Yes, preemies can sleep with a pacifier (and in fact, offering one at nap- or bedtime may help lower SIDS risk) — but it’s critical to always follow safe sleep guidelines.
Regardless of whether you’re offering a pacifier to a preemie or older baby, keep these safety tips from the AAP in mind:
Keep pacifiers loose in the crib. Never attach a pacifier to your child’s hand or neck, to their crib or car seat, or to a lovey or stuffed animal. Pacifier clips and other such accessories that might attach to a pacifier (including ribbon, string, cord, chain, twine, leather or yarn) are incredibly dangerous.
Look for one-piece pacifiers. Pacifiers molded from one piece of firm, solid plastic (as opposed to multiple small parts) are safest, according to the AAP. Pacifiers should also have ventilation holes.
Check the measurements. According to the AAP, pacifiers should be at least 3.8 centimeters across to ensure they can’t fully fit into your child’s mouth.
Never use the top and bottle nipple as a pacifier. They could come apart and pose a choking risk to your baby.
Inspect your child’s pacifiers regularly. Make sure that the material isn’t deteriorating or torn, and if it is, replace ASAP.
Keep size in mind. If your child continues to use a pacifier past the preemie stage (or even into the toddler stage), regularly replace them to ensure your little one is using an age-appropriate product.
When can I introduce a pacifier to a preemie?
If you’re nursing, you might choose to wait until breastfeeding has been established (usually around three or four weeks) before offering a pacifier, according to the AAP. If you’re bottle-feeding, you can introduce a pacifier any time you’d like.

Baby's
first bath
can be nerve-wracking for new parents. Placing a tiny newborn into a slippery tub is certainly not for the faint of heart. But as time goes on, most parents come to love the ritual of giving their baby a bath — and many babies can’t seem to get enough of it. In fact, bathtime can serve as a bonding experience as well as an integral part of your baby’s bedtime routine.
Bath toys aren't necessary for infants, but as your little one gets older, toys can help keep him engaged and happy during tub time. Before you know it, your teeny little baby will be splish-splashing around and ready to play with all sorts of bath toys.
Baby bath toys are available in many different styles and materials for various age ranges. In fact, there are nearly as many toys designed and developed for use in the bath as there are toys for outside it, which can make choosing the right ones tough.
How We Chose the Best Baby Bath Toys
We consulted the
American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
for any safety guidance. Per their recommendations, all the toys on this list are specifically meant for babies and toddlers (ages 0-36 months) to ensure each item is safe and developmentally appropriate.
We turned to the What to Expect community to gather consensus on brands and specific bath toys for babies that real parents have used and loved. Based on their feedback, we made sure that every baby bath toy on this list:
Is easy to clean and/or made of mold- and mildew-resistant materials.
Has overwhelmingly positive reviews for their durability and function.
We also prioritized BPA-free products where possible, although not everything on this list is BPA-free.
How To Clean Baby Bath Toys
Because of their constant exposure to water, bath toys are prone to developing mildew and mold if not cleaned properly. This is especially true of squirt toys and others with small crevices where water can get trapped inside. Considering how often your little one will use these toys — and how prone babies and toddlers are to putting things in their mouths — it’s really important to keep your bath toys clean. Here are some tips for getting the job done:
Empty water completely out of all toys. If it can be disassembled, do so to ensure the best possible clean.
Wipe toys down with a washcloth and some mild dish soap. Or check the product’s label to see if it’s safe to throw in the top rack of your dishwasher, which is the case for many plastic products.
Let dry completely before giving back to your child.
To help your bath toys dry out (and reduce the risk of mold and mildew buildup), enterprising WTE parents recommend storing your toys in a large mesh garment bag and hanging it up in the bathroom to air dry. When the bag itself gets grody, you can throw it in the laundry for a quick clean.
To help guide you in your search, here are the best bath toys for babies and toddlers that are sure to make your little one's bathing experience all the more joyous.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

. The hanging organizer has three small mesh pockets and then a large mesh pocket below — perfect for storing toys, baby shampoo, bubble bath and more. Other Factors To Consider When Purchasing a Baby Bath Toy
When shopping for bath toys for your baby or toddler, it’s important to keep a few things in mind:
Easy-to-dry shapes:
Bath toys get wet (that’s kind of the point….), so you’ll need them to dry quickly and completely to prevent mold and mildew. Avoid toys that seem hollow or have lots of nooks and crannies that might stay damp.
Material:
As mentioned, bath toys can develop mold or mildew if you’re not careful. Look for materials that don’t retain moisture and that are easy to wipe clean, like BPA-free plastic or silicone. Even better if the toys are dishwasher-safe for easier cleaning.
Age appropriate-ness:
Per the AAP, age recommendations on toys are a crucial way to understand how safe a particular product is for your child and whether it’s developmentally appropriate. (Read: Don’t give your baby a toy designed for 3-year-olds!) Products should also be larger than your child’s mouth and shouldn’t have any small, easily detached parts he could choke on.
Educational elements:
Since bathtime will become part of your regular routine, you may want to consider bath toys that offer some sort of educational benefit, be it interesting textures, funny sounds or toys that help teach baby new vocabulary. While not every single toy has to be educational, it can be a nice perk.
