If you’ve started your hunt for the best stretch mark cream, you’ve likely noticed that the many options on the market can be overwhelming. Combine that with conflicting information about which skincare products are pregnancy-safe and what will actually work to get rid of stretch marks, and you may want to give up the search entirely. But don’t give up just yet. To help make the decision easier for moms-to-be, I did the research on everything you need to know when buying stretch mark cream, which options are the best, and what to look out for to ensure they’re pregnancy-safe.
According to the
American Academy of Dermatology (AAD)
, stretch marks appear when rapid changes in elastin and collagen production, such as a growing belly, cause the skin to rupture, scar, and then heal. Many factors impact whether you get stretch marks, including hormone levels and genetics, but creams and topical remedies can offer some relief.
"While there's no magic bullet cream to definitively prevent stretch marks, some products may help soothe itchy skin during pregnancy and may also improve the appearance of stretch marks," says Annabelle Garcia, M.D., a board-certified dermatologist at
Sonterra Dermatology
.
How I Chose the Best Stretch Mark Creams
To ensure the safety and efficacy of the stretch mark creams on my list, I consulted several dermatologists, including Garcia and Emily Wood, M.D., a board-certified dermatologist at
Westlake Dermatology
. They provided guidance on which ingredients are safe to use during pregnancy, and I cross-referenced this with the AAD and
Cleveland Clinic
' recommendations. Through my research, I ensured that all the stretch mark creams featured were free of the following:
Retinol
Salicylic acid
Alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs)
I also prioritized products that contained at least one of these ingredients, which have been shown to help with skin elasticity:
Shea butter
Cocoa butter or coconut oil
Jojoba oil
Vitamin E
Centella asiatica extract
Hyaluronic acid
Aloe vera gel
I further narrowed down my list based on results from the
2024 Pregnancy-Safe Beauty Awards
, where over 700 moms voted on their favorite stretch mark cream. Finally, I spoke to two moms and looked to the What to Expect community to see what moms-to-be were using and what they found effective. Below are my recommendations for the best stretch mark creams on the market today.

What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

Trofolastin
not only comes highly recommended by dermatologists but is also a favorite among moms in the WTE community — and for good reason. This cream is the only one on the list with solid clinical testing showing that it actually works. According to Dr. Wood, who also recommends this product, the cream’s efficacy lies in its ingredients, specifically the addition of pregnancy-safe centella asiatica. “Centella asiatica is a plant found in the wetlands of Asia, which has been shown to increase collagen production,” she says. Other ingredients, like vitamin E, can help add moisture to the skin, which may in turn improve the appearance of stretch marks, but centella asiatica is the only clinically tested ingredient shown to reduce and potentially prevent the appearance of stretch marks.
Aiding in collagen production is key to diminishing the appearance of stretch marks, and Trofolastin helps regenerate, repair, and heal rapidly stretching skin. It’s been shown to prevent the appearance of stretch marks in 89 percent of its users, while offering gentle hydration to dry pregnancy skin. Though it is a bit on the pricier side compared to other options on this list, the results from Trofolastin speak for themselves. To apply, simply massage the cream onto your skin twice daily.

A Note About Stretch Mark Creams
It’s important to remember that there isn’t a singular solution for stretch marks that works for everyone. The
AAD
, along with the doctors I interviewed, states that whether or not you get stretch marks, and the severity of those stretch marks, depends on many factors beyond our control, such as hormones or genetics. As a result, a bit of trial and error may be necessary to find what truly works for you.
While creams containing centella asiatica are a good place to start due to their proven clinical efficacy for preventing stretch marks, remedies with popular ingredients like vitamin E or cocoa butter can help reduce the appearance of stretch marks if they do appear. The AAD recommends massaging the cream into the skin when you apply it, as massage can enhance the cream's effectiveness.
At the end of the day, though, none of these remedies are likely to cause negative effects, as long as you test a small patch on your skin to ensure you don’t have a reaction. Dr. Garcia notes that many of these remedies can at least alleviate itchy skin that often accompanies pregnancy. For others, these creams offer a healthy dose of hydration, which is important for maintaining your skin barrier, both during pregnancy and beyond
FAQs Best Stretch Mark Creams
What cream is best for pregnancy stretch marks?
According to the Cleveland Clinic, there’s some research suggesting home remedies with aloe vera gel, hyaluronic acid and centella asiatica herb may help moms and moms-to-be treat or prevent stretch marks. That being said, pregnant women should speak with their healthcare providers before trying out a stretch mark cream.
When should you start using stretch mark creams during pregnancy?
“I would recommend starting to use a stretch mark cream as soon as you know you are pregnant,” Dr. Wood says. This way, you can start treating skin as soon as hormones begin to fluctuate and skin begins to stretch.
What if stretch mark cream isn’t working?
If you’re not seeing results from one of these top-rated creams, ask your dermatologist about in-office treatments such as microneedling and laser to help reduce the appearance of stretch marks.

When you’re pregnant, there’s a long list of things to give up (alcohol, unpasteurized dairy, deli meat) or consume in moderation (looking at you, coffee). But figuring out which beauty and personal care products to skip can be trickier, particularly when it comes to nail polish. Many moms-to-be find themselves confused about what’s okay when it comes to
prenatal manicures and pedicures
. As one
What to Expect Community user
asks: ‘Am I safe to do my nails at
all
throughout my pregnancy?’
Nail polish does contain chemical compounds, and more research assessing their safety during pregnancy is needed. There have been concerns about some ingredients in these formulas, such as formaldehyde, a common preservative often used to harden nail polish, and phthalates like dibutyl phthalate (DBP), used to prevent polish from cracking. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) doesn’t directly address nail polish use, although it does
recommend some personal care ingredients to avoid
when possible.
The good news? Using any kind of
nail polish during pregnancy
is probably perfectly fine. “We tell our patients that nail polish and nail polish remover are safe,” says
Jennifer Wu
, M.D., a board-certified OB/GYN with her own private practice in New York City, Women's Health of Manhattan, and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board.
While chemicals in nail polish can be absorbed through the nail bed and into the body, “the exact amount that is absorbed and whether or not this is harmful remains unknown,” explains
Jeriel Weitz
, D.O., a dermatologist with Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City. The likelihood of these compounds getting into the bloodstream of a pregnant person after applying them to the nails is very small. Long story short: you don’t have to stress much about the type of polish that you choose.
But if you are concerned about chemicals or want to be extra cautious, “it’s certainly reasonable to consider a non-toxic polish,” adds
Marisa Garshick,
M.D., clinical assistant professor of dermatology at New York Presbyterian-Cornell. Adds
Joshua Zeichner
, M.D., a dermatologist and Director of Cosmetic & Clinical Research in Dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital: “Whether nail polishes with these ingredients pose any risk is up for debate, but the good news is that there are products on the market that you can purchase that do not contain them, so there are options for everyone.” (If you haven’t been using a non-toxic polish, though, you don’t need to be too worried!)
How I Tested and Selected the Best Pregnancy-Safe Nail Polish
If you’ve ever found yourself in the nail polish aisle wondering which bottle is safe to bring home, I’ve been there too. During both of my pregnancies, I caught myself squinting at tiny labels and Googling ingredients. So when I set out to create this list, I wanted to take that guesswork off your plate. I pulled from my own experience as a manicure-loving mom and paired it with research deep dives, leaning heavily on expert guidance to choose polishes that are readily available at drugstores, align with the ACOG's recommendations for
safer beauty products in pregnancy
, and receive rave reviews from moms in the community and on staff. Here’s exactly how I narrowed things down:
I referenced ACOG’s guidance on
avoiding toxic chemicals during pregnancy
. When possible, the organization stresses skipping beauty or personal care products that contain phthalates, parabens, oxybenzone, triclosan. Again, experts say it’s not necessary to exclusively use “non-toxic” polishes during pregnancy.
But to be extra safe, I only considered options that were at least “3-free,” meaning they do not contain formaldehyde, toluene (a less-common solvent), or the phthalate DBP. These three chemicals “may pose risks to fetal development,” says
Navya Mysore
, M.D., a primary care physician and women’s health expert based in New York City.
To refine the list of nail polishes that fit this criteria, I referenced the Environmental Working Group’s
Skin Deep Ratings
for nail polish, and only considered polishes that had a score of no more than 5 on the EWG’s scale, meaning their ingredients have a relatively low hazard risk.
I also consulted eight experts to better understand how moms-to-be can use nail polish safely during pregnancy:
Jeriel Weitz
, D.O., a dermatologist with Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City
Marisa Garshick, M.D., clinical assistant professor of dermatology at New York Presbyterian-Cornell
Joshua Zeichner
, M.D., a dermatologist and Director of Cosmetic & Clinical Research in Dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital
Jennifer Wu
, M.D., a board-certified OB/GYN with her own private practice, Women's Health of Manhattan, in New York City, and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board
Maya Thosani
, M.D., a dermatologist at Modern Dermatologoy in Arizona
Navya Mysore, M.D., a primary care physician and women’s health expert based in New York City
Megan Bernstein
, M.D., assistant clinical professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA
Kecia Gaither
, M.D., a double board-certified in OB/GYN and maternal fetal medicine specialist, and Director of Perinatal Services/Maternal Fetal Medicine at
NYC Health + Hospitals/Lincoln
in the Bronx
I then scoured What to Expect’s community forums and message boards, where moms-to-be share honest reviews of beauty products like nail polish.
In summary, based on the above research, I made sure the seven recommended polish brands featured on this list are:
Easy to find in stores or available online
Certified “3-free” at minimum, though most of the products on this list have eliminated even more potentially concerning ingredients
Have an EWG Skin Deep score no higher than 5, indicating its formula is made with ingredients that are the lowest level of concern
Have many positive reviews from online retailers and in the What to Expect Community

Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

A Doctor’s Note on Pregnancy Manicure Safety
Painting your nails while pregnant is generally safe, and so is going to a nail salon to get a professionally done manicure or pedicure.
However, there are some things to keep in mind to ensure you have a safe and optimal mani experience.
Choose a salon you trust.
Dr. Weitz says you should go to a high-quality place that you know properly sanitizes its tools to reduce your risk of infection. This is always true, but especially important during pregnancy because your body might be less able to fight off infections (or have more severe symptoms) while you’re pregnant.
And if you’re getting a pedicure, opt for portable foot baths over the kind built into spa chairs, as the latter is a potential source of bacterial infection.
Consider bringing your own tools.
For even more peace of mind, you could bring your own manicure tools to the salon, Dr. Zeichner says.
“In the event of a cut in the skin and exposure to unclean tools, it could result in a skin infection requiring antibiotics to treat.”
Call ahead.
I
f you’re being choosy about what type of nail polish you use during pregnancy, such as using a formula that doesn’t contain formaldehyde or phthalates, you’ll want to inquire about what nail polish the salon stocks, and if necessary, bring your own.
Get some air.
It’s a good idea for everyone to use nail polish in a well-ventilated room, Dr. Zeichner says, and that’s especially true during pregnancy. Fumes from these products can sometimes “contribute to nausea during some women's pregnancies,” Dr. Thosani adds. Choosing a seat at the salon that has good air flow or opening the window when using polish at home is your best bet. “Always use polish in a well-ventilated area, avoid inhaling fumes, and wash your hands afterward when the nail polish has dried,” says Dr. Mysore.
However, professional manicurists, who are consistently exposed to these chemicals due to their work, may be at an increased risk of birth defects. If you’re pregnant and work in a nail salon, wearing protective equipment like masks and gloves, improving ventilation at work and taking regular breaks for fresh air may help reduce your risk.
Jessica Migala
originally contributed to this article.
Pregnancy-Safe Nail Polish FAQs
Is gel polish safe during pregnancy?
As with “regular” nail polish, more research is needed about the chemicals used in gel manicures. “Gel manicures use specific ingredients to help the polish adhere to the nails, [and] some experts suggest sticking to regular manicures rather than gel manicures to avoid exposure to those chemicals,” says Dr. Zeichner.
Gel manicures also use a UV lamp to dry the polish, and some moms-to-be might find that this process irritates their skin. “Skin can be more sensitive in pregnancy, so keep that in mind when using UV lights to cure gel manicures,” says Megan Bernstein, assistant clinical professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. “You might want to wear sunscreen on your hands or wear gloves if you are noticing more skin sensitivity.”
Keeping your treatments simpler, such as by opting for a less-involved manicure, can also reduce your exposure to fumes, says Dr. Weitz. But as with nail polish in general, the choice is ultimately yours. If you have questions about your personal risk, have a discussion with your doctor.
Can I use standard nail polish remover during pregnancy?
Nail polish remover isn’t thought to be unsafe during pregnancy, Dr. Wu says. But the smell can be unpleasant, and Dr. Zeichner recommends opening a window when using acetone nail polish remover to avoid inhaling the chemical for long periods of time. Acetone can also be irritating to the skin, so you might choose to wash your hands or feet after using it. Another option is to look for (or ask your salon) acetone-free remover, Dr. Thosani says.
Any tips on how I can chose the right nail polish?
As mentioned, you really don’t have to stress much about the type of polish that you choose. But “non-toxic” in this case typically means free of ingredients like formaldehyde. This is simply a term for certain ingredients that the polish does not have. Here’s a breakdown of labels you might encounter while shopping:
“3-Free” formulas: These do not contain formaldehyde, toluene (a less-common solvent) or DBP, which are considered the most problematic ingredients, says Dr. Garshick.
“5-free” formulas: Like a 3-free formula, these do not contain formaldehyde, toluene, and DBP. They also lack formaldehyde resin and camphor, which may cause allergic contact dermatitis in some people, notes Dr. Weitz.
“7-Free” formulas (and up): In addition to being free of everything in a 5-free formula, these formulas also typically lack ethyl tosylamide (which can cause allergic reactions in some people) and xylene (which can irritate the eyes and throat when inhaled in large amounts). “8-free,” “10-free,” and other such formulas will also lack other potentially irritating/harmful ingredients, depending on the product.
Vegan: If a product has a
certified vegan logo
, that means it doesn’t contain any animal-derived ingredients or animal by-products, nor was it tested on animals. (Certain common nail polish ingredients, like shellac,
come from animal secretions
, while some pigments like carmine are made from insects.) Don’t conflate this label with “plant based,” which simply means that there are ingredients derived from plants in the product. (And cruelty-free means the product was not tested on animals.)
Non-toxic: Usually, brands use this to mean that their product doesn’t include ingredients that are believed to be potentially harmful. (For nail polish, brands will often pair this with “3-free” or “5-free” messaging.) But remember, this is primarily a marketing claim without a standard legal definition, so take these claims with a grain of salt.
Can I still go to the salon while pregnant?
Painting your nails while pregnant is generally safe, and so is going to a nail salon to get a professionally done manicure or pedicure. However, there are some things to keep in mind to ensure you have a safe and optimal mani experience.
For starters, Dr. Weitz says you should go to a high-quality place that you know properly sanitizes its tools to reduce your risk of infection. This is always true, but especially important during pregnancy because your body might be less able to fight off infections (or have more severe symptoms) while you’re pregnant. Don’t let your manicurist cut your cuticles either, she adds, because it could also cause an infection. And if you’re getting a pedicure, opt for portable foot baths over the kind built into spa chairs, as the latter is a potential source of bacterial infection.
Choosing salons with a well-ventilated area “reduces inhalation of chemical fumes,” Dr. Gaither notes. You can also consider wearing a mask at the salon for extra protection, she adds.
If you’re being extra choosy about what type of nail polish you use during pregnancy, you’ll want to inquire about what nail polish the salon stocks, and if necessary, bring your own. Ideally, you’d also be keeping your treatment simple, Dr. Weitz says. “The more involved the manicure, such as with acrylics and gels, the longer the duration and the potential for greater exposures through fumes and potential risk for infection,” she says.

As I prepared for my daughter's first beach trip three years ago, I made sure to have all the essentials:
bathing suits
,
baby-safe sunscreens
,
baby sunglasses
and a baby beach tent to keep her safe from the sun. Thought, I’ll be honest, I was hesitant about the latter. I like to pack light when I go to the beach, and the idea of lugging another bag wasn’t appealing. Plus, I figured my daughter would be fine with the typical sun gear. (Heck, I was a tent-free beach baby and I turned out fine.) But I was immediately proven wrong after talking to fellow moms and our pediatrician
"Sun protection needs to be multifaceted since — let's face it — we aren't perfect when it comes to applying sunscreen," says
Hayley Goldbach
, MD, FAAD, FACMS a double board certified dermatologist and dermatologic surgeon at Brown University. She recommends keeping your baby out of the sun during peak hours (from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.) when the UV rays and heat are the strongest. One way to do that is to utilize a baby beach tent, says Dr. Goldbach.
Baby beach tents, which can also be used at parks, playgrounds and your backyard, are made of sun protective fabric to protect your little one’s skin from the sun’s rays while giving them a comfy spot to stay cool — and even nap. But narrowing down the choices can be tricky, especially if you’re not used to using a beach tent for yourself. So to save you some time, I've done the research for you and found the best baby beach tents for your al fresco hangs.
How I Chose the Best Baby Beach Tents
Sun protection is, of course, the top priority when selecting a beach tent for your baby. But you also need to make sure that the tent allows for air flow to avoid overheating and just keep your baby comfortable. I spoke to Dr. Goldback and consulted recommendations from the
American Academy of Pediatrics
and
Skin Care Foundation
to learn what beach tent features keep your baby safe. Per their guidance, all beach tents on this list are
made of UPF 50 fabric
and
feature mesh or roll-up windows
to provide proper airflow and keep the space from getting too hot.( It’s worth noting that mesh windows won’t offer the same sun protection those made of the tent fabric and, therefore, should be placed away from the sun.)
With this information in mind, I then considered what I looked for when shopping for my first beach tent. I also spoke to a colleague who takes her son to the beach regularly, and turned to the What to Expect community to ensure my criteria met the needs of the masses. Based on this feedback, I made sure all of the baby beach tents on the list received positive reviews for:
Security
: Some tents have sand pockets to help hold them in place while others have stakes. Ones with stakes can also be used at older sibs soccer games, backyard play dates or when you’re camping.
Portability
: If you have a lot of children or tend to go to the beach without your partner, portability should be at the top of your list. Look for lightweight tents and one that comes with a carrying bag. Similarly, if you are going on a beach vacation, lightweight beach tents with carrying bags will be easier to pack.
Ease of use
: Pop-up tents are the easiest to set up and take down. For others, you may want to check out a YouTube video before hitting the beach for the first time.
Durability
: Sturdier tents are built to withstand strong wind gusts and will last more than a summer. They also tend to cost more, an investment that is worth it if your family spends a lot of time outdoors or you plan on having more children.

was the first baby beach tent I tried, and it truly checked all the boxes. And it doesn't hurt that it has thousands of 5-star ratings.
Made of a water-resistant, UPF 50+ polyester, this pop-up tent has three large windows and an open front to ensure plenty of ventilation. As much as I like to soak up the sun, I found myself escaping to the tent with my daughter when temperatures got a little too hot.
And that fact that it's not a total pain to carry or set up adds to the appeal. The tent is very lightweight — comparable to a camping chair, one user noted — and can be easily folded and stored in the included carrying case. As for set up, all you have to do is pull the two strings at the top of the tent and it'll pop into place. Just be sure you secure the tent with the four included sand stakes and sand pockets.
Another thing that drew me to the Pacific Breeze was its durability. “This is the third beach tent that I’ve purchased and the only one that has made it through multiple trips to the beach,” one parent says. I've had my tent for two years and though it's a little scuffed up, it still does its job.
When unfolded, the tent has enough room for four people, and features several pockets where you can store your phone, sunscreen or even a portable white noise machine.
So what's the downside? Unfortunately, there is no way to close the opening. So if you want complete privacy when breastfeeding or need to contain a super antsy baby, this may not be the tent for you.

Tika Fender, Art Director and mom of one, lives in sunny California and invested in this tent to maximize her son's outdoor time while keeping him safe from the rays.
"I love it because it's a super big tent and I can comfortably fit inside and play with my toddler," Tika says.
Although I don't own the California Beach Co tent, I was lucky enough to enjoy it when we went away with friends who bought it. It was so nice to place all three children (all under 1 at the time) in the tent so they could play together outside without being exposed to the sun. And we didn't have to worry about them crawling away, thanks to a mesh zip-up panel.
It’s roomy enough to fit at least three kids and a grown up or two. The mesh sides allow the cool ocean breeze to flow through freely.
If you foresee your child taking a lot of naps in the tent, you can add-on the mattress and mattress cover to create a cozier environment. Tika does warn that the inflatable mat takes forever to deflate and she often finds herself "having to wrestle it to make it fit in the little carrier." But if you don't mind a little work and need something spacious, the California Beach Co Tent is a worthwhile investment.

Your baby may be soft and squishy now, but their skin is oh-so-delicate. Lotions can do a lot to keep them comfortable not only this winter, but year-round. “Consistent use of bland moisturizers can definitely maintain the skin barrier, minimize dryness and itching, and improve the symptoms associated with eczema,” says
Patrick McMahon
, M.D., pediatric dermatologist at
HMGS Pediatric Dermatology
in New Jersey.
Finding the best baby lotion, however, isn’t always simple. Like many parents, I’ve spent more late nights than I’d like to admit poring over ingredient labels, watching TikTok product reviews, and worrying about what might happen if my child ever had a bad reaction.
That anxiety-fueled research, along with caring for two young daughters with
eczema-prone skin
, has made me something of a lotion expert. I’ve tested dozens of formulas in search of that elusive “baby-soft” skin feel everyone is always talking about. Along the way, I've discovered which baby lotions work well for both of my kids, some that only worked for one, and a few I would never purchase again.
And while every baby is different, the lotions listed below have earned my repeat purchases for good reason. They’re moisturizing and gentle enough for even the most sensitive skin, leading to softer (never greasy) cuddle sessions.
How I Chose the Best Baby Lotions
Although I have years of personal testing as a parent and one too many American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) deep dives about
dry winter skin
under my belt, to ensure my picks are safe and effective, I also referenced previous What to Expect interviews with Dr. McMahon and Dr. Latanya Benjamin, M.D., a pediatric dermatologist in Florida, and Society for Pediatric Dermatology board member. Here's everything I considered:
Ingredient safety:
Following Dr. Benjamin’s guidance, I avoided lotions with potential irritants like parabens, phthalates, sodium laureth sulfate, and triclosan. I also skipped undiluted essential oils, which are not deemed safe for babies under 6 months old — and some, like lavender oil, have even been flagged as potential hormone disruptors in young males.
Moisturizer type:
As Dr. Benjamin notes,
lotions
are the most lightweight, containing the highest water content;
creams
are thicker and more nourishing; and
ointments
are the richest and best for sealing in moisture.
According to the
AAP
, thick creams and ointments are the best choice for eczema flare-ups or severely dry skin.
Poor past experiences:
With two kids who’ve both battled dryness and eczema, I’ve tried dozens of lotions firsthand. Personally, I wouldn't use Pipette, Babyganic, or Hello Bello. While my children never had a poor reaction to any of these products, I found that the lotions were never as thick, creamy, or hydrating as I wanted them to be.
Community and expert consensus:
I read hundreds of reviews from parents in the What to Expect community to see what they loved and what they found less than impressive. While many were mentioned, I found that brands such as Aveeno, CeraVe, and Mustela were talked about the most.
Below, you’ll find the baby lotions that consistently received overwhelmingly positive reviews. Each product is gentle, effective, and approved by dermatologists who specialize in baby skin. Note that my choices range from the inexpensive and no-frills to options that appear more high-end, to accommodate various budgets.

Why We Love It
For babies who have normal skin, Dr. Benjamin recommends
this lightweight (read: not greasy!) formula
, as it was developed with pediatric dermatologists to help prevent dry skin.
CeraVe's baby lotion
is not only free of fragrance and parabens, but it also includes ceramides (which are found naturally in the skin and make up about half of the lipids in the skin’s natural protective barrier), hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide to lock in moisture and soothe dryness.
The
National Eczema Association
has also given CeraVe its official seal of approval, so you know it's a safe bet for babies with sensitive or eczema-prone skin — and that includes both of my daughters.
I use this regularly and love how quickly it absorbs without leaving residue. During colder months, however, I switch to something richer.

How to Apply Baby Lotion
Make lotion time part of bathtime. After rub-a-dub-dubbing in the tub, get your baby out, pat the skin dry and apply a lotion within two minutes to lock in moisture, recommends Dr. McMahon. Massaging the lotion into baby’s skin can promote more than bonding — it can help decrease the symptoms of atopic dermatitis, adds Dr. Benjamin.
Dr. Benjamin also emphasizes daily moisturizing — not just during flare-ups — is key to keeping your baby’s skin healthy, resilient, and itch-free.
Cassie Shortsleeve originally contributed to this article.
Baby Lotions FAQs
Can I use regular lotion on my baby?
If you’re going to use lotion on your little one, whether they have dry skin or not, you’ll want to stick with a baby lotion made specifically for their age range rather than lotion you might use on yourself. Baby lotions are generally made with more gentle ingredients for their super sensitive skin and usually don’t contain as many harsh irritants as adult lotions may contain.
Any ingredients I should try to avoid in baby lotions?
Even some baby lotions will contain ingredients that you may want to avoid. Dr. Benjamin recommended avoiding ingredients that are known to cause irritation, like parabens, phthalates, sodium laureth sulfate and triclosan, as well as essential oils for babies under 6 months of age.
How often should I apply baby lotion?
You can apply baby lotion to your child’s skin once a day, or even every other day if their skin is very soft and not dry or eczema-prone. Baby lotion can be applied to damp skin immediately after a bath. If they have eczema or very dry patches, you can apply lotion or ointment as needed, but check with your pediatrician to get their recommendation.

When I was pregnant, I knew I’d be spending some money prepping for my baby’s arrival. After all, even the most affordable car seats and strollers are an investment. But I didn’t realize how much money would go toward those seemingly inexpensive items (the burp cloth bill can quickly add up!). Fortunately, thanks to many other moms, I learned that numerous retailers and baby brands offer free samples of bottles, blankets, formula, clothing, and so much more. By signing up for one (or many!) of these free baby samples, you can save money up front and in the long run. Every baby is different, so the samples allow you to try various products and find what works for your little one without having to buy each one in bulk right off the bat.
(And if you want more suggestions for baby gear based on your unique preferences, check out
What to Expect's Registry Builder
, which also recommends great baby registries tailored to your needs.)
How I Chose the Best Free Baby Samples
Curated a list of brands and retailers that offer free baby samples
Evaluated each brand’s or retailer’s offerings using firsthand experience and customer reviews
Reviewed the requirements to obtain free baby samples, such as paying for shipping, creating a gift registry, or signing up for a rewards program or newsletter
Using this information, I identified which brands and retailers offer the best value through their freebie programs—without too many strings attached. The result: a list of free baby samples that brings you one step closer to being a budget-conscious, in-the-know parent.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

Recurring Resources for Families
Raising a baby is expensive, and many families need more than just one-time freebies to help reduce the overall costs. If you or someone you know requires additional assistance in securing free or low-cost baby essentials, here are some helpful resources:
National Diaper Bank Network
: Partnering with Huggies, this organization collects, stores, and distributes free diapers to families across the country. The website provides a state-by-state list of diaper banks so you can find the nearest one to you.
Free Formula Exchange
: This nationwide network connects families in need of baby formula with others who have formula to donate, free of charge.
Women, Infant and Children
:
Commonly referred to as WIC, this program offers supplemental foods, health care referrals, and nutrition education for low-income mothers, infants, and children up to age five who are at nutritional risk. You must apply to be eligible for the program.
FAQ
How can I get free baby stuff?
Creating a registry and signing up for promos aren’t the only ways to score free baby items. Some other ways to snag free (or significantly cheaper) baby gear include:
Asking family and friends for hand-me-downs:
When I was pregnant, I quickly learned how much parents like to declutter. My sister-in-law was more than happy to unload boxes of clothes, toys, and even a high chair.
Joining your local “Buy Nothing” Facebook group:
Again, parents love to get rid of unwanted items, and many are doing so through neighborhood- and town-based Facebook groups. The only downside is you need to check often and act fast, so this may be better for non-essential items.
Getting a
breast pump through insurance
:
Thanks to the Affordable Care Act, many new moms are eligible for free (or reduced-price)
breast pumps
. The coverage will vary based on your provider, and you may have to do a little legwork. But given that some breast pumps can cost up to $400, it’s worth the effort for such a helpful device.
Utilizing your FSA money on eligible items:
There are a surprising number of
FSA-eligible baby items
, including baby monitors, diaper rash cream, and even postpartum recovery kits. Although you’re still paying for these items, you’re using pre-tax money, which saves you some money.
Is it ok to buy second hand baby stuff?
Although it's totally fine to buy some second hand baby gear, not every product is safe to buy used. The
American Academy of Pediatrics
, advises against used car seats, for example, because they could be expired or missing parts. There is similar concern with strollers and cribs.
If you accept or buy
used baby gear
, do your due diligence. Always check that the item hasn't been recalled, and look closely to ensure it’s not damaged or missing any parts.

The best infant life jackets keep your child safe around any body of water, whether you’re headed to the lake, beach or pool. Based on advice from sailing instructors and fellow boating parents, the Stearns Kids Life Jacket is a top choice because of its snug yet comfy fit and affordable price point.

Because
drowning is the leading cause of death
for children between ages 1 and 4, you’ll want to make sure you’re equipped with the right safety gear. And one of the most important items you can have, whether boating or hanging at the pool, is an infant life jacket.
In fact, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says that
babies should wear a life jacket whenever they’re near water
, even if you don’t plan on going for a dip. Even an inch or two poses the
threat of drowning
, especially for infants and young kids who can’t swim. Of course, life jackets “only work when they are worn,” points out Angus Robertson, sailing director at the
Lewes Yacht Club
in Lewes, Delaware.
And I know all too well that getting a squirmy baby to wear one without screaming is a tall order. As a lifelong sailor, I’ve been taking my four kids on boats as soon as they were able. Nonetheless, some were fussier than others when it came to putting on a vest. Through trial and error, I’ve learned that fit and weight can make a massive difference in how likely your little one will enjoy the experience. My recommendation is to look for comfy padding and adjustable straps, in addition to a U.S. Coast Guard (USCG)-Approved Label.
How I Chose the Best Infant Life Jackets
I spoke with two sailing instructors (Robertson and Ricky Nelson, owner and general manager at
Annapolis Sailing School
in Annapolis, Maryland), along with
Natalie Livingston, CPRC, AFO
, a lifeguard instructor trainer and co-founder of
Alive Solutions, Inc.
, to understand what types of life jackets and safety features to prioritize when compiling my list of the best infant life vests. I also consulted
guidance measures
outlined by the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG).
As a mom of four who spends most of her free time on or near water, I relied heavily on my firsthand experience when considering different brands and products. But I also spoke with Emily Longmire, a fellow boater and mom, and reviewed recommendations from parents in the What to Expect community to survey as many options as possible. In the end, I narrowed down my list to the seven best infant life jackets using expert advice and parent feedback to ensure each pick is safe and comfortable for baby. All of the below infant life jackets are:
USCG-certified:
Believe it or not, there are some life jackets available to purchase that do not officially meet USCG standards.
Type II PFDs:
Personal floatation devices (PFDs) are categorized as Type I, Type II, Type III, and Type V. Type II is specifically recommended for infants — or those weighing less than or equal to 33 pounds — as it provides greater buoyancy and features a face-up design. The padded neck collar also best supports baby’s head. Also keep in mind that the USCG doesn't recommend boarding with a little one until they are at least 18 pounds.
Available in vivid colors:
Aquatic experts prefer bright hues for improved visibility. Plus, playful patterns and color palettes may also warm a choosy little one up to the idea of wearing a life vest altogether (whatever works, right?).

Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

The vest features closed sides to offer a tighter, more secure fit, even when your little one squirms or splashes around. (This means you're always within arm's reach of the child).
While I’m a fan of the extra padding (it's buoyant enough to keep baby’s head up and dry), some little ones who aren't quite mobile yet may have trouble looking around and get frustrated as a result. Parents also noted that some older children were capable of figuring out how to pull the zipper down part way, so you may want to reserve it for younger children with less dexterity. Still, keep Nelson’s advice top of mind: “Zippered personal floatation devices can have a more secure fit and thus be safer.”

Not to mention, the open design of the sides and back allows baby more freedom when moving their arms around. I started using this life vest with my second son and it’s been passed down to his two little sisters since. Jamison Hermann, a former video producer with What to Expect, has used this vest for his toddler, Elena. “We've used it for beach and boat stuff — mostly canoes and rowboats — since she was about 18 months old and it's been great,” he says. “The vest feels very sturdy, and it's easy to make it fit snugly, which is best for safety. I like the bright color, too, as it's easy to spot her when she's on the move.”

I grew up using West Marine life jackets, so it felt natural to use them for my kids as well. (Longmire has also used West Marine life jackets for her son.) A big perk of the
West Marine Deluxe Kids’ Rapid Dry Life Jacket
(and the main reason it's worthy of its price tag) is the fact that it dries quickly thanks to special “rapid dry” technology. I’m confident you and your little one will appreciate that fact on cooler days!
The vest comes with an adjustable front strap for a secure fit, plus side-release buckles and a zippered front for simple on-and-off access. There’s also a padded crotch strap to lower the risk of chafing. The closed-sided design stays snug on the child no matter how much they move around without feeling bulky. For an under-$30 infant life jacket, try

It looks more like a floatable swaddle blanket than a classic life vest, with several features designed for baby’s comfort. In fact, many parents report that their baby felt so snug, they took a nap while wearing it.
The elastic material at the crotch helps guarantee a more secure fit that won’t squeeze baby’s legs. And, of course, the oversized collar provides better head support, which might be more comfortable, especially when floating in the water.
Given its unique design, however, you may need to upgrade your baby’s life jacket sooner than if you used a more classic style. But the $20 price tag makes the shorter lifespan well worth it.
Features to Keep in Mind When Shopping for Infant Life Jackets
At baseline, it’s important to follow the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG)
guidance
. Based on this, all infant life jackets should be USCG-certified and Type II PFDs. Yet whatever baby life jacket you choose, it’s crucial to always practice good water safety. "Life jackets are not a ‘set it and forget it’ type approach,” says
Natalie Livingston, CPRC, AFO
, a lifeguard instructor trainer and co-founder of
Alive Solutions, Inc.
, an educational and consulting firm focused on aquatic safety. “They do not take the place of adult supervision or of learning to swim.”
The AAP
recommends
always being within arm’s reach of your child when in the water with them, even if they’re wearing a life jacket.
Experts I spoke with also recommend:
Choosing a life jacket with a grab handle, crotch strap and neck collar, as you want to easily be able to lift your little one out of the water.
Sticking to vivid colors, as aquatic experts prefer these to see baby better. “High visibility should be a top priority,” stresses Nelson.
Testing a zipper before buying. Because getting your little one secured quickly is important, it’s best to choose a life jacket with a zipper that goes up and down easily. That, and getting out of a life jacket more quickly when back on land may avoid a meltdown.
Double-checking the weight and size of your little one. Infant life jackets are designed to fit children who weigh 33 pounds or less, per USCG standards. (The next size up is a “child” life jacket, which is made to support kids between 33 pounds and 55 pounds.)
FAQs
What type of life jacket is best for infant?
The USCG
recommends
that babies wear an infant Type II PFD when they are on a recreational boat. These life jackets are designed to turn the wearer’s head from a face-down position in the water into a face-up position so they can breathe. These life jackets often come in infant- and toddler-specific sizes, which is important because you should always make sure that baby’s life vest fits correctly.
Should a newborn wear a life jacket?
Although infant life jackets are designed for anyone under 30 pounds, the USCG doesn’t recommend taking infants under 18 pounds on a boat as the life vests might not fit properly. Therefore, a newborn shouldn’t wear a life jacket because it won’t be small enough and could even potentially pose a suffocation risk if it slides up and covers their mouth.
Do infants need life jackets on boats?
Yes, the USCG
recommends
that babies wear a Type II infant life jacket when on a boat. However, note that this may not be until they weigh 18 pounds, or around when they turn 1 years old, because the life vest may not fit them properly yet to work correctly. But once baby is old enough for a life jacket, they should always wear one on a boat.

As soon as the temperatures start to rise, I know my four kids will be begging to swim. And I’m happy to oblige. Whether it’s the main activity for the day or a quick pit stop, you can find us at the neighborhood pool or my sister’s backyard oasis — and always with a big bag of the best pool toys in tow.
Admittedly, I might have a pool toy problem. They’re fun for the whole family — including me! — and I can’t help but add to our collection every year. I’ve purchased everything from a
canopied float
my little ones bobbed around in as babies to wind-up and dive toys they chase after for hours now as active tots. Needless to say, I’ve learned that the best pool toys can make any
water experience more memorable, which makes them just as important to pack as towels and
sunscreen
.
Curious which pool toys have passed the entertainment test for my babies and toddlers? Scroll on.
How I Chose the Best Pool Toys
I’ve spent over a decade researching, shopping for and testing dozens of different pool toys. So I know firsthand which are the most entertaining and undeniably durable. That’s why I only included toys that have survived at least one summer in my home (for context, my children are notoriously tough on their gear and playthings). I also limited considerations to toys designed for those between the ages of 3 months and 5 years.
But because every family is different, I also looked into which pool toys parents in the What to Expect community recommend and love. Based on their suggestions and reviews, I whittled down a list of contenders from 50 to just 15 pool toys that check the following boxes:
Safety:
All of my favorite toys are free of small parts that can easily detach and become choking hazards.
Materials:
Plastic and foam are durable and great in the water, and they’re also resistant to mold and bacterial growth. I focused on toys made from these materials.
Versatility:
While not all pool toys can or should be used elsewhere, I made sure to include a variety of products that can also be used in the bath or at the beach.
Size:
Not every family has a ton of space for toys, especially pool toys. That’s why I made sure to include products with a range of sizes, including toys that can be deflated or broken down easily for storage.
Durability:
Pool toys should last more than a single season. The toys that made the final list should withstand regular use in the water and won’t pop or break easily, even in the hands of a toddler. My 2-year-old tends to throw things when she gets mad or frustrated — everything on this list has survived a summer or more in her hands.
Before diving into my list of favorites (all of which you can find in my overflowing garage), it’s essential to note that children should never be in the pool unsupervised and that you should never leave pool toys in the water once your child has finished playing. Otherwise, the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) warns that they can become a drowning hazard for curious toddlers. I recommend investing in a
large mesh bag
to house your pool gear after the fun is over — it’s airy enough to help your toys dry off and the open weave makes it easy to spot what’s inside.

FAQs
Should pool toys be left in the pool?
Even though they’re made to be played with in the water, you shouldn’t leave pool toys in the pool when they’re not in use. Most pool toys and floats are made with PVC, which can slowly break down over time the more it is exposed to chlorine and sunlight. This can result in tears, leaks and cracks, which not only can make them unusable, but can also leak into your pool and clog a filtration system.
What can I do with my toddler in the pool?
There are lots of ways to entertain your toddler in the pool whether they can swim yet or not. Offering them simple pool toys, like something that glides through the water for them to chase or buckets they can fill and dump, is one way to keep them entertained. Plus, you’re helping them hone important fine motor skills at the same time.
Just remember to never leave your child unattended
while in any amount of water
— always ensure an adult is within arms’ reach of them.
How do you keep pool toys clean?
Taking proper care of your pool toys is the first step in keeping them clean. Always remove them from the pool once you’re done using them. Dry them off and be sure no water is stuck in a hidden crevice to avoid mold buildup. Deflate your inflatables after use and then, if necessary, clean them with a mix of either soap and water, vinegar and water, or baking soda and water. For smaller pool toys, remove them from the water and dry them off, then wipe them down with a mild soap and water or vinegar and water.
How do you store pool toys?
Pool toys should be stored in a cool, dry place. A shed can be a great option, especially one that is close to the pool for convenience. You can also buy an outdoor storage bench or bin or keep them in a garage. It’s best to put inflatables in a heavy duty bag or back in the box it came in to keep them protected from snags or nicks that can lead to tears and rips.

Stroller walks — or just getting outside in general — provide physical and mental health benefits for both parent and baby. While keeping infants indoors on hot days is ideal, as a mom of three, I know that’s not always possible. I often had to bring my baby along to my older kids’ outings, like swim classes and park playdates. In those instances, I’d always bring a stroller fan (or sometimes two!) to keep my youngest cool and safe.
But even if you have a stroller fan at the ready, it’s important to keep an eye out for
signs of overheating
when temperatures start to soar later this year.
Gina Posner, M.D., F.A.A.P.
, a board-certified pediatrician practicing at MemorialCare Medical Group in Fountain Valley, California, warns that sweating, tiredness and clammy skin are all indicators of a heat-related illness.
How I Chose the Best Stroller Fans
Thanks to the wide selection of portable fans available — miniature clip-ons, bladeless styles and foam propellers — finding the right one for you and your baby (and stroller!) can be overwhelming. I narrowed down my top picks based on the following criteria:
Durability and ease of operation
Battery duration
Accessibility to a power supply
Price range and availability
I also spoke with
Steven Abelowitz, M.D., F.A.A.P.
, a board-certified pediatrician and medical director of Ocean Pediatrics in Orange County, California, to learn if stroller fans are
actually
helpful (spoiler alert: they are), what features to look for and other heat-protecting measures parents can take.
This still left me with dozens of very similar-looking choices, however, so I dug a little deeper into the What to Expect community to see which stroller fans parents were recommending and how effective they found them. I also relied on my personal experience with multiple brands as a longtime parenting editor and mom of three who lives in a city that can be unbearably hot in the summer months.

Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

Tips For Buying a Stroller Fan
Selecting the right portable fan for your baby’s stroller can come down to personal taste, but it may help to keep the following features in mind when you’re shopping:
Solid construction:
The most common materials used to make portable fans are hard plastic, silicone and metal. For fans made with foam blades, the foam should be soft and pliable but solid (read: doesn’t feel as if it will fall apart). The fan enclosure should be sturdy and the slats or grill openings should be wide enough for good airflow, but narrow enough to prevent small hands and fingers from sliding in.
Accessible, portable power supply:
Unlike standard fans that have outlet plugs, portable fans are powered by replaceable or rechargeable batteries, and sometimes USB ports.
No sharp edges:
Rounded designs and minimally exposed joints are preferred, with metal components covered or concealed.
Secure mounting system:
Whether using clip-on or flexible wrapping legs, the mounting system should be secure and stable. If you’re planning on running often or walking on uneven terrain with the stroller, you may prefer a flexible leg mount as I find they can often be attached tighter than clip-on counterparts.
FAQ Stroller Fans
What are the different types of stroller fans worth considering?
A wide variety of manufacturers produce small, portable fans that can be used with strollers. These portable fans primarily fall into three categories:
Standard portable fans: These fans are miniature versions of traditional fans, with blades that create air movement blown through a self-contained frame or cage.
“Bladeless” fans: Rather than having standard revolving fan blades, “bladeless” fans are equipped with a cylindrical drum that has multiple leaves that create air movement when spun and blown through a slotted enclosure.
Foam-bladed fans: Whether they are housed in an enclosure or are fully open, these fans have soft, bendable foam blades that don’t hurt or cut skin when touched during operation.
There are also four main portable fan mounting styles:
Clip-on mount: These use a squeeze clip to secure the portable fan.
Flexible wrapping legs, either tripod or monopod: These are a common mounting style and allow for the most customizable setup on a stroller.
Handheld: Mini, portable handheld fans are useful for older kids and adults, not so much for babies for obvious reasons
Around the neck: This collar-style fan typically has two cooling elements that hang around the neck and would only be suitable for older children and adults.
Are stroller fans a good idea?
Stroller fans are definitely not a must-have, but experts agree that “stroller fans can be beneficial, especially on hotter days in warmer climates,” says Dr. Abelowitz, because they circulate the air around your little one, he says.
It’s important to note, though, that while fans can provide comfort, they won’t prevent heat-related illness when temps near three digits, according to
the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
. Fans don’t actually cool the air, and shouldn’t be used in extreme heat. Plus,
the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
warns that when the temperature is higher than your body temp, it may even cause you to
gain heat rather than lose it
.
Dr. Abelowitz adds that children at any age should avoid being out in the heat for extended periods during very warm temperatures — especially at a heat index at or above 90 degrees Fahrenheit, which can pose a significant risk to kids. And make sure to follow other important
tips for protecting your little one in hot weather
, like dressing them in lightweight clothing and keeping them hydrated.
Do I need a stroller fan?
While Dr. Abelowtiz and Dr. Posner agree that a portable stroller fan isn’t absolutely required, they can be helpful for a stroller-bound baby or toddler in a number of ways, such as circulating extra air around them and providing comfort in an otherwise uncomfortably hot situation.
That said, keep these considerations in mind when you’re using a stroller fan:
Make sure the portable fan is mounted securely and in the appropriate position so that it doesn’t accidentally fall out of place or blow air directly on your little one, as it might dry out her mouth and nostrils or circulate any allergens.
Make sure the fan’s slats or grill openings are narrow enough so that small hands or fingers can’t get through and cause injury.
And of course, a child should never be left unattended in a stroller or car seat under any circumstances — even if there’s a fan running.
Where is the best place to put the fan on my stroller?
Where you place the fan depends largely on your stroller. Many parents choose to attach clip-on stroller fans to the belly bar or snack tray bar since the canopy will often be too flimsy to support the weight of the fan. Portable fans with flexible legs can possibly be attached onto the canopy frame as well as the handlebars.
If the stroller seat is front-facing, you can attach the fan to either the parent handlebar or parent stroller organizer.

You probably know to stock up on
baby mittens
,
snowsuits
, and warm hats before your little one’s first winter. But one item you might not have on your radar is a stroller footmuff.
Also called stroller buntings, footmuffs attach to your stroller to keep baby warm and dry during cold-weather walks. They look like little sleeping bags, cocooning baby in insulated, water- or wind-resistant materials for added comfort.
A stroller footmuff might not be a must-have for every parent, but they can come in handy depending on where you live — especially in colder climates where most days are plagued by freezing temps, snow, or rain. And, unlike a blanket, footmuffs aren’t easily kicked off by a wiggly passenger.
As a mom of two living in Brooklyn, New York, I relied on mine for four winters. While not exactly an essential product, I absolutely found my footmuff much easier to use and more secure than wrapping my babies in multiple blankets during walks.
A Doctor's Note on Footmuffs
“If you live in a city and are walking around with your child in a stroller, a footmuff can be really helpful, especially for babies who are not as good at regulating temperature,” says
Micah Resnick
, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician in Cincinnati, Ohio, with TriHealth and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board. Of course, you can still bundle up baby in layers, he notes, but a footmuff provides “a great level of convenience and ease.”
Just note that any footmuffs designed for car seats should never include a layer of fabric between baby and the car seat or harness straps, and their face should always be uncovered in the car, per the
American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
. Any added bulkiness is unsafe because it can impede the way the harness works. “If using a footmuff with a car seat that you put in the stroller, remember to ALWAYS remove the footmuff before putting the car seat back in the car, as the fabric behind baby is not safe to be in the car seat when operating the vehicle,” says
Tina Feeley
, M.D., M.P.H., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at Chestnut Hill Pediatrics in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts and member of the
What to Expect Medical Review Board
.
How I Chose the Best Stroller Footmuffs
When putting together a list of the best stroller footmuffs for babies, I started by comparing feedback on stroller footmuffs from What to Expect community and staff members. Referencing their reviews and recommendations, I compiled a list of around two dozen stroller footmuffs that received praise for their quality, compatibility, and ease of use.
Next, I interviewed three pediatricians (Dr. Resnick;
Gina Posner
, M.D., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at MemorialCare Medical Group in Fountain Valley, California; and Dr. Feeley, for additional information about stroller footmuffs, including how to use them safely. I also referenced information from the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP). And since I’m a mom of two and a former parenting editor who has tested several stroller footmuffs myself, I took my own experience into consideration, too.
Based on all of this research, I narrowed down our list of the best stroller footmuffs to the top 10 that checked the following boxes:
Made from comfortable, weather-resistant materials
Easy to use and adjust
Has anti-slip features to prevent bunching
I also awarded “bonus points” for any compelling additional features, such as extra insulation (for footmuffs for babies in very cold climates), universal compatibility, and machine-washable constructions (they tend to get pretty dirty after walks in the snow or slush).
Ready to make your winter walks warm and cozy? Below are all of the infant- and toddler-sized bunting bags What to Expect editors and parent testers highly recommend — including the very footmuff I used throughout multiple winters without any issues.

Christine Mattheis, Group VP of Content & Brand Solutions at What to Expect, used the JJ Cole Bunting Bag with daughter Rose for two winters — first when she was between 3 and 7 months old, and again between 15 and 19 months — and found it well-insulated and easy to use.
Indeed, the ease of use is a quality many parents mention. Most rave about the multiple access points — zippers on both sides and buttons on the front — make it a breeze to adjust if the weather changes during your walk. The footmuff includes three elastic straps, one at the top and two at the sides, that fit most strollers. It also comes with a removable back panel so you can ensure baby's back remains flat when strapping them in to prevent any sliding.
Another pro for parents: JJ Cole's bunting bag is machine washable. "It got super dirty every winter and we'd throw it in the wash at least a couple of times each season, especially after we had a big snow," Christine recalls.

The footmuff rolls up into a little storage bag, making it a breeze to take with you when traveling or store during the warmer months when you don’t need it. I also appreciated that you could fold up the YOYO while the footmuff was still attached.
What to Look for in Stroller Footmuffs
To make sure you are going to get the right stroller footmuff for your family, these are some important aspects to keep in mind when shopping for a footmuff:
Material:
Just like when you're shopping for a coat, the climate you live in will most likely inform what type of material to look for in a footmuff. For instance, if you live in colder climates, you might want to look for bunting that's insulated with multiple layers of protection. However, if your area doesn't get too cold, opt for a more lightweight option to prevent overheating.
Size:
Most footmuffs are designed either for newborns to 6 months or 6 months to 4 years old. When in doubt, look to the sizing guide for each product to make sure it will fit your child. “Ideally, a footmuff comes up to baby’s armpits, so the face should always not be obstructed,” says
Tina Feeley
, M.D., M.P.H., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at Chestnut Hill Pediatrics in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts and member of the
What to Expect Medical Review Board
.
Adjustability:
There are a few features that can make it easier to adjust your footmuff. Some, for example, prioritize designs that include sections that you can unzip to extend the length of the bag to fit baby as she grows. A few others on our list also provide front panels that can fold down to allow more air in if it isn't too cold out or fold up to keep baby more bundled. Your footmuff may also have an adjustable harness to ensure it's secured to the stroller.
FAQs
Are footmuffs safe?
Footmuffs are perfectly safe to use as long as they're the appropriate size for your child and properly fit your stroller. If the footmuff doesn't fit the stroller or baby correctly, the fabric could potentially cover baby's mouth as a result of bunching or the footmuff moving and pose a suffocation risk. That’s why Dr. Posner recommends footmuffs with anti-slip features to ensure your little one can’t move in their harness.
It’s also important to monitor your little one for
signs of overheating
, adds Dr. Resnick. “If your baby feels warm to the touch, is sweating, if their skin is red and clammy, or if they are breathing fast, unzip the footmuff.”
How do I determine if a footmuff is compatible with my stroller?
The easiest way to ensure that a footmuff you’re considering works with your stroller is to buy one provided by the same brand. (For example, if you have a Nuna stroller, you’d purchase the brand’s compatible footmuff.) But that shouldn’t rule out other universal footmuffs. For these, check the product description to see if the manufacturer lists specific brands or styles it’s compatible with. Or, prioritize  adjustable features that work on a variety of strollers, such as adjustable straps and zippers, a removable back panel or expandable fabrics.

Nothing ruins a pool day faster than a sudden evacuation — especially if it was triggered by your baby who pooped. (Hey, accidents happen!) But you don’t have to avoid public watering holes or hold off on swimming lessons until your child is
potty trained
. You just need one of the best swim diapers.
Designed to contain a baby’s fecal matter — not pee — swim diapers fit like
regular diapers
but look and feel like a bathing suit. Most importantly, they won’t swell after coming in contact with water. Most pools require young children to wear swim diapers because they can help contain bowel movements, which pose a risk to other swimmers. So lest you want to recreate the doodie scene from
Caddyshack
, you should invest in some swim diapers ASAP.
How I Chose the Best Swim Diapers
I spoke to What to Expect editors to learn which brands their children have worn without worry. I also combed through the community boards, where plenty of pool- and beach-going parents shared their favorites. Based on their feedback, I weeded out options that didn’t fit the following criteria:
Adjustable, with the exception of pull-up disposable diapers
Available in a wide range of sizes
Machine-washable, in the case of reusable diapers
But bear in mind that the below list is not fail-proof. You’ll want to check on the state of your little one’s swim diapers frequently (an hour or so is ideal!).

Why We Love It
An overwhelming majority of parents in the What to Expect community swear by
Green Sprouts
swim diapers (formerly
i play
). The rebranding only improves upon the original — thin enough to wear under a swimsuit without the extra bulk and side snaps for easy changes. Still available in a whole rainbow of shades and patterns, these swim diapers include three different layers of material: A wicking liner that helps pull moisture away from baby’s skin, a second absorbent layer that keeps messes in, and a third outer waterproof layer to help prevent messes from leaking out.
The gussets, a new feature on this year’s diapers, add extra leak protection. Many caregivers appreciate the triple-layer design to mitigate accidents while maintaining a reasonable price point. (It’s also machine washable, and can be put in the dryer on low.)
What really stands out, however, is the snap design, with three on one side of the diaper. This makes taking them off after an accident much easier than pulling the whole thing down and potentially making a mess. The snaps also allow for quick diaper checks.
Leah Rocketto, Associate Commerce Director at What to Expect, has used this swim diaper with her daughter, Olivia. “It was easy to put on because it snaps only on one side,” she says. “Olivia was in a wriggly stage so you have to hold her down to get things on, it made it easier that it was just one side and not both sides. Would use again!"
Another bonus: the fabric is UPF 50+, which helps block out harmful UV rays from the sun — crucial for protecting your baby’s sensitive skin. One important thing to note before buying is that some parents said these diapers run small and that they had to size up for their child, especially for bigger babies.

FAQ
Do swim diapers actually work?
Yes, to some extent. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), swim diapers
are designed to hold solid feces
, but no manufacturer claims they are 100 percent leakproof. Still, most pools require swim diapers because they can help prevent or slow downcertain infection-causing germs and parasites (like
Cryptosporidium, which causes diarrhea
) from leaking into the pool as possible. Swim diapers are not designed to contain pee or diarrhea; if the latter occurs it’s important that you take your baby out of the pool as quickly as you can and change their diaper.
What is the difference between disposable swim diapers and reusable swim diapers?
Much like regular diapers, disposable diapers are meant to be tossed after each use while reusable diapers are typically made of multi-layered, waterproof fabrics. In the case of swim diapers, disposable diapers are cheaper and good if you aren’t a frequent pool-goer. Reusable swim diapers, on the other hand, are better if you essentially live at the pool (or beach, or lake.) They are also preferred by most swimming instructors. For younger babies, diapers with adjustable features or newborn-sized disposables are best.
Do swim diapers catch pee and poop?
Swim diapers catch solid poop (not diarrhea), per the CDC. They are not meant to absorb water, including urine. That’s why you should regularly check swim diapers (around every 60 minutes), change in an area away from the pool, and use regular diapers when your little one is not in the water.
Do you need to put a regular diaper under a swim diaper?
You do not need to (and shouldn’t!) put a regular disposable diaper on under a swim diaper. A swim diaper (whether it’s reusable or disposable) covered by a swimsuit is perfectly sufficient. If you add a regular diaper to the mix, it will only swell when submerged in water and could make baby uncomfortable or break apart, leaking not only waste but absorbent beads.
Take it from one
What to Expect mom who used to work at a public pool
: “They can explode when they get too full (which they will get full fast of pool water), and the stuff that helps the diaper absorb water will be ALL over the pool. It’s so gross and hard to clean up! I used to work at a public pool, and once someone snuck in a regular diaper (against the rules), and it was a disaster…”
How should swim diapers fit?
For a swim diaper to do what it’s made to do — hold accidents in — they need to fit a bit more snugly than your average diaper. That’s why many have cinched sides, waists or leg openings. Like regular diapers, most pool diapers are sized by weight, so check the packaging and manufacturer sizing charts for guidance. And don’t be surprised if the diaper seems a little on the tight side.

— and quite honestly, I don’t think I fully understood how short a lifespan that purchase would have. When I was pregnant with my second, I immediately purchased a convertible car seat, knowing I didn’t want to have to replace a very expensive piece of baby gear a year later.
A convertible car seat can change to adapt to your growing baby’s needs. Install it as a rear-facing car seat when they’re a newborn, then turn it around when your toddler outgrows the rear-facing height or weight limits. Brilliant, right? Well, there is a catch: To pack in all that flexibility, a convertible car seat will be heavier and larger than an infant car seat. You also can’t pop a convertible seat out of the base and into a stroller, a feature many parents love (especially when they’re running late.) Rather, you'll need to remove your baby each time. Still, that lack of portability may be worth it to you for the value and convenience you get in return.
