It’s no secret that having a baby is basically synonymous with spending money. Not only do babies require a lot of stuff, but so do pregnant and recovering postpartum moms. Fortunately, a Flexible Spending Account (FSA) can help you stock up on pregnancy and baby essentials, while saving money in the long run.
According to the
U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
, an FSA is a type of health plan that allows you to set aside pre-tax money to pay for certain out-of-pocket health care costs. And, with most plans, that includes purchasing health-related essentials as well as covering doctor’s visits. (A
Health Savings Account
(HSA) is another health plan that works similarly to an FSA and can also be used on many of the items below.)
There is one caveat: Only specific baby, maternity and postpartum items are going to be eligible for purchase with FSA money. That said, there is a surprising amount of FSA-eligible baby items covered and include many that all new moms need to have on hand for a smooth recovery, as well as taking care of your newborn.
Find all of our favorite
FSA-eligible pregnancy, postpartum, and baby essentials
in our Amazon storefront.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

I loved wearing this for the first few weeks after I gave birth; it alleviated my discomfort because it was so supportive. It’s a great way to use your FSA money because it’s something people likely aren’t going to buy for you at a bridal shower and it’s not covered by insurance. Another FSA-eligible option is the

FAQs
Are diapers FSA-eligible?
Although diapers are a non-negotiable for babies, they’re unfortunately not FSA-eligible. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
considers
baby diapers personal care items and not medical expenses, and FSA reimbursement is only available for medical expenses. Other baby items that are surprisingly excluded from FSA eligibility include infant formula and bottles.
How do I use FSA money on baby items?
You can typically access FSA dollars through insurance plans and company benefits. These accounts are a place to set aside pre-tax money and use it on qualified medical expenses. This includes things like prescription medicines and eye exams, but it can also cover certain baby, maternity and postpartum essentials that are determined medical expenses. The advantage of using pre-tax dollars to buy these items is that you end up saving money that you would otherwise be putting towards your federal and state taxes.
Your insurance policy will dictate whether you need to shop directly from the official
FSA
stores, or if you can buy items directly from retailers like Amazon, Target or Walmart, or a pharmacy like CVS or Walgreens. Some insurances will give you a debit card to purchase these items, while others will require you to submit receipts. Either way, make sure that the item is explicitly stated as FSA eligible before purchasing.

Growing up, my parents went out of their way to stuff my Christmas stocking with fun surprises. Needless to say, I’ve carried on that tradition in my own household as a mom to four young kids. Over the years, I’ve filled my fair share of the holiday staple with dozens upon dozens of trinkets, toys and treats, and have learned that the best baby stocking stuffers keep the fun going long after each gift has been unwrapped.
Whether you’re celebrating your child’s first Christmas or they’re pushing 2 years old, my recommendations for baby stocking stuffers include proven crowd-pleasers that my own crew loved (think: bubbles, teethers and books), along with recommendations by fellow parents in the What to Expect community.
How I Chose the Best Stocking Stuffers
Stocking stuffers for babies nail that sweet spot of being fun and useful, while still being small enough to squeeze into an oversized sock. To choose the best baby stocking stuffers, I relied on my personal experience as a mom of four. But because every family is different, I also pored over the What to Expect community message boards to see what other parents loved gifting.
Since babies generally fall into the newborn and 2-year-old age range, it’s important to consider where your child lies within that window. For very young children, I’ve found it’s better to choose something entertaining, like a rattle, or to opt for something useful that you as a parent will appreciate, such as binkies and onesies. You can get a bit more creative as your little one — and their development — grows.
I also ensured every item is either tiny to begin with or can be rolled into a smaller size to fit into a stocking. Finally, I kept most of the products to $10 or less. After all, this isn’t the gift category where you want to spend a ton of money.

Baby Stocking Stuffers FAQs
About how much should I anticipate spending on stocking stuffers?
This ultimately depends on your budget, but speaking from experience, you can get a lot of cute stuff for under $10. I included a few items that cost a little more, but only for products that you’ll get a lot of mileage out of. Also, keep this in mind: Your child will have no idea what their stocking stuffers cost. What matters is that they’re a good fit for them.
Where can I buy cute, unique stockings for kids?
You can find adorable stocking options nearly everywhere. However, if you want a few options to start, check out Target, West Elm Kids, Pottery Barn Kids and Maisonette. Amazon is also an excellent spot to score cute, unique stockings at a low price (What to Expect editors recommend Creative Co-Op’s rustic designs.)

It can be heartbreaking to watch your little one deal with itchy, inflamed skin that often accompanies
baby eczema
. Trust me: I watched my two sons battle with eczema for years. But one important item to have in your medicine cabinet that can help soothe the irritation and keep their skin properly moisturized is baby eczema cream.
Of course, every baby’s skin is different, and what works for one may not work for another. The eczema creams we used to keep my oldest’s skin moisturized, for example, didn’t help my youngest’s. So, it’s no surprise that parents often go through multiple products before
finding the best baby eczema cream
(or combination of treatments) that finally works to relieve irritation and help hydrate their skin.
As someone who has had my fair share of experience with eczema as a parent and even as a sister when growing up, I’ve applied my own experience — as well as expert advice — to find the best baby eczema creams worth trying out. (And don't forget that there are gentle
baby washes
and
lotions
designed for eczema-prone skin that will help, too!)
How I Chose the Best Baby Eczema Cream
When considering the best eczema cream for babies, I not only leaned on my personal experience but also reviewed feedback from parents in the What to Expect community:
I considered more than 50 of the most recommended eczema creams for babies to compile a comprehensive list of the best options available.
Then, I sought expert guidance from
Julie McClave, MD, FAAP
, a pediatrician with Akron Children’s Pediatrics, to learn what to look for in eczema creams for babies. According to her recommendations, I ensured that the products I considered:
Are thick moisturizers like creams and ointments rather than lotions
Are free from perfumes, dyes and additives, which could aggravate sensitive skin
Keep skin moisturized
Protect the skin’s moisture barrier
I also paid particular attention to eczema cream options that were given a seal of acceptance by the
National Eczema Association
, as these are guaranteed free of fragrance, known irritants or allergens.
By ensuring that each product recommendation met expert guidance, was easy to apply, and proved effective according to parents who tested them, I was able to narrow my list down to the nine best baby eczema creams.
A Doctor's Note on Eczema Creams
“The most important aspect of choosing the right moisturizers for your child is finding one that they seem to tolerate the best and can be used daily,” says Dr. McClave.
Although cream or ointment-based moisturizers tend to be most effective, sometimes the ointment can be too greasy, or a child may not like having it applied, Dr. McClave advises. In this case, it might be best to have a more lightweight option that they’ll tolerate to keep your child’s skin hydrated.
“Fragrance-free and dye-free ‘hypoallergenic’ moisturizers also tend to work well,” she says. This is the most important aspect to look for when buying an eczema cream, Dr. McClave adds.

What to Know When Buying Baby Eczema Cream
In addition to expert guidance to choose eczema creams that are thick and free from fragrances and dyes, there are a few other important factors to keep in mind when buying a baby eczema cream:
Cream formulas don't necessarily need to be organic.
Just because you see “all natural” or “organic” on a product, does not automatically mean that the product is fragrance-free or does not contain irritants. A cream you can find at the drugstore may be just as effective, or even better, for your little one.
Some creams may not work right away.
“I typically recommend thick moisturizers — creams and ointments tend to work a little better than lotions — and frequent application daily,” says Dr. McClave, noting that consistent application is the key to treating baby eczema. Don’t get discouraged if your baby’s eczema doesn’t get better right away. It may take time — up to two weeks — for a product to start working. (But there may still be trial and error involved after that.) You will, however, want to stop using a product if their eczema gets worse or seems to be reacting badly to the cream. “If you notice any yellow crusting, sores, or blisters on the eczema patches, it is important to see your child's doctor to have it evaluated,” says Dr. McClave.
Only use steroid-free creams, unless directed by a doctor.
If the cream you’re considering has an added steroid like hydrocortisone, it’s important to check with your doctor to ensure that it is safe for your baby. Not every infant with eczema will require steroid treatment, and not all steroid creams are safe for babies.

When my son first started daycare, he must have brought home every single cold known to man within the first month. He was — quite literally — up to his ears in boogies.
Besides the fact that it was impossibly sad to watch a four-month-old wheeze and struggle to breathe through tiny nostrils stuffed with mucus he didn’t know how to expel, I wasn’t sleeping a wink because of said mucus.
We were all miserable.
I wasn’t getting anywhere with the bulb-shaped snot sucker they give you at the hospital, plus the device kind of grossed me out — how in the world are you supposed to clean those things?
So I broke out the one gift I didn’t register for, but got anyway, because all of the moms I knew said they swore by it: the
Fridababy NoseFrida Snotsucker Aspirator
($21 on Amazon).
What is the NoseFrida?
The product is undoubtedly a little intimidating. A long mouthpiece connects to a mesh filter housed inside a blue tube that sits right at the base of baby’s nose. And when you suck on the red mouthpiece, the gentle force of your air draws the baby’s snot out of their nose and into the blue tube where it collects.
I can already hear your thoughts, because I had them too:
I have to do
what
?
How to use the NoseFrida
To use, the large tube is placed at the base of baby’s nose, creating a seal. Next, a parent or caregiver applies gentle suction through the mouthpiece and then — you guessed it — literally sucks the snot out of baby’s nostril.
Yes, you do have to hold that blue tube up to your baby’s tiny nostril and suck on the opposite end to draw the snot out. But I promise, you will not get a single ounce of mucus in your mouth.
There’s a disposable filter in the tube that blocks snot
and
germs, so none of the gross stuff makes its way to you. (NoseFrida says the disposable filters are clinically proven to prevent the transfer of mucus or bacterial germs to the snot sucker.) The grossest part of the whole process is the sound it makes, so at the end of the day, it’s really nothing more than a mental hurdle to overcome.
You don’t have to worry about hurting your baby, either. While you’re bound to hear a few cries — ok, screams — it’s not because you’re using too much force. According to the company, it’s nearly impossible to suck too hard, and the device is safe to use up to four times a day. So, more than likely, it’s simply a new and uncomfortable sensation for baby.
There’s a little trick to make things a easier, though: saline solution. Before using the NoseFrida, put a couple drops of saline solution in each nostril. According to both the company and my pediatrician, this helps loosen thick mucus, making it easier to more effectively expel it.
Our review
The first time I used the NoseFrida, I had to really talk myself into it. (What can I say, I’m squeamish!) I sprayed a little saline in my son’s nostrils, then started sucking. What came out was truly horrifying and satisfying all at the same time — more than a full inch of thick green boogers.
My son, admittedly, hated every second of it. He cried and cried during our snot sucking adventure, but shortly after I finished and he realized he could breathe more adequately, his cries subsided and he dozed off to sleep.
Before I tucked myself in, I gave the NoseFrida a quick rinse.
Pro tip: It’s much easier to clean when the mucus is fresh.
I simply use the power of the faucet to let the boogers slide out and down into the drain, toss the filter, then place the product in the dishwasher following package instructions for a full clean.
Another thing to note: As baby gets older and more mobile, it’s harder to keep them still for such an invasive activity. I found that holding their arms down helped, but I definitely felt guilty for having to put them through it — even though I knew how much it was ultimately helping.
My baby is now 3.5 years old and way past the NoseFrida days (he hasn’t let me come anywhere near him with the thing since he was about a year old), but I have three more kids who have found relief from colds through the wonders of the product. And since a happy baby is a happy mom, I’ll happily reach for the NoseFrida to suck up snot whenever a cold strikes.

Mastering the art of sucking my baby’s snot did not come easily to me as a first-time mom. I was terrified to poke the pointy end of a nasal aspirator into my son’s teeny-tiny clogged nostril. Like so many gross parenting tasks, I eventually got the hang of it out of sheer necessity because — spoiler alert! —
babies can’t blow their own nose
…and most toddlers won’t either.
As any new parent quickly discovers, congestion can derail sleep, feedings, and everyone’s sanity. That’s why finding the best baby nasal aspirator is so important. Alongside your trusty
thermometer
and
humidifier
, a nasal aspirator is one of those
cold and flu essentials
you’ll reach for again and again. But with so many options to choose from (there’s everything from high-tech electric devices and old-school bulbs), it can be confusing to figure out what’s actually worth it.
That’s why, as a mom of two and parenting writer who has researched and tested her fair share of nasal aspirators, I rounded up the most effective, safe, and easy-to-use tools for baby congestion relief below, so you can both breathe a little easier.
How I Chose the Best Baby Nasal Aspirators
When considering the best baby nasal aspirators, I relied on three key factors to influence the final list:
Expert insights:
I consulted both the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) and the following experts, who provided advice on how to use a nasal aspirator and what to look for when buying one, focusing on styles and features that will help suck up the most mucus in an easy, efficient, and safe way:
Kaitlin Wiseman
, M.D., family physician and Chief Medical Officer at Playhouse MD
Robert Quillin
, M.D., board-certified pediatrician at Pediatrix Medical Group in Fort Worth, Texas
Shannon Godsil
, M.D., pediatrician at Children’s Hospital & Medical Center in Omaha
Christine Kingsley
, APRN, health and wellness director at the Lung Institute in Connecticut
Parent-tested favorites:
I sorted through recommendations from the thousands of parents in the What to Expect Community to learn which nasal aspirators other parents say truly work well to clear their baby’s mucus. Their honest feedback was invaluable in separating the must-haves from the meh.
Selection criteria:
Every aspirator on this list is safe for babies of all ages, boasts gentle yet powerful suction, has easy-to-clean parts, is simple to operate, and is designed to be as comfortable as possible for small, sensitive noses.
Stuffy noses are inevitable — but with the right nasal aspirator, helping your baby breathe easier doesn’t have to be intimidating.
A Doctor’s Note on Clearing Congestion
“The most important factor is the ability to provide gentle, superficial suction,” Dr. Wiseman said. “You want to clear congestion effectively without irritating delicate nasal tissue.”
She suggests parents should focus on five basic components: Ease of use, comfort, ease of cleaning, design, and cost. “It is best to use one designed specifically for babies, one that offers a soft, flexible tip, and provides gentle suctioning,” she explained.

Other Factors to Consider When Buying Baby Nasal Aspirators
Choosing the best nasal aspirator will depend on personal preference as well as product performance. Here are points to consider when selecting what’s best for you and your baby.
Manual vs. Electric:
There are two types of nose suckers on the market: manual and electric. Both work well, with the cost being higher for  electric nasal aspirators. There are, however, convenient advantages such as multiple tip sizes that allow use for a wider range of ages, and literal bells and whistles, like music and lights, to distract your child during the process. Manual aspirators, on the other hand, are simple, but can be just as effective. Most models are the bulb-style that’s used to clean baby’s airways after birth. To use this type of nose sucker, caregivers simply squeeze the bulb first, then insert it into baby’s nostril and release pressure on the bulb to suck out the snot. Another type of manual sucker is one that features a tube for parents to literally suck the snot out with their mouth. It’s not for everyone, but parents find that these aspirators are less intimidating and invasive to baby and therefore, easy to use.
Ease of cleaning:
Nasal aspirators need to be cleaned well after each use. Those that can easily be pulled apart to clean and dry are ideal and reduce the risk of bacterial build up. You may want to look for one that has the least amount of parts and no small nooks or crannies to avoid buildup. Some nasal aspirators are dishwasher-safe while others are hand-wash only, so look for whichever type works best for your lifestyle.
Age appropriateness:
The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
notes that nasal aspirators
are most commonly used for babies under 6 months, but not every snot sucker will be suitable for all babies. Check the manufacturer's age recommendations before purchasing a nasal aspirator to ensure it’s the correct range for your child. “It's important to go with an age- and size-appropriate aspirator, otherwise it may cause no improvements or even result in greater harm,” says Kingsley. Having the right size will make the experience more comfortable for baby and avoid damaging their nostrils.
Amber Leventry
originally contributed to this article.
Nasal Aspirator FAQs
What age can I use a nasal aspirator?
“The great news is that you can use a nasal aspirator as soon as you come home with your baby,” says Dr. Godsil. Typically, babies under 6 months of age need a snot sucker because they can’t blow their nose. You can use one on older babies and toddlers, but know that they might be more likely to fight the sucker.
Depending on the size of your child’s nostrils, you may need to experiment with different-sized nose tips of the aspirator. Bulb aspirators can vary in size and are recommended based on your child’s age, so be sure to read the product’s description before making a final choice. For electronic nasal aspirators, look for products that offer different nose tips so that you can be sure you get the right size for the age of your child. Some products can be used from infant to toddler ages, but others are designed specifically for toddlers.
How do I use a nasal aspirator?
First, you’ll want to lay baby on his back before using the aspirator. Dr. Quillin suggests adding a couple drops of saline before using a nasal aspirator to thin out mucus, limit nasal irritation and prevent damage to the inside of the nostril. Make sure the air is out of the bulb, or chamber if you are using an electric one, by squeezing the bulb. Next, place the tip inside baby’s nostril, and release the bulb or activate the suction on an electric model. Once you’ve sucked up the mucus, you can discard it and repeat on the other nostril.
Dr. Wiseman advises using a nasal aspirator before your child feeds, as clearing out the mucus may help them drink and eat better. And if you notice their nostrils becoming irritated, you may need to suction their nose less frequently.
Is it safe to use a nasal aspirator on a baby?
It’s safe to use a nasal aspirator on an infant — just be sure to use one designed for your child’s age. If using an electric aspirator, start with the lowest suction and work your way up if necessary to not irritate baby’s nostrils. “The safest way to clear a baby’s nose is to start with a gentle saline spray or drops to help loosen mucus, followed by superficial suctioning if needed,” Dr. Wiseman says, noting this can be with a nasal bulb, mouth-to-nose style aspirator, or electric nasal aspirator.
However, if the nasal congestion doesn’t seem to be bothering your child, leave it alone. You don’t need to suction out their nose just because they “sound” congested. Instead, remove mucus if they aren’t feeding or sleeping well, or if the congestion is affecting their breathing. And always clean the nasal aspirator after each use.
How do I clean a nasal aspirator?
“Choosing a device that is easy to clean and sanitize is crucial as it is important to prevent the spread of germs and infection,” says Kingsley. “Consider a disposable aspirator or one with removable parts over the traditional ones, as they are easier to clean thoroughly after each use.” When cleaning a nasal aspirator, follow the instructions according to the manufacturer's recommendations, as each device is a little different. Some can be cleaned in the dishwasher or can be sterilized. Others are cleaned with soapy water and left to air dry.

Maybe you've been hearing a lot about probiotics for babies and how beneficial they can be for your infant’s gut health and even immunity. But with so many options on the market, it can be nerve-wracking to first decide whether or not to give one to a young baby. And then, assuming the answer is "yes," how do you figure out which baby probiotic to choose?
First, the benefits: There’s evidence to suggest that giving babies a probiotic product may help support digestion and immune response. Probiotics appear to be effective at treating acute viral gastroenteritis and preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea, according to research from
the American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP). Additionally, some research
also indicates
that having a balanced microbiome may help kids fight off future infections.
Your doctor might recommend a daily probiotic if you’re trying to treat colic, or they may advise you to give your baby a probiotic only when your little one has an issue that warrants it, such as a stomach virus or if they’re starting an antibiotic. To be safe, always talk to your doctor before starting probiotics. From there, they can recommend a brand to try, or you can opt for one of these pediatrician-approved picks.
How We Chose the Best Baby Probiotics
In order to learn about what you should look for in a baby probiotic and how they can help infants’ digestion, we spoke with two pediatricians:
Jenelle Ferry, M.D.
, a neonatologist and the director of feeding, nutrition and infant development at Pediatrix Medical Group of Florida, and
Gina Posner, M.D,
, a board-certified pediatrician practicing at MemorialCare Medical Group in Fountain Valley, California and member of the
What to Expect Medical Review Board
. We also consulted the AAP’s
guidance on probiotics
for babies and referred to
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) 2023 letter
on probiotic safety considerations for premature babies. Finally, we utilized feedback from parents in the What to Expect community to see what brands they found worked best for their little ones — plus, which probiotics they felt were worth the price.

Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

unless they’re consuming more than 27 ounces per day of vitamin D-fortified formula. as well as

(BB-12), which occurs naturally in the intestines. It comes in a liquid formula, and a dropper is included.
Given that it’s a two-in-one product, Culturelle’s price — just
$.66 per serving — is also a big selling point, though some parents do say that the consistency is a little on the thick side and can be harder to administer with the dropper.

What To Look for in Baby Probiotics
Based on our interviews with Dr. Ferry and Dr. Posner, advice from the AAP and feedback from parents in the What to Expect community, these are the factors to consider when buying baby probiotics:
Quality assurance
: Probiotics are a type of supplement, which means — like all supplements marketed for adults or children — they have not undergone FDA’s rigorous testing process to evaluate their safety, effectiveness and quality as medications. For this reason, it’s critical to choose a probiotic product from a reputable brand and seller. Each baby probiotic in our list is from trusted brands that pediatricians frequently recommend — and we made sure to get our list vetted by a pediatrician. When in doubt, you can also speak to your doctor about the types of probiotic products they recommend for your baby specifically.
Ingredients
: Two of the most common strains in particular to look for when buying a baby probiotic are lactobacillus (such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus or Lactobacillus reuteri) or bifidobacterium, according to Dr. Ferry, as they have data supporting their benefits for GI issues. All of the products on our list contain either or both of these strains. In addition, the probiotic formulas we’ve selected are non-GMO, dairy- and gluten-free to ensure they’re safe and easy on baby’s stomach.
FAQs
Should babies be given probiotics?
"According to a
statement by the AAP
, probiotics appear to be modestly effective at treating acute viral gastroenteritis and preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea," says Dr. Ferry. "There is encouraging but preliminary data for their role in helping irritable bowel syndrome, ulcerative colitis, atopy and infantile colic, and even more conflicting data on the potential for probiotics to reduce food allergies.”
Many pediatricians also recommend probiotics for infants who are on antibiotics. “Probiotics can be helpful to counteract the good bacteria that are destroyed from antibiotics,” explains Dr. Posner.
However, it’s important to note that probiotics aren’t right for all infants, and premature babies or those who are immunocompromised
should not be offered them
, Dr. Posner says. Always ask your doctor to make sure probiotics are appropriate for your little one before starting them.
Are probiotics safe for babies?
While probiotics can be beneficial and safe for many infants, they’re not considered safe for premature and/or immunocompromised babies. In 2023, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration
sent a letter
to health care providers warning them about potentially serious risks that probiotic products could pose to premature babies in a hospital setting. Probiotics had been given to hospitalized preemie babies to prevent an intestinal disease called necrotizing enterocolitis, but some products were attributed to adverse outcomes, including one infant death. Babies who are immunocompromised should also not be given probiotics for the same reason, Dr. Posner says.
“For that segment of kids — preemies or immunocompromised babies — I’d stay away from a probiotic,” she says. “Other than that, by the time they’re no longer preemies and out of NICU, probiotics are safe to use.”
Which probiotic strain is best for baby?
Lactobacillus and bifidobacterium are the two most common strains found in baby probiotic products, according to Dr. Ferry. The lactobacillus strain may be particularly beneficial for little ones suffering from colic.
What is the best probiotic for baby’s immune system?
There’s
some research
to suggest that having a balanced microbiome — which probiotics can help to achieve — may help children fight off future infections.
Still, Dr. Posner cautions against thinking about probiotics — or any kind of supplements for that matter — as a cure-all. “I’m a big fan of probiotics, but [they] tend to be best for more GI issues,” she says. “Parents shouldn’t think of them as a miracle cure.”

What Is It?

Chances are, you’ve seen someone rocking a
Lululemon Everywhere Belt Bag
at the playground or in your Mommy and Me class. Despite watching this accessory grow in popularity over the years and hearing rave reviews from friends, I was hesitant to jump on the trend. Didn’t fanny packs go out of style in the '90s? How could this compact bag possibly hold everything I need as a mom of three?
Eventually, though, I no longer needed the massive space my
diaper bag
provided and decided to give Lululemon's popular belt bag a try. Worst-case scenario, it wouldn’t work for me, and I could just pass it on to one of my kids. That was a few years ago, and now this elevated fanny pack has become a wardrobe staple. It carries everything I need to get through errands or outings with the kids — without ever weighing me down.
If you've been on the fence about adding the belt bag to your cart, here are a few reasons why it’s worth purchasing.
The Pros
Spaciousness
I’ve owned some similarly sized bags before and could never fit everything I needed. The Everywhere Belt Bag, however, stores all my essentials — phone, wallet, keys, stick sunscreen, lip gloss, hand sanitizer, and random hair ties — with ease. This makes sense, given the bag boasts a 1-liter volume and measures 7.5 inches long, 2 inches deep and 5 inches tall.
Plus, zippers and pockets keep the bag from becoming a disorganized mess.
Esther Carlstone
The outer zip pocket is especially useful for stashing my car keys, so I don’t have to dig around to find them. There are also a couple of smaller interior compartments where I tend to keep things like gum and credit cards when I'm not carrying a wallet. Yet, no matter how much stuff in it, the belt bag remains shockingly lightweight. And for lighter loads, I hardly feel it at all.
In an ideal world, it would also fit a small pack of baby wipes or a diaper or two. But in those instances, it might make more sense just to bring a backpack.
Versatility
Whether I’m running errands, at the playground, or out for date night, this bag is my go-to. Not only is it great on its own, but it also prevents my other bags from becoming bottomless pits. For instance, I can see it perfectly accompanying a giant tote or beach bag, keeping your small essentials safe and easily accessible.
Esther Carlstone
That's why I never travel without it: It's an easily accessible, smaller bag that keeps my carry-on a little more orderly. (Have you ever tried fishing for your ID with a child in tow?) Thanks to the easy-to-adjust straps, the bag can be worn as a fanny pack or a crossbody, which has definitely come in handy in these instances.
Durability
Made of sturdy, water-resistant nylon, the Lululemon Everywhere Belt Bag is as durable as advertised. I’ve carelessly tossed mine on the ground, spilled water on it, and have even had kids accidentally trample over it, and it still looks fantastic. (Pro mom tip: the black color definitely hides any wear and tear.)
Similarly, the straps haven’t frayed and are still easy to manipulate.
Color Options
I definitely know more than a few friends who own it in multiple colors to coordinate with various outfits, and I can’t say I haven’t been tempted myself. While I find that black goes with everything, there are also bright pastels and earthy hues to choose from. The style comes in a
miniature size
and a slightly roomier
2-liter version
, too.

Belly Bandit
Every new mom adapts to her post-pregnancy body differently. In the early days after birth, some women may feel their best in loose, lightweight clothing. Others may feel more comfortable and supported in postpartum shapewear such as postpartum belly bands.
Postpartum belly bands, also known as postpartum belly wraps and postpartum shapewear, are meant to be worn around the waist and are designed to support your body after childbirth. They're usually made of adjustable elastic materials that cover your torso from ribs to hips.
The point of a postpartum wrap isn't to the shape of your body (you just made a baby, after all!). Rather, they're designed to support you and make you feel more comfortable after pregnancy, which can strain your abdominal muscles and possibly contribute to
postpartum back pain
.
You may also be dealing with lingering symptoms of
symphysis pubis dysfunction (SPD)
— also called
pelvic girdle pain
(PGP) — a condition that occurs when the ligaments that keep your bones aligned become too relaxed during pregnancy, destabilizing the pelvic joint and possibly triggering pain.
This is where a postpartum belly band or wrap might be helpful, as these garments may provide extra support to reduce pain. While there’s not much research-based evidence that wearing a belly band offers significant medical benefits for women postpartum, “many women with back pain and pubic symphysis pain report that they find the bands comfortable after pregnancy,” says Susan Lareau, M.D., an OB-GYN at UPMC-Magee Women’s Hospital in Pittsburgh. “But,” she adds, “it’s very dependent on the woman and her body if she will find it comfortable.”
In addition to potentially helping reduce pain, some new moms also turn to postpartum belly bands and wraps to better support and align their abdomen, provide light compression or take the pressure off a healing cesarean incision. Indeed, a small 2019 study published in the
The Eurasian Journal of Medicine
found that women who wore wraps or binders after getting C-sections were able to walk longer distances and had less pain than those who did not wear those products in the first 48 hours post-operation. However, you should wait 2-4 weeks after a C-section (and get your doctor’s signoff) before wearing a postpartum belly band to avoid irritating your healing incision. Be careful when putting on and removing your belly band, too.
Other moms also appreciate that postpartum shapewear products can have a smoothing effect that might make it a little easier to fit into non-maternity clothes.
Still, there is no clear evidence that postpartum belly bands or wraps can help you lose any weight you gained during pregnancy, or reshape your stomach or hips. So take many of these products’ claims with a healthy dose of skepticism. It's also very important to avoid any postpartum shapewear product that constricts your movement or breathing.
Types of postpartum belly bands
Postpartum belly bands (also called postpartum wraps or even postpartum shapewear) come in a few different varieties, so it may require some trial and error to find what feels most comfortable for you. Here are a few of the most popular styles:
Wraps:
These belly bands can wrap around your entire midsection, from your hips to your lower rib cage.
Belts:
These belly bands tend to be thinner than other types of wraps, and fit around your hips and belly.
Multi-part bands:
Some belly bands feature two or more bands, which can be adjusted to provide that just-the-right-amount of compression.
Many of these postpartum bands are made of soft, stretchy materials such as spandex, viscose and nylon.
How to choose the best postpartum belly band
Look for a product that's adjustable and made of soft, comfortable materials.
Make sure that the postpartum belly band or wrap fits you properly and isn't too restrictive. “Any band that is so constricting as to be uncomfortable should be avoided,” says Dr. Lareau.
Avoid waist trainers, cinchers or corsets, which are made of stiffer materials and are usually less about healing and more about appearance.
You should not wear a postpartum belly band or wrap all day, every day. Some experts say that relying on the support for too long will cause your core muscles to weaken even further, which could then worsen your back and hip pain.
How we made our picks for the best belly bands, wraps and shapewear products
We started by scouting out the most popular belly bands on the market, including What to Expect readers’ favorites, and narrowed down our picks to the best rated and reviewed products. Then we selected bands with unique features (machine-washable fabric, pockets for hot/cold packs, extra compression, etc) designed to help new moms.
Here, our top picks for the best postpartum belly bands, postpartum belly wraps and postpartum shapewear products to keep you more comfortable and supported after childbirth.

I Tried 7 White T-Shirts While Pregnant: This $10 Amazon One Won
by
Elizabeth Buxton
| April 8, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Nothing I owned was fitting in my third trimester, so I tried something I never wear.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
Getting dressed during this pregnancy has been harder than I expected. By the middle of my second trimester, my usual clothes stopped working. Pants were easy enough to solve with stretchy styles or a couple pairs of maternity jeans, but tops were the issue. Everything I tried either swallowed me or clung to my bump in a way that felt too revealing and uncomfortable. Timing didn’t help. With my first, I had a September due date and could rely on flowy dresses. This time, I’m in that winter-to-spring transition where you actually need practical outfits, and nothing quite fits right.
I usually like getting dressed and feel like I have my style figured out, but for a few weeks, I felt completely stuck. So I started paying attention to what other women were actually wearing during pregnancy, specifically the ones who still looked like themselves. The common denominator was a good white t-shirt. It’s basic, but for a reason. It works during and after pregnancy, layers with everything, and can be dressed up or down. The challenge is finding one that actually fits well with a bump.
I ordered seven from Amazon, Gap, Old Navy, and a few other brands. Most got one thing right and everything else wrong. Some were long enough but too tight in the arms. Some were comfortable and incredibly soft, but too thin and see-through. Others were oversized in a way that made me look bigger than I already felt (woof).
Liz Buxton
Then I tried the
$10 Amazon Essentials crewneck
. I ordered a large, even though I’m usually a small or medium, and it hit exactly the balance I was looking for. The length covers my bump without looking oversized. The fit is slightly boxy but still structured. The sleeves aren’t tight. The neckline is high and substantial. It’s also 100% cotton, which makes it soft and breathable without feeling thin (a rarity at this price point).
Liz Buxton
I wear it with everything: maternity leggings, lower-rise maternity jeans, lounge pants, under sweaters, with cardigans, with a trench.
Liz Buxton
I wear it often enough that I bought a second one just to keep it in rotation. More than anything, it solved the daily question of what to wear. It’s one piece I can rely on that feels comfortable, looks put together, and works with the rest of my closet, and I’ll keep wearing it long after this pregnancy is over.

I Wish Someone Had Told Me to Pack This $14 Item in My Hospital Bag
by
Lia Beck
| April 23, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Sarah Darby
The first postpartum pee would have been a lot easier with this tool.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
When it came to preparing for my son’s arrival two years ago, I didn’t go overboard with purchases. I made a spreadsheet of minimal gear I’d add to my registry, secondhand scores from Facebook Marketplace, and new items my husband and I would purchase. I truly went the “we’ll figure out the rest as we go” route rather than the “buy multiple types of everything and test them out” route.
I was so focussed on setting up for baby, attending my midwife appointments, and satisfying my endless cereal craving that I overlooked items meant for, well, me. I hadn’t thought about packing my hospital bag or prepping a postpartum care station. As I panic-read through forums, I decided to splurge on the
Frida Labor and Delivery + Postpartum Recovery Kit
. Every review said it was a treasure trove of self-care goodies: a nursing gown and no-slip socks for labor comfort, ice pads and perineal foam for postpartum healing, even disposable underwear to lighten the laundry load. It seemed well worth the $100 for a shortcut to stock items I’d use, right?
Well, while I used a few things from the kit, the contents didn’t live up to the hype. The disposable underwear, while comfortable, didn’t have built-in absorption. The icy pads were equally unabsorbent, and not as cooling as expected. The nurse put the hospital-provided socks on me before I could grab the ones from my kit. The witch hazel liners went unused, given how many the hospital provided.
But there was one item that outperformed its hospital counterpart, providing instant relief and easing those postpartum bathroom visits: the
Frida Mom Upside Down Peri Bottle
.
No one prepared me for the first post-delivery pee. I couldn’t feel my legs (thanks, epidural!), and was practically hanging on to the nurse to avoid falling. When I was done, I was handed a little squirt bottle to clean down there since toilet paper was a no-go. But it hardly did the job. The spray was minimal, and I couldn’t exactly bend my body to get a full washing.
Sarah Darby
That’s where the Frida Mom peri bottle stood out. It’s marketed as, “a bidet for your vajay,” and that’s not too far from the truth. Rather than a straight design, the Frida Mom’s bottle has a bent neck (i.e. upside down), which lets you point the stream right where you need it instead of letting it dribble down. The long neck gives you more control of your aim without contouring your sore body. It was also easier to squeeze, giving me more control of the flow. I noticed that the stream was much more forceful, but still gentle on the swollen, tender area. It wasn’t a shower-like washing, but it was enough to clear out the discharge and left me feeling relatively clean when I was finally home.
Sarah Darby
Even though the hospital provides a peri bottle, I’d rather pay $14 to upgrade to the
Frida Mom Upside Down Peri Bottle
. To be honest, I’d probably pay double. The
Frida Labor and Delivery + Postpartum Recovery Kit
may not have been $100 well spent, but it brought me to my postpartum MVP, so it wasn’t a total waste.
Frida Mom Upside Down Peri Bottle
Your Postpartum Bathroom Bestie

My first pregnancy happened during COVID and a frigid winter. I barely left the house, so investing in a full maternity wardrobe felt unnecessary. My second pregnancy was the opposite. I was back in the office, juggling birthday parties, playdates, and the occasional date night. One pair of maternity jeans and stretchy leggings suddenly weren’t cutting it. Still, I couldn’t justify spending hundreds on clothes I’d wear for just a few months.
The solution came from the
What to Expect community
:
Nuuly
. I had not seriously considered a clothing rental service, but the praise was hard to ignore. One mom-to-be wrote, “If I have something I need to dress up for, I do Nuuly and I love it.” Another shared, “I just got my first Nuuly box and it is awesome.”
And right now, you can take

Why Nuuly Is Worth It For Maternity Clothes
A legit maternity section with actually stylish pieces
I tried several clothing subscriptions pre-kids, and they all had one thing in common: an abysmal maternity section. The options were slim and, frankly, dated. Not
Nuuly
.
For $98 a month, you can rent six pieces at a time and swap them out each month. Its virtual closet holds more than 300 maternity pieces (yes, even jeans) designed to be worn with a growing bump. You’ll find baby shower dresses, office-ready trousers, and effortlessly cool matching sets from brands like
Ingrid & Isabel
,

,
Emilia George
, and more.
It can cost less than buying a temporary wardrobe
$98 a month is not insignificant. But maternity denim alone can cost $150 or more. Add a few dresses, work staples, and event outfits, and you can easily spend several hundred dollars on clothes you will wear for a single season.
If you use Nuuly for four or five months during peak bump growth, the total can be comparable to buying a short-term wardrobe outright. The difference is you do not have to store or resell anything afterward.
Plus, there’s no need to store bins of maternity clothes or figure out how to resell them later. When you’re done, you simply send everything back using the pre-paid label.
It works postpartum, too
We do not talk enough about postpartum clothes because they barely exist as a category. You’re either still wearing maternity pieces that now feel too loose, squeezing into pre-pregnancy clothes that do not fit comfortably yet, or buying new items that may not fit in a few weeks.
Nuuly offers a fourth option: renting clothes that fit your body right now.
Most pieces are available in a wide size range (typically 00 to 16), making it easy to size up or down as your body continues to change. And because the selection rotates seasonally, you’re not stuck trying to make a linen dress work in 30-degree weather.
It’s a flexible, low-commitment way to feel put-together during a phase when getting dressed can feel surprisingly hard.
Is Nuuly Right for You?
If you’re pregnant, attending events, or commuting to an office and don’t want to build a temporary wardrobe from scratch,
Nuuly
is definitely worth considering.
The $98 monthly fee may not make sense if you only need a pair of jeans and a few tees. But if you have multiple social plans, work events, or special occasions, renting can be the more flexible option.
As one What to Expect community member put it: “Given how fast the body changes, renting clothes feels like the more sustainable and affordable route than purchasing a bunch of new clothes.”
For me, it made pregnancy and postpartum style easier, far less wasteful, and a lot more fun. Interested? Right now, you can take

When you’re pregnant, you expect your belly to grow and your cravings to take interesting turns. But some bodily changes may catch you off guard. Your feet typically stop growing by early adulthood, yet by the third trimester, they may feel like they’ve doubled in size.
Swollen feet and ankles are common pregnancy symptoms caused by the extra weight you're carrying, hormone shifts that loosen ligaments, and an increase in water retention (hello,
edema
!). Shoes that fit just fine before your pregnancy announcement may suddenly feel too snug, and if your feet are sore after periods of standing or walking, it could be a sign it’s time to shop for new footwear.
Sure,
compression socks
can help with swelling, but they aren't a cure-all for most foot discomforts brought on by pregnancy. That's why finding pregnancy-friendly footwear is more than a fashion choice — it's about making yourself feel a little more comfortable and supported before (and after!) baby arrives.
How We Chose the Best Shoes for Pregnancy
There are a dizzying number of shoes on the market, and pretty much all of them claim to be comfortable! Finding a pair that can adapt to the swelling and shape changes caused by pregnancy can feel a lot like searching for a needle in a haystack. To help narrow down the options, we combined expert advice from two podiatrists and hands-on testing feedback from moms in the What to Expect community and editors on staff.
First, we spoke with
Ashley Lee
, D.P.M., a foot and ankle reconstructive surgeon in Hinsdale, Illinois, and
Emily Splichal
, D.P.M., a podiatrist based in New York City, to idenfity the most important features in pregnacy-friendly footwear:
Supportive arches and cushioned inserts to alleviate fatigue and pain
Breathable and flexible material constructions that stretch with swelling and make it easy to put on and take off (because at some point you're no longer going to be able to bend over!)
Adjustable features, whether that be stretchy laces, velcro straps, buckles, or
slip-on styles
A wide and roomy toe box to prevent pinching, rubbing, and other irritations
We also referenced the
American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA) Seal of Acceptance Program
, which awards a seal to products that promote good foot health. (Many of the shoes selected for this list have received that award!)
And, as it's important to note that you won't know how comfortable a shoe is until you've walked a mile in it, we also assessed personal experiences from moms who wore them throughout every trimester and beyond.
We prioritized shoes that testers reached for the most often, especially after birth, when they were juggling newborn care and toddler daycare drop-offs or playdates at the park. Style also plays into this level of longevity, but it wasn't the main feature we looked into.
But since everyone's pregnancy and parenting journey is different, it's essential to keep your lifestyle in mind when reviewing our curated list of picks below.
By marrying medical know-how with mom-vetted brands, the result is 12 of the best shoes for swelling caused by pregnancy that you'll still enjoy wearing long after your little one arrives.
Doctor's Note on Why Feet Swell (And How Shoes Can Help)
A growing belly isn't the only thing changing in size right now —
edema
affects about three-quarters of pregnant women. It can start as early as the middle of the second trimester, and when it does appear, it will likely stick around until you give birth.
“This is due to the extra fluid in the body and the pressure from a growing uterus,”
explains Dr. Lee.
“Gravity pulls this fluid to the feet and ankles, which can cause painful swelling.”
“Pregnancy usually results in weight gain, which is normal, but this can cause problems with your feet,”
Dr. Lee adds. That's because you’re experiencing increased weight on your feet, as well as swelling in your feet and ankles due to your body increasing its water content during pregnancy.
Plus, at the same time that you're experiencing swelling, the ligaments and tendons in your feet may also go through changes due to an increase in
hormones like relaxin
.
“During pregnancy, it's common for these
ligaments and tendons to relax
, causing the feet to ‘expand,’”
says Dr. Lee. It might also make your arches flatten and cause your shoes to feel a little tight.
You may be wondering: Will my feet
ever
go back to normal? In fact, it's actually a pretty common ask in the
What to Expect community forums
. Many moms shared their personal experience with swelling postpartum — one user noted that it took
roughly eight weeks for their shoes to fit again
, whereas
another
shared, "My feet ended up a half size bigger with my first and did not return to original size."
Experts recommend giving yourself time and drinking lots of fluids. In the meantime, your pregnancy-friendly shoe purchase will certainly come in handy! Dr. Lee suggests buying wider shoes or sizing up, because wearing too-tight shoes can lead to pain and long-term complications.

What To Look for in Pregnancy Shoes
Based on feedback from Dr. Lee and Dr. Splichal,
information from the APMA
and feedback from moms on our editorial team and in the What to Expect community, these are the factors to consider when buying shoes for swollen feet caused by pregnanc:
Comfort:
It’s no surprise that comfort is key when it comes to pregnancy shoes. Look for features that prioritize comfort, such as a contoured footbed, shock-absorbing foam, adjustable straps and lightweight, breathable materials.
Ease of use:
It’s no secret that the further along in pregnancy you get, the harder it is to see your feet — making it increasingly tricky to put on your shoes, especially in the third trimester. Slip- or pull-on styles can be very helpful for this reason, so you can put on your shoes without needing to bend over so much.
Type:
The podiatrists we spoke to noted that sneakers generally tend to be some of the most supportive pregnancy shoes, so that might be the best style to opt for when shopping. With other styles such as flats, boots and sandals, you should prioritize wider shoes because too-narrow options could be constricting when you’re experiencing foot and lower leg swellings. If you want a shoe that you can use to dress up, look for low wedges or flats over heels, as these options provide support to the entire bottom of the foot, whereas heels put pressure on only the ball and heel of your feet, according to Dr. Lee.
Arch support:
This is essential in pregnancy shoes, Dr. Splichal says. “Foot support during pregnancy is particularly important as the woman enters the 3rd trimester,” she explains. “Increasing body weight coupled with elevation of the hormone relaxin places high stress to the arches of the feet, [which] can result in foot pain and arch fatigue.” Given this information, you should look for shoes with built-in arch support. Dr. Splichal also notes that you may want to consider insoles (she likes the ones from
Powerstep
) for additional support.
FAQs
What are the best shoes to wear during pregnancy?
Ultimately, the best shoes to wear during pregnancy are whichever pair you feel comfortable in that provide support and aren’t overly tight — and that’s especially important as you enter the third trimester. Shoes that come with the American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA)’s seal of acceptance, a special seal given to products that promote good foot health, are especially good choices.
In general, gym shoes and sneakers tend to be the most supportive options for moms-to-be. Any flats you choose should have good arch support with soft, flexible uppers to accommodate swelling, Dr. Splichal says. And if you want something a little dressier, Dr. Lee suggests flats or low wedges over heels, as these options provide support to the entire bottom of the foot, whereas heels put pressure on only the ball and heel of your feet. Not to mention, there’s lower risk of falling when in these shoes, she says.
What shoe styles help with ankle and arch support in pregnancy?
To help minimize lower extremity swelling, Dr. Lee recommends
wearing compression stockings
, limiting your salt intake, and elevating your feet when seated. The right shoes can also help keep you comfortable. To give your swollen feet the most support, Dr. Lee says to turn to gym shoes and sneakers, particularly those with cushioned midsoles.
Should I size up during pregnancy or after swelling?
If your shoes feel snug now, don’t wait until swelling peaks — it’s better to size up (or choose a wider width) during pregnancy to prevent discomfort and long-term foot issues, according to Dr. Lee. Swelling can come and go throughout the day, so adjustable shoes that can expand with your feet are ideal. Many moms find their shoe size returns to normal in the weeks after birth, but for others, ligament changes can make those new measurements permanent.
Are slip-ons better than lace-up shoes for late pregnancy?
Moms and moms-to-be are equally big fans of
slip-on shoes
. These hands-free designs are easy to put on and take off, especially when you can no longer bend over to see your toes. According to one of What to Expect's contributing writers, Jessica Booth, she says she reaches for these types of shoes more than any other option in her closet. And now, with a 3- and 5-year-old in tow, slip-on shoes help her get out the door even faster.
Which shoes can handle both indoors and outside with swelling?
Slippers are a super popular slip-on shoe that moms love to wear indoors, but not all can be worn outside. You'll want to pay close attention to design details such as non-slip, durable soles with decent tread. For instance, our favorite pair of cozy slip-on shoes — the
Minnetonka Tempe Slipper
— can take on all terrain.
Other indoor- and outdoor-friendly brands that moms love include
Crocs
and other clogs, such as
HEYDUDEs
.

The timeline will be different for everyone, but there's a lot to think about when it comes to adding maternity items to your closet.
Back to Top
In This Article
When to buy maternity clothes
What to look for when buying maternity clothes
9 maternity clothing essentials
When it comes to buying maternity clothing, there are no “rules.” Some moms-to-be start shopping shortly after seeing that positive
pregnancy test
; others wait until their pre-pregnancy clothes become a squeeze.
Most importantly, you should simply wear what makes you feel good during pregnancy, says
Sherry Ross
, M.D., an OB/GYN, women’s sexual health expert and author. “Comfort is king while wearing maternity clothes,” she says.
Here are some tips to keep in mind if you choose to buy
maternity clothes
— such as signs it might be time to make the transition and which comfy features to look for when you do — plus pregnancy-friendly stores at every price point.
When to buy maternity clothes
How you approach maternity dressing is a personal choice, and again, there are no “rights” or “wrongs” here  — when and if you choose to wear pregnancy-specific styles is entirely up to you.
But if you do intend to purchase maternity clothes, you’ll likely want to get your money’s worth out of them. For this reason, many moms-to-be start thinking seriously about maternity clothes around the end of the first trimester or beginning of the second. Though everyone’s
baby bump grows at a different rate
, it’s common to feel like you’re starting to “pop” around this time.
“I have been wearing maternity clothes since 14 weeks,” says one mom in the What to Expect Community. “I was surprised by how quickly I needed to start wearing them, but all my clothes felt so uncomfortable.”
Many moms-to-be find that their feelings on maternity clothing evolve over the course of their pregnancy. For example, you might be initially resistant to buying maternity clothes only to change your mind once the waistband on your pants become painfully tight. On the other hand, you may be pleasantly surprised to discover that some of your looser dresses or shirts continue to fit as your pregnancy progresses.
If you do decide to buy maternity clothes, these are a few signs it might be time to put your pre-pregnancy items into short-term storage:
Waistbands feel terrible.
The classic “rubber band trick” (looping a hair tie or elastic band around your belt loop and button) or a
maternity belly band or pants extender
help some moms-to-be keep wearing their favorite pants or shorts for longer. But at a certain point, you may find it’s worth getting at least one pair of maternity jeans, pants or leggings — even if that’s the only item you buy.
Clothes ride up or feel painfully tight.
Shirts that keep riding up in a way that makes you feel exposed or dresses that painfully pinch your waist or ribcage may need to be replaced with something roomier.
The fit is uncomfortable.
As your body changes, your pre-pregnancy clothes may start to fit a little differently, even if you can still get them on. Buttons or clasps on shirts or dresses may suddenly dig into your skin at a painful angle, for example. Or you may find that fabrics you used to love now irritate your newly
sensitive skin
.
You’re spending a lot of time thinking about how your clothes fit (or don’t).
If you're stressing about whether your pants are sliding down or whether your pre-pregnancy clothes are becoming a daily source of frustration and discomfort, it might be worth investing in at least a few maternity-specific replacements.
What to look for when buying maternity clothes
While the best maternity clothes for you will depend on your lifestyle and personal style, asking yourself these questions may make shopping for pregnancy-friendly outfits a little easier.
1. Fabric: Is it comfortable?
“Soft and breathable materials are ideal for pregnancy,” Dr. Ross says. “It’s best to avoid polyester and nylon fabrics that don’t breathe well.” She recommends clothes made from fabrics such as cotton, spandex, jersey, knit, bamboo, lyocell and modal that allow for airflow without irritating skin.
2. Fit: Is it forgiving?
Styles that are either very loose or made from stretchy fabrics (such as spandex) are more likely to accommodate your bump, Dr. Ross says. And expectant moms agree: “I'm almost six months and I haven't bought any actual maternity clothes,” says a mom in the WTE Community. “I've just been buying dresses and skirts with a stretchy band for the waist.”
3. Size: How big should I buy?
A number of moms in our WTE Community note that they just assumed they should size up when shopping for clothes from maternity brands, only to discover that their original size was usually best.
“What I learned during my first pregnancy is to just buy whatever size you normally are in maternity,” says a WTE Community mom. “So if you wear a medium, buy a medium in maternity clothing. The maternity style clothing is meant to stretch and will fit you through any stage of your pregnancy.” When in doubt, check the brand’s sizing chart.
4. Postpartum use: Can I wear it after giving birth?
You'll definitely want to think about continuing to wear roomy silhouettes and stretchy fabrics for a few months or more after giving birth, too. During this
postpartum recovery stage
you’ll still be craving cozier options — your uterus will be gradually returning to its pre-pregnancy size, you’ll be experiencing postpartum bleeding, called
lochia
, and may still have
perineal pain
or sensitivity around your
C-section incision
.
“People told me that I would only wear maternity clothes for a month or two, and that was not true,” says a WTE Community mom. “It took me a while to lose the weight postpartum, and maternity clothes were the most comfortable in the meantime.”
Still, some pregnancy-friendly styles work better for the
postpartum period
than others. If you’re nursing, for example you’ll probably prefer styles that give your baby easy access to your breasts throughout the day, such as
tops
or dresses with necklines that can be unbuttoned or pulled aside.
5. Seasonality: When am I due?
If you live in a climate with four distinct seasons, you’ll want to think about the timing of your pregnancy with the weather. If you’ll be in your third trimester during the winter, you’ll likely need a
maternity coat
that can button or zip around your bump. On the other hand, moms-to-be with summer due dates might want to stock up on dresses that are loose or stretchy enough to comfortably expand as their bump grows, and may also want to invest in a
maternity swimsuit
.
6. Lifestyle: Do I need office-appropriate clothes?
The type of maternity clothes you need will also heavily depend on how you spend most of your days. Moms-to-be who work in an office will likely need to stock up on more maternity pants and button-down shirts, for example. If you work from home, you may need more basics like leggings, cardigans, sweatpants and jeans.
9 maternity clothing essentials
Your lifestyle, budget, style and the season you’re due will all play a role in what’s essential for you. Here are some of the main types of maternity clothes to consider shopping for (think of it as a maternity "capsule wardrobe," if you will):
Maternity jeans:
If you only buy one maternity clothing item, there’s a strong case to be made that it should be a pair of
maternity jeans
. “Maternity jeans are so much more comfortable than finding ways to extend use of regular jeans,” says one WTE Community memberPregnancy-friendly jeans usually have an under-the-bump band, side paneling or over-the-bump paneling to hold your bump in place and keep your jeans from sliding down.
Maternity dresses:
Not only are
maternity dresses
designed with your bump specifically in mind, but many maternity dresses have nursing-friendly features so you can continue wearing them after giving birth if you’re choosing to breastfeed.
Maternity tops:
Maternity tops are longer and roomier, and as with maternity dresses, many include
nursing-friendly
features.
Maternity leggings:
Leggings are a go-to in pregnancy, and the best
maternity leggings
should feel comfortable and supportive but never too tight. Many regular leggings can still work in pregnancy, especially if you size up — but some have too much compression or seams in the waistband that can dig into your bump, so it’s important to read reviews closely or try them on in the store if you’re going the non-maternity route.
Maternity workout clothes:
In addition to leggings, you may want to invest in a few other pieces of maternity activewear like tops or sports bras. Your breasts may grow during pregnancy, so you might want to head to the store for a fit check, or order a couple different sizes to try.
Maternity coats:
If you’ll be in the third trimester during winter, a
maternity coat
is a must. Alternatively, you can try a jacket extender (insert panels that can be added to your existing winter gear) to accommodate your bump.
Maternity swimsuits:
Maternity swimsuits are designed to grow with your bump — perfect if you prefer high-waisted or one-piece fits — and many moms say they’re able to wear them postpartum too.
Maternity underwear:
You can continue wearing your regular underwear if it fits or purchase a few pairs in a larger size, but
maternity underwear
can be blissfully comfortable. Maternity underwear has a waistband that won’t dig into your bump as it expands, which also makes them super comfortable postpartum.
Pregnancy-friendly shoes:
Feet can also swell when you’re pregnant, which is called
edema
.
Pregnancy-friendly shoes
are wider shoes and offer more arch support and other comfort-focused features.
There are maternity clothes for every price point
Everyone has a different budget, so to help you shop, here's a guide to stores with maternity
clothes at every price point
.
Maternity brands
A clothing brand dedicated to maternity-specific styles will give you the biggest selection and easiest shopping experience, as you won’t have to filter out non-maternity items or guess whether something is pregnancy-friendly. Here are a few of our favorites:

If you don’t love the thought of buying lots of clothes you may not wear long term, a clothing rental service can be worth looking into. These services, which generally allow you to rent a few items per month for a membership fee, can be especially helpful if you have an event coming up or you're heading on a babymoon. Renting a dress for a wedding can be much more cost-effective than buying a new one, for example.

The Real Reason Your Pregnancy Belly Band Isn't Fixing Your Hip Pain (and What to Use Instead)

Leah Rocketto
| April 9, 2026
Latest update:

Leah Rocketto
Experiencing lightning-like zaps in your hip? A belly band won’t fix it.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
I went into my second pregnancy feeling a little overconfident: no nausea, no major discomfort, and every intention of keeping up my workout routine. I even added tennis lessons, because what’s cuter than a pregnant woman in tennis whites? But those outfits collected dust. By my second trimester, I was dealing with sharp, stabbing pain that bounced between my hips and groin. I bought a standard belly band and tried to power through, assuming it was just my body adjusting or an old injury flaring up. Then one night, I got out of bed, my hips foze, and my legs gave out completely. My husband had to carry me back while I tried not to cry from the pain.
That’s when I decided it was time to see a pelvic floor physical therapist, who clocked the issue immediately. The surge of relaxin (the hormone that loosens your ligaments for birth) was creating instability in my hip and pelvic joints. “And that,” she said, pointing to my belly band, “isn’t helping.”
To be clear, belly bands aren’t useless. They’re great for relieving lower back pain and supporting the weight of your bump. But that wasn’t my problem. I didn’t need a lift; I needed stability, specifically support for my sacroiliac (SI) joints. That’s when I was introduced to the
Serola Sacroiliac Belt
.
Leah Rocketto
Unlike stretchy belly wraps, the Serola Belt is designed to actually stabilize your pelvis. It uses a two-layer system: a base layer to anchor the belt in place, and a top layer that applies targeted pressure to your joints. The tighter the top layer, the more stability you get. It sounds intense, but it doesn’t feel restrictive. It feels like your hips are being held in place, which, it turns out, is exactly what I needed.
Within minutes of putting it on, the sharp, lightning-like pain started to ease. And, over time, paired with stretching and strengthening exercises, I was able to move through the rest of my pregnancy without that same level of instability.
Leah Rocketto
It’s not as thin or discreet as a typical belly band, but that’s the point. I was still able to wear it under looser clothing without it being obvious, and it didn’t trap heat the way I expected. It’s also incredibly durable. I wore it daily through my second and third trimesters and into postpartum, but it still looks brand new.
If you’re dealing with intense pelvic pain during pregnancy, it’s definitely worth seeing a pelvic floor or physical therapist. But, if that’s not immediately accessible, this is one of the few things that can actually help stabilize what’s causing the pain. It’s not the most subtle option, but being able to walk, stand, and get out of bed without pain made that tradeoff an easy one.

Baby floor seats can be a godsend for both you and your child. Parents like these seats because they provide a safe place to keep your little one secured and occupied when you need your hands free, whether you’re folding laundry or starting dinner. A baby seat can also give your little one a chance to sit up and have an exciting new vantage point from which to view the world before they’re able to sit up on their own.
These floor seats, which are best suited for babies 3 to 5 months old who are able to control their heads, can help your little one learn how to sit up, a very important milestone.

What to consider when buying a baby floor seat
Baby floor seats come in different styles, be made of different material, and feature different add-ons like activity centers or snack trays. Here are some factors to consider as you start your research.
Fit:
Babies come in all shapes and sizes, and even if they fall within the weight and height guidelines for a certain seat, they may not necessarily fit comfortably in it. For instance, one common complaint of floor seats is that the leg holes aren’t large enough for chubby thighs. If you can't try the seat in person to see how it fits your baby, order from a site with an easy return policy just in case it isn’t comfortable for baby. "The best and most development-friendly baby floor seats will provide enough support for your baby without being too restrictive," says Dr. Hunter. In short, you’ll want a seat that baby can’t fall or wriggle out of, but also one that isn’t too constricting.
Ease of cleaning:
Floor seats get gunky quickly, so consider how you're going to degrime it. Plastic and foam are simple to wipe down, and if your seat has fabric panels, they should be easy to detach and machine wash. This is especially important if your floor seat doubles as a booster chair and you're planning to use the seat at mealtimes.
Interactiveness:
"Look for seats with developmentally-appropriate toys to help stimulate your baby’s development," says Dr. Hunter. This may include an activity center with buttons, knobs and rattles to encourage fine motor skill development, or a musical bar that will introduce them to new sounds. Your baby floor seat may also include a removable tray. "This is convenient for feeding or playtime and provides additional support to prevent the baby from toppling forward," says Dr. Hunter.
Age-appropriateness:
Some seats are meant for young babies only, while others can convert into booster seats and be used well into the preschool and toddler years. These seats can be good investments because you can use them for many years, but might not be necessary if you already have a high chair or other feeding gear.
Portability:
You’re likely planning on using a floor seat around the house, whether you need to sit baby on the floor while you fold clothes or in the kitchen as you cook. Because of this, it may be ideal to prioritize seats that are lightweight and easy to move around without hassle. Some are designed to fold easily while others are made of lightweight material like foam.
Are baby floor seats safe?
Baby floor seats are safe when used correctly. Here's what you need to know about how to safely use a baby floor seat.
Keep it on the floor:
Sometimes reviewers' online photos show baby floor seats placed on tables or counters, but this is a serious no-no. “As the name implies, baby floor seats should only be used on the floor, not higher surfaces such as a table, bed or counter,” says Dr. Hunter. “No matter how safe the seat looks, there is still a chance that the baby can topple over.” The exception: Some floor seats come with straps that attach to high-backed chairs and can do double-duty as boosters. Under no circumstances, however, should these be used on a backless chair or stool.
Wait until your baby has neck strength:
Make sure your baby has proper head and neck control before setting them up in their new spot. "It is very important to not use floor seats until your baby can hold their head up on their own,” says Dr. Hunter, which
usually happens between three and five months
.
Set up safely:
"Floor seats should be kept out of range of dangerous objects such as electrical sockets, cords, and sharp objects," says Dr. Hunter. Find an open space where your baby won't be tempted to grab anything that could harm them.
Limit the time:
Dr. Hunter recommends only allowing your baby to use the floor seat for a total of 30 minutes each day, broken up into 15-minute increments. "When babies are confined to a 'container' such as a baby floor seat, they lose some freedom of movement,” says Dr. Hunter. In fact, this containment can be restricting, especially to their spine and hips. It can potentially impact their anatomical development and cause delay in gross motor skills, she adds.
Encourage movement:
No matter how cool your new chair looks, or what the company claims, it isn't going to teach your child how to sit — the muscles needed for sitting must be developed simply by using them. "You want to make sure your baby has plenty of free time away from their seat to learn to use their muscles and gain strength," says Dr. Hunter.
Supervise:
You'd be surprised by the trouble babies can get into even when you just duck out for a second to answer the doorbell. "Parents should never leave their baby unattended in a floor seat," says Dr. Hunter. Floor seats should not be used as a replacement for supervision and should always be used while you’re with baby.
