As a mom of two, I can tell you the journey from
bottles
to
open cups
isn't always a smooth one. Both of my boys eventually made the switch, and sippy cups were an incredibly helpful stepping stone during that time. Not only are they easier for most babies and toddlers to drink from and hold independently, but they’re also typically less messy (weighted bottoms and covered tops prevent most puddles from appearing on your floor). Sippy cups are also more portable, allowing you to easily pack them in a bag for on-the-go activities like play dates and daycare.
But how do you know when is the right time to introduce your little one to a sippy cup? The
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) now recommends starting to wean off bottles somewhere between 6 and 9 months. Understandably, there is quite a learning curve at this stage. While some experts recommend going straight to open containers from the breast or bottle, most families (mine included) found that the best sippy cups can help
bridge this gap
.
How I Chose the Best Sippy Cups
To learn about must-have features and any safety considerations when using training cups before ensuring every recommendation was backed by both experience and expertise, I combined firsthand parenting know-how with insights from trusted professionals and organizations:
Interviewed pediatric and dental experts:
I spoke to
Lauren Crosby
, M.D., a pediatrician at
La Peer Pediatrics
in Beverly Hills, California, and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board; and
Michelle Kelman
, D.D.S., a pediatric dentist in Los Angeles, California, and a member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board.
I also referenced information from the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP) and the
American Dental Association
(ADA). The latter recommends avoiding designs with no-spill valves, as it will encourage your child to suck rather than sip, which may impact oral motor skills and overall teeth health. That’s why I made sure to include drinking vessels featuring straws or lids with spouts, though there’s a variety to suit a range of needs and comfort.
Priotized parent-tested picks:
As both a mom and former parenting editor, I have tested many sippy cups to find ones that work for my two sons, so I made note of the products that I’ve personally found most helpful and easiest to use. Next, I spoke to What to Expect staff members with four kids between them and then canvassed the What to Expect community boards to learn which sippy cups parents felt were easiest to clean, and for babies to hold and drink from.
Reviewed feedback from previous award results:
For the
2024
What to Expect Feeding Awards
, where hundreds of parents voted for their favorite baby products, sippy cups were included.
By blending expert guidance with parent reviews, this list spotlights the best sippy cups that are durable, easy to use, and (mostly) spill-proof — so you can focus more on your little one’s progress and less on mopping up messes.
A Doctor's Note on Sippy Cups
Dr. Kelman says she generally prefers that parents transition from a bottle directly to an open cup, but if you do go the sippy cup route, she suggests a spoutless model. “Although there have been some concerns regarding positioning of the tongue with [spoutless] cups, they aren’t as damaging to the teeth as traditional sippy cups,” she explains.

Many babies initially struggle to learn how to use a straw, especially if they’re exclusively breastfed and haven’t yet been introduced to bottles or cups of any kind. If that’s the case with your little one, you might consider offering her the
TalkTools Honey Bear Drinking Cup
, often simply called “the honey bear cup” by devoted customers.
Developed as a feeding therapy tool for occupational therapists, this cup disperses liquid very easily — the BPA-free plastic is thin and lightweight, and liquid squeezes up at the slightest bit of pressure. That, combined with the thinness of the straw and soft texture, seems to make the cup very manageable for babies to hold and use. There are countless stories within the What to Expect community from parents whose little ones finally learned how to drink from a straw after using this cup.
Heavily influenced by the many What to Expect parents who recommended it in my Birth Month Group, I purchased this cup for my youngest son when he was around 8 months. To my surprise, he understood almost immediately how to drink from this cup. And while he’s now capable of using “regular”-sized straws, we still have the Honey Bear around for water use.
Just note that this is not the best sippy cup for milk. While it’s dishwasher-safe, the straw is incredibly thin, which makes it difficult to clean. For this reason, many parents prefer to use the Honey Bear cup solely as a tool to introduce straws and as a water cup thereafter.

It may not be the first material you think of when shopping for sippy cups, but stainless steel has some undeniable benefits. It’s sustainable, does not come with any of the concerns about chemicals that can be found in plastic and is highly durable.
Pura’s stainless steel bottles
, which have a hugely loyal following, are virtually indestructible, parents say. This brand specializes in stainless steel feeding products that will last for years. Each of their drinking vessels can be used from the newborn stage and beyond: First, as a bottle with a nipple top; as a sippy cup when you swap in the silicone sipper spout; as a straw cup with the straw top; and finally as a regular water bottle with the sport top. All of these tops are compatible with the same stainless steel base. In other words, while it’s undeniably an initial investment (the cups are $28 each), you won’t have to continuously replace them as your child gets older.
Although this sippy cup will last years, the one downside is that it may not be the most comfortable for a younger baby who is learning how to use a sippy cup. With its bigger, clunkier size and heavier weight (while relatively lightweight, it’s still stainless steel and weighs more than a plastic cup), the Pura is more like a water bottle, making
it a little tricky for 6-month-olds to hold and manage themselves. In this case, you might want to try introducing a sippy cup with one of the other models on this list first.

smaller baby sippy cups
are $10 and the

are $13.

What to Know Before Buying a Sippy Cup
Comfort:
This is particularly important when shopping for a sippy cup for a younger baby. The littlest hands may prefer cups made from materials that are soft, such as silicone, as well as those that have a softer spout that more closely resembles a bottle nipple.
Design:
First, you’ll want to consider what type of sippy cup you’d like—hard spout, soft spout, straw, or flat lid. Cups that are designed to be easy to manage and hold, such as models with handles or grippy material, are often easier for little hands to pick up. It’s also smart to look for a sippy cup designed to prevent leaks: After all, one of the biggest benefits of using a sippy cup is that they help prevent spills as your child learns to drink from a cup. Some models on the market are truly leak-proof, while others are more what we'd call leak-resistant.
Ease of cleaning:
Straws and spouts are a perfect place for gunk to build up and germs to grow, which means ease of cleaning is incredibly important. The best sippy cups are those that come completely apart and can be washed in the dishwasher to avoid the possibility of mold.
FAQs
What kind of sippy cup is best?
There are four main types of sippy cups: Hard spout, soft spout, straw and flat lid. We’ve featured each of the four types on our list of the best sippy cups, but it can be difficult to decide which is best for your child. Soft spouts and straws are popular choices, as they more closely resemble nipples and are easier for tots to learn how to drink from. “Straws are better for oral motor development, but most babies can't figure out how to use them before they are 9 to 12 months old,” says Dr. Crosby.
Besides straw and spout, many experts also recommend flat lid or spoutless cups. “I always suggest a spoutless one as the first option,” says Dr. Kelman.
Do pediatricians recommend sippy cups?
You don’t have to offer your child a sippy cup (you can go straight from the bottle to an open cup — and in fact, some experts recommend this), but the AAP says sippy cups are just fine to use while transitioning baby from the bottle to a “real” cup, which you should ideally do by about age 2. But they recommend that sippies are only used while your child is learning to make this jump.
At what age should babies start using sippy cups?
Although you don’t have to give baby a sippy cup, many parents do choose to offer one to babies in their first year, especially because an open cup can be difficult and messy for young children.
“We recommend
introducing a sippy cup
around 6 months old so the child becomes familiar with it and proficient so that by their first birthday they can use them and start weaning off bottles,” says Dr. Crosby.
Your child can begin using a sippy cup as soon as she can sit in a high chair to eat solid foods. “A cue that your child is ready for a cup is that they are sitting upright on their own,” says Dr. Kelman.
What cup should an 18-month-old use?
As your toddler approaches her second birthday, give her more opportunities to sip from an open cup or straw cup (such as when she’s sitting in her high chair eating). The AAP recommends that children be weaned from sippy cups by age 2.
A good rule of thumb? Try to think of the sippy cup as a bridge to the real thing, and switch to a real cup once she gets the hang of holding it upright, rather than letting it become a comfort object. “Toddlers don't need to carry around a cup all day like a security blanket,” says Dr. Crosby. “That tends to encourage over-drinking which can fill them up so they don't eat their meals.”

If you've decided to pump — whether you're
exclusively pumping
,
traveling without your baby
or
preparing to go back to work
— you'll need a breast pump.
Fortunately, there are a variety of pumps to choose from, including double-electric, hands-free, manual and more.
The many options on the market these days certainly make the pumping process a little bit easier. But as a pumping mom, a good breast pump is usually just the beginning of what you'll need.
More often than not, it’s the accessories (what you pack your pump in, what you store your milk in and what you use to clean everything up) that ensure your experience is as seamless as possible.
The good news? With a little bit of prep, you can put together a pumping essentials package that will make both at-home and on-the-go pumping sessions a breeze. Here are some pointers to keep in mind:
How to prepare for pumping and storing breast milk
Do your research ahead of time.
Since no one wants to be on the hunt for a pump room or a place to store your milk, foresight can pay off in spades. Before you leave the house (if possible) do some digging on where the pump rooms at your workplace are located, for example, and what resources the space provides.
Practice.
It can be helpful to start pumping before you need to so you can get the hang of it and your baby can get used to taking a bottle.
Consider an extra
pump
.
If you’re going back to a full-time job and hope to feed your baby only (or mostly) breast milk, a double-electric pump is usually most efficient. But some moms prefer handheld pumps, especially if they won't be pumping every day, while others invest in wireless models they can use hands-free. Depending on when and where you'll be pumping, you may want more than one.
Keep cleaning in mind.
Does washing your pump parts in a communal sink make you nervous? You might want to be prepared with your own wipes, microwave sterilizing bags and extra pump parts. Knowing yourself as well as your environment can help you figure out the additional products you’ll need.
Remember to relax!
Easier said than done, we know, but in order to trigger letdown to release milk, it helps to be relaxed. Letdown naturally occurs in the presence of your baby, but it’s possible to recreate the sensation with photos or videos of your little one, for example. Knowing this can help you in the moment when you’re ready to start pumping away from baby.
Milk storage matters.
Whether you pump directly into bottles or bags, it’s important to
store your milk at the right temperature
.
Here, all the products you need to get from session to session, no matter where your pumping journey takes you.

Every family’s baby-feeding journey is unique. Whether you’re
breastfeeding
,
formula-feeding
, pumping and bottle-feeding (or doing some combination of all three), the truth is that you often need quite a lot of stuff to support you and your baby. And the need for the right gear continues once you start to
introduce solid foods
.
But knowing where to start can be a daunting task. Which breast pump should you choose? Is a
bottle warmer
worth it — and if so, which one is best? Which of the many baby bottles on the market is a reliable choice? While a lot comes down to personal preference (including what your baby responds to), it can help to learn which products have worked well for experienced parents who’ve been there.
That’s why we set out to ask the experts — parents like you! — about their tried-and-true baby-feeding products for the fourth annual What to Expect Feeding Awards. The winners include beloved products trusted by the What to Expect community in 24 different categories.
How the What to Expect Feeding Award Winners Were Chosen
First, we created a list of the items we knew were key for feeding your little one, from the
best breast pumps
(we’re talking electric,
wearable
and manual) to the best baby food brand.
We then selected a thorough list of contenders for each category based on what our community of parents have recommended time and time again, as well as products parents on the What to Expect editorial team have tested themselves.
From there, we polled parents in our community, asking them to vote for their absolute favorite feeding-related products in each category. This year, nearly 6,000 votes were cast to help finalize the list of winning products.
Below, the winners of the What to Expect Feeding Awards.
Why Trust Us?

When I was pregnant with my first child, I couldn’t wait to get my hands on one of the high-tech wearable breast pumps that were hitting the market. Now, four years after I started testing them, the range of hands-free breast pumps has greatly expanded, offering even more options. Still, one thing hasn’t changed: The best wearable breast pumps are those that allow moms to pump hands-free just about anywhere.
Traditional
breast pumps
protrude outside your bra and you have to be connected to an outlet to use them. Wireless pumps, however, offer much more comfort and mobility, fitting snugly into your normal bras. I really appreciated this convenience as I was getting the hang of breastfeeding and trying to multitask around the house, as well as
pumping in public places

What to Look for in a Wearable Breast Pump
Buying a wearable breast pump is highly personal, and what makes sense for someone else may not be right for you. Keep the following considerations in mind to find the
best wearable breast pump
for your lifestyle and preferences:
Comfort:
When choosing any type of breast pump, comfort is a top priority. Wearable breast pumps should feel comfortable when worn and fit properly inside your bra. Remember: Finding the right breast pump flange size is crucial to getting a comfortable fit on any breast pump, wearable or otherwise, so make sure to measure yourself using the manufacturer’s size guide.
Suction:
Breast pump suction is measured in millimeters of mercury (or mmHG), and higher suction power means the pump is able to express milk more efficiently. Breast pumps usually have a maximum suction of around 220 to 350 (on this list, the range is from 220 to 320 mmHG) with hospital-grade pumps in the higher end of that range. While some moms may choose to invest in hospital-grade suction to express the most milk in the shortest amount of time, others might find stronger suction to be uncomfortable and may prefer a pump that’s a little gentler.
Ease of cleaning:
Wearable pumps have a number of parts to clean after use — but those parts do tend to be smaller and a little more fiddly than those of electric pumps. Models with dishwasher-safe parts are generally a little easier to keep clean.
Price:
Wearable pumps tend to be more expensive than plug-into-the-wall units, ranging in price from $100 to over $500, says Kincer. “Most of these pumps also have custom milk storage bags that are more expensive than the other ones on the market, so your upfront and long-term costs will also be higher than other pumps," she adds.
FAQs
Are wearable breast pumps covered by insurance?
Since the passage of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) more than a decade ago, health insurers
are required to cover
breastfeeding support supplies, including wearable breast pumps. However, coverage can vary depending on your health plan (for example, some may only cover hospital-grade pumps while other employers may have “grandfathered” plans that don’t require them to provide coverage for any pump). And if you’ve already used your benefit to cover an electric or hospital-grade breast pump, you may have to purchase an additional wearable pump out of pocket.
“Insurance coverage varies with insurance plans, it's best to contact your insurance provider for more specific details and find out if there is any co-pay or deductibles and if you will require a prescription,” says Chan. “Some insurance companies have specific time frames when you can qualify for a breast pump benefit. Some can be purchased prior to birth and some within a week of birth.”
Also helpful: Some brands, including
Willow
and
Elvie
, have information on their website about how to check if your insurance will cover the cost of your pump, which can be useful as you make your decision.
Do wearable breast pumps actually work?
Wearable breast pumps absolutely work, but some moms do find the suction on some models to be a little less strong than that on electric pumps — or that leakage and other issues can crop up if you’re moving around. That’s why many experts recommend having both a standard breast pump and hands-free option available, especially if you’re going to be pumping exclusively.
For this reason, wearable pumps aren’t considered  a must-have for everyone who pumps. “[Wearable pumps] are not necessary for every parent,” says Chrisie Rosenthal, an international board-certified lactation consultant and consultant relations manager with
The Lactation Network
. “Most pumping parents do great with a traditional high-quality double electric breast pump.”
That being said, hands-free pumps are great because they’re portable and allow you to multitask or pump on-the-go. “For the mother who truly needs to be multitasking, a wireless pump will allow her to continue to produce milk for her baby where this otherwise wouldn’t have been possible,” says Kincer.
Considering that a typical pumping session takes about 20 minutes, sitting near a power source for that much time can feel frustrating (plus a little boring and lonely) when you have so many other things to do.
“Parents who find these pumps most helpful are parents who have multiple children, and parents who have jobs that make taking scheduled pump breaks difficult,” adds Rosenthal.
Other benefits of wearable pumps include:
They’re more discreet:
Wearable pumps and in-bra collection cups make pumping easier when it’s less obvious. For instance, you can feel less worried about someone walking in on you pumping with these devices or even wear them while you commute.
They may feel more comfortable:
You might find yourself hunched over a lot when using a more traditional pump. This can cause back pain, so some parents find that a hands-free pump can actually make pumping much more comfortable.
Is there a hospital-grade wearable breast pump?
Although it’s true that most wearable breast pumps aren’t considered hospital-grade (that’s because they have a lower range of suction power), there are a few hospital-grade models on the market. On this list of the best wearable breast pumps, both the Elvie Stride and the Baby Buddha Single or Double Portable Breast Pump have hospital-grade power.
Can you lay down with a wearable breast pump?
Wearable breast pumps are designed to slip inside a bra so you can wear them and pump completely hands-free. Most of these pumps work very similarly to an electric breast pump: You put the flange in place over your nipple, turn on the pump and wait for your milk to collect.
However, though wearable pumps do let you multitask — making it possible to bend over or move around — some are designed in such a way that it is possible for them to overflow or leak should you lie down completely. Check the specific instructions for each brand, however, as some may be used lying down: For example, you can recline completely while wearing Willow pumps if you’re
using the brand’s spill-proof bags
.
How do you clean a wearable breast pump?
As you may already know, it’s important to
clean your breast pump and pump parts
after each use. Washing a wearable breast pump is
similar to washing a regular one
: Each piece should be washed using dish soap and warm water, then left to air dry on either a paper towel or dish rack (avoid towels because they can harbor bacteria). Or, simply wash it in the dishwasher on the top rack if it’s dishwasher-safe.
But what’s the main difference between cleaning a regular pump versus a wearable one? Wearable pumps actually tend to be easier to clean because they typically include fewer parts.

Although they aren’t nearly as cute as your
baby’s going-home outfit
, postpartum pads are just as essential to pack in your
hospital bag
. Most maternity wards will supply mesh underwear and heavy-duty hospital pads, but bringing your tried-and-true favorites along can help you feel a little more like yourself post-delivery. And since bleeding after birth (called
lochia
) can last up to 6 weeks, you’ll want to stock up on plenty for home, too.
Because
tampons and menstrual cups can introduce bacteria
to your healing vagina and uterus, they’re typically off-limits until your doctor gives the green light. That means pads and other absorbent products like
disposable underwear
will be your best friends in those early weeks postpartum.
However, each person’s postpartum recovery journey might look a little different: Some new moms prefer thick, super-absorbent pads in the first couple of days, while others might be fine with thinner and lightweight options. You might even find that period underwear feels more comfortable than pads altogether. Whatever the case, I’ve rounded up our top picks — whether you’re looking for the best postpartum pads for heavy bleeding or the best organic postpartum pads.
How I Chose the Best Postpartum Pads
In order to recommend the best pads for postpartum recovery that work well for a wide variety of women, I combined hands-on testing with feedback and reviews from numerous sources:
First, I considered the postpartum pads I tested and used after giving birth to my two children, taking note of absorbency and comfort throughout the day (as new mom life doesn’t offer many opportunities to sit still!).
I also spoke with three moms on the What to Expect staff who have given birth at least once each and tested several different types of pads while recovering from both vaginal deliveries and C-sections.
I then reviewed thousands of reviews from moms in the What to Expect community to increase my initial list and learn what other brands earned high praise for leak protection, softness, and overall value.
Lastly, I sought expert insights from
Shannon Smith
, M.D., a board-certified OBGYN and partner at Brigham Faulkner Associates (in affiliation with Brigham and Women's Hospital) in Boston, Massachusetts. She shared her clinical perspective on what new moms need most out of postpartum pads in the first few weeks after delivery. She also explained the typical experience you might have with postpartum bleeding. Based on her guidance, I also ensured that none of the recommended products feature added fragrance, as Dr. Smith notes that "your tissue is very sensitive postpartum."
A Doctor's Note on Postpartum Bleeding
"After delivery, the uterus has to shed the thickened lining that supported the pregnancy. The shedding is helped along by the sudden drop in estrogen and progesterone after delivery that signals to shedding of this remaining endometrium," explains Dr. Smith. "Additionally, when the placenta separates from the uterus, it leaves a raw surface with open blood vessels. These contribute to the heavier bleeding in the first few days after delivery."
While everyone is different, Dr. Smith notes that after the first week, you can generally expect your bleeding to lighten up.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

What To Look For in Postpartum Pads
Based on research and feedback from moms, these are the factors you should consider when buying postpartum pads:
Absorbency:
You'll want highly absorbent pads that can withstand some wear before they need to be changed, as you might find changing your pad to be uncomfortable right after giving birth. For this reason, you may want to consider overnight pads (typically size 4 or 5), because they’re the most absorbent.
Comfort:
You’ll likely already be experiencing some pain after giving birth, so the last thing you want is to add an uncomfortable pad to the mix. You'll want something soft but not bulky, and will want to consider features like wings to hold the pad in place and long, wide backs to help avoid leaking.
Value:
If you’re going to need enough pads for six weeks or longer, you probably don’t want anything too expensive.
FAQs
What pads should I use after giving birth?
There’s no rule on which specific postpartum pads to use, although you’ll likely want something soft, comfortable and absorbent enough to handle a heavy flow and wear constantly. We like Always Infinity Pads best because they’re absorbent enough for overnight wear but still have a thin and flexible feel. If you’d prefer to use something organic, Rael Organic Cotton Pads are ideal for sensitive skin and have a comfortable fit. Using ice packs in your underwear is also a great way to relieve pain and inflammation, and Frida Mom has 2-in-1 ice packs and pads that absorb liquid and keep you cool. If you hate pads, try disposable underwear, like Always Discreet.
"Whatever pads you choose to use, ensure they are fragrance-free," notes Dr. Smith. She also advises to layer with witch hazel or cooling packs. "Peri bottle with warm water while using the bathroom is key — and then always pat, don't wipe."
How often do you change your postpartum pads?
You should change your postpartum pad as often as you feel is necessary, depending on how full your pad is or how long you’ve been wearing it. In the first few days or week, that might be every hour or more. As time goes on, you may be able to go several hours or even through the night without changing your pad.
When should I switch from heavy-duty to thin pads?
"Everyone is different, but generally after the first week, you can change from extra heavy, hospital maternity pads to more 'normal' period-appropriate pads," shares Dr. Smith. "Then, around 2 to 4 weeks postpartum, most women will be able to change to a light pad or panty liner."
Are reusable postpartum pads safe?
"I would not recommend use of reusable pads in the first one to two weeks due to the higher infection risk in this period," stresses Dr. Smith. "After that time, if you choose to use them, I would ensure they are cleaned thoroughly with hot water and with fragrance-free detergent to prevent vulvar irritation."

I knew I’d feel uncomfortable in those first weeks postpartum, but I didn’t anticipate just how
long
that discomfort would last. Like many new moms, I experienced soreness, swelling, and bleeding for around six weeks after I gave birth — and I quickly learned my regular underwear was not suited for helping my recovery. So, following many friends’ advice, I invested in a few pairs of postpartum underwear to help me feel a little more supported while I healed.
When it comes to
all the stuff you buy to aid your recovery
, the best postpartum underwear is often overlooked. But it can really come in handy. Just take it from
Rebecca Amaru
, M.D., an OB/GYN practicing in New York City and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board. "It prevents you from ruining your own underwear when you are invariably bleeding heavily and unpredictably postpartum,” she says. “And, it’s more comfortable than most of the underwear you would typically wear at a time when your perineum is sore and you need to accommodate heavy absorption pads.”
How I Tested and Chose the Best Postpartum Underwear
To find the best postpartum underwear, I spoke to three OB/GYNs:
Rebecca Amaru, M.D.,
an OB/GYN practicing in New York City and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board;
Rebecca Levy-Gantt, D.O.
, an OB/GYN based in Napa, California; and
Jill Hechtman, M.D.
, an OB/GYN based in Tampa, Florida. I asked each of these experts about the most important features to look for in postpartum underwear based on the type of delivery a mom had, as well as the postpartum symptoms she might experience. Along with their insights, I referenced guidance on postpartum care from the
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
(ACOG).
Next, I consulted several moms on the What to Expect editorial team about their experiences trying different postpartum underwear brands.
I also canvassed the What to Expect Community message boards to learn about the postpartum underwear new moms in our community felt were most comfortable to wear and use. And since I’m a mom of two and former parenting editor who has
also
tried a number of postpartum underwear styles, I took my personal experience into account, too.
Based on all of this feedback, I reviewed and selected the best postpartum underwear based on the following criteria:
Comfort:
I chose products with not-too-tight waistbands to avoid unnecessary pressure, and prioritized those available in a variety of styles to suit different postpartum needs.
Material:
Breathable fabrics like cotton or microfiber, as well as stretchy materials, like nylon-spandex blends, are best. I also included some made with a light compression material that will give you a more sucked-in feeling (but not as much as shapewear), which some moms like for extra support postpartum.
Size:
I prioritized postpartum underwear that’s available in a wide range of sizes.
Extra features
: Details like silicone panels to help soothe C-section scars or a designated space to hold an ice pack were sought after to help hasten recovery.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

A Doctor's Note on Postpartum Bleeding
Let’s talk about something every new mom goes through but few are prepared for:
postpartum bleeding
, or lochia. Whether you had a vaginal birth or a C-section, your body will shed the extra tissue from pregnancy.
Bleeding is typically heaviest in the first week postpartum, or the first stage of lochia, before gradually lightening over time. During the second stage of lochia, you can expect pink or brown blood for roughly 12 days. In the final stage of lochia, you'll likely see spotting or a yellowish discharge for up to six weeks.
During this time, postpartum underwear is your first line of defense. These super-comfy panties are roomy enough to hold maxi pads or ice packs for soreness; you shouldn't use tampons or menstrual cups until your doctor gives you approval, as there is a heightened
risk of infection
during this time.
FAQs
What type of underwear is best after giving birth?
The best postpartum underwear for you will depend on personal preference. For instance, do you prefer a compression panel? How do you feel about the environmental impact of disposables?
It will also depend on how you gave birth. New moms who had a C-section usually prefer a higher waistband, for example.
From disposable underwear to underwear with built-in silicone pads to cover a cesarean incision, the best type of postpartum underwear will vary from person to person.
How many pairs should I buy for early postpartum?
This depends on a number of factors, including the type of postpartum underwear you’re thinking of getting. Many women find that they only need to use disposable underwear for the first week or so after giving birth, after which point they switch to regular underwear with a pad. So if you’re going the disposable route, you may find that you just need enough for a few weeks. (Assume you’ll be changing them often in the first few days.)
The quantity of non-disposables you need just depends on how frequently you want to do laundry. Even with a pad, it’s possible to experience leaks in the early days, so having a few more pairs than you think you need is always a good idea.
Are disposable underwear good for postpartum?
Immediately after delivery, you'll likely wear the disposable undies you're given in the hospital. In fact, docs often suggest stashing a bunch of these to take home, if you can.
If you prefer disposable mesh underwear, know that you can also buy more pairs to use at home in those first few weeks. Disposable postpartum underwear means less laundry, but it also means buying more packs.
Can I wear normal underwear after a C-section?
If you’re a C-section mom, you should avoid bikini briefs (or anything that hits low) for several weeks, since most people have a surgical incision right above where their pubic hairline starts. High-waisted underwear is usually what those who had a C-section opt for, as well as underwear that has some compression or support to hold you in. There are also some pairs of postpartum underwear that have a silicone band designed to go over your incision to help prevent it from getting irritated.
How long do you need to wear postpartum underwear?
This can vary a lot from mom to mom, but most women experience their heaviest
lochia
, or postpartum bleeding, for the first 10 days after giving birth. After that, lochia usually transitions into lighter bleeding or spotting for four to six weeks. Postpartum underwear will probably come in handy the most during these first few weeks and months. But many moms find postpartum undies to be especially comfortable and continue wearing them beyond that point (in fact, some of the pairs on this list have rave reviews for working as “regular” underwear, too).
What size postpartum underwear should I get?
When shopping for postpartum underwear, you may want to order a size larger than you normally would to accommodate your postpartum body and have room for pads, particularly if the underwear is a non-postpartum style. If you’re buying underwear specifically marketed for maternity or the postpartum period, it might be safe to go with your regular size — just check the brand’s sizing chart to be sure.
How many pairs should I buy for early postpartum?
Think of postpartum underwear like burp cloths — you’ll want more than you think. My advice is to have enough to keep on rotation without having to stress about doing laundry on the daily. I consider 6 to 10 pairs a general sweet spot, though it'll depend on your personal needs. As far as disposable underwear goes, make sure you have enough on hand for the first week.
What styles work best with maxi pads or ice packs?
High-waisted, full-coverage pairs of underwear are best. However, if you've had a C-section, be mindful of where the band sits on your incision.
How do I wash postpartum underwear safely?
It's always best to check with the brand's care instructions. In general, to keep your underwear clean and extend its lifespan, I recommend washing these on a gentle cycle with a mild detergent. Line dry when you can, otherwise, opt for low heat.

Once I hit my second trimester and my OB/GYN told me to start sleeping on my side, I knew my bedtime routine was about to change. As a lifelong back sleeper, I worried that this new position would keep me up all night. My OB/GYN, physical therapist, and a few wise mom friends suggested I get a pregnancy pillow. Not only would it encourage a
pregnancy-safe sleep position
, but it could also ease some of those oh-so-common pregnancy aches and pains by cushioning everything from my neck to my bump to my knees.
And let me tell you: They were right. My pregnancy pillow became one of my most-used sleep sidekicks.
How We Chose and Tested the Best Pregnancy Pillows
Finding the best pregnancy pillow isn’t a one-size-fits-all task — because no two pregnancies (or sleep needs) are exactly the same. To put together this guide, I combined hands-on testing with expert input and tons of feedback from real moms. Here’s how we narrowed it down to the 11 best:
I tested six different pregnancy pillows between my two pregnancies, sleeping with each one for at least two weeks. I evaluated their size, shape, firmness, and how well they relieved common pregnancy symptoms like hip pain, backaches, and
round ligament pain
. Because one pregnancy was in winter and the other in summer, I also paid attention to heat retention (hello, sweaty sleep).
I pulled insights from the
What to Expect Mom Must-Have Awards
, where more than 1,200 community members voted for their favorite pregnancy pillows. I looked at the top vote-getters, as well as voter feedback to identify standout picks for specific needs (like extra back support or cooling comfort).
I spoke to five What to Expect staffers and contributors who’ve tested many of these pillows across eight pregnancies. They shared what mattered most to them — from fill type and pillow shape to how easy it was to repurpose the pillow for postpartum support.
I
scoured What to Expect’s community forums and message boards to
which pillows moms truly loved — especially those that helped them sleep better through hip pain, growing bumps, or the dreaded third-trimester insomnia.
I consulted
Amy Wetter, M.D.
, a board-certified OB-GYN at Pediatrix Medical Group, and reviewed guidelines from the
American College of Obstetrics and Gynecologists
(ACOG) to better understand what makes a pregnancy pillow not just cozy — but supportive and safe, especially for specific symptoms like sciatica or pelvic pain.
Based on parent input, expert guidance, and research, e
very pillow we recommend:
Supports side sleeping
— the safest position for pregnancy
Eases pressure
on your back, hips, knees, and belly
Helps you fall asleep
faster and stay asleep longer (at least as much as possible with a baby-on-board bladder!)
Ashley Jones contributed to this article.

What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.

easily earned the MVP title. Both my OB/GYN and pelvic floor therapist recommended the C-shaped option, saying it would provide the ample, full-body support I needed to combat round ligament pain. And, to no surprise, they were right.
The secret is the extended C-shaped design: it wraps around your entire body, from back to belly, ensuring proper alignment to reduce strain on your achy back and hips. In the center, there’s a curved space that provides more room in the shoulder and hip areas to better cradle your belly.
And if you have a tiny bladder, like me, you’ll really appreciate the pillow’s C-shape. The lack of backing made it easy for me to roll out of bed and waddle my way to the bathroom. (If you need a laugh, ask a pregnant woman to climb over a U-shaped pillow to pee in time.)

Several other What to Expect moms agree with me, believing the unique fill allows the pillow to stay firm longer. In fact, one What to Expect mom said she’s used the pillow for four pregnancies.
Another potential downside is the size. Although my pillow, dog, husband, and I were able to fit comfortably in our king-sized bed, it probably wouldn’t work if we had a smaller bed—or if my toddler insisted on sleeping with us, too.

How to Pick a Pregnancy Pillow
For many What to Expect staff and community members, the best pregnancy pillow is the
Momcozy U-Shaped Pregnancy Pillow
. But depending on your needs and bed size, you might need a different pregnancy pillow. Some things to consider when looking for the best pregnancy pillow include:
Fill Material:
Most pregnancy pillow fillings are made from polyester and designed to hold their shape. However, just like a regular pillow, you may prefer a fill type that is more or less firm. Memory foam is firmer and may offer increased support, while down can be snuggled and squished against the body more easily.
Shape:
There are three common pregnancy pillow shapes: J-shaped, C-shaped or U-shaped, and the one you choose “may depend on how much support you need,” says Dr. Wetter. C-shaped pillows curve to tuck under your head and between your knees, while J-shaped pillows run parallel to your body with one curve that can either go under your head or between your knees. Or, if you often switch the side that you sleep on during the night (and expect to continue doing so, even as your bump makes it difficult), you might opt for a U-shaped pillow that you won’t have to readjust every time you move.
Size:
A pregnancy pillow won’t do you any good if it takes up too much room in bed. Fortunately, there are some pregnancy pillows with detachable extensions that allow you to customize the fit, as well as wedge pillows to use under your back for added support without taking up a ton of space.
FAQ
What type of pregnancy pillow is best?
There are three common types of pregnancy pillows: J-shaped, C-shaped or U-shaped, and the best type of pregnancy pillow “may depend on how much support you need,” says Dr. Wetter. For many moms-to-be, U-shaped pregnancy pillows are the best because they provides full-body support. With support on both sides and an opening at the bottom, it cradles your head, neck, back and belly.
On the other hand, C-shaped pillows curve to tuck under your head and between your knees, while J-shaped pillows run parallel to your body with one curve that can either go under your head or between your knees.
At what week should you start using a pregnancy pillow?
There's no set time that you should start using a pregnancy pillow. Some moms-to-be begin using one during the first trimester, while others are much further along. That said, most moms begin using a pregnancy pillow around halfway through pregnancy, when their expanding bellies begin making it more difficult to shift positions during the night.
What is the best pregnancy sleeping position?
Doctors typically recommend that a moms-to-be sleep on her side during pregnancy, and a pregnancy pillow can make that more comfortable. That said, if you find yourself waking up on your back, don't sweat it.
What are the different types of pregnancy pillows?
C-shaped: These pillows tuck under your head and between your knees.
J-shaped: Similar to C-shaped, but a little more streamlined.
U-shaped: U-shaped pillows have two panels that run parallel to your body, with one curve that can either go under your head or between your knees.
Wedge: A smaller pregnancy pillow that nestles under your belly to offer extra support.
Butterfly-shaped: A smaller pregnancy pillow that supports your back and belly at the same time.

By the time I waddled into my second trimester, my sweet little bump was making a big impression — especially on my
round ligaments
and
lower back
. That’s when my OB/GYN gently nudged me toward trying a pregnancy belly band, and let’s just say…game-changer.
If you're wondering what a belly band actually does, you're not alone. “Belly bands can help support the uterus and, if worn lower on the abdomen, can help pull the baby off the pelvis,” says
April Dunmyre, D.O.
, an orthopedist and assistant director at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital Womancare Associates in Pittsburgh. Translation? Less pressure, more comfort — especially in the second and third trimesters when every step can feel like a stretch.
Doctor’s Note: “Not only are pregnancy bands safe, but they are a wonderful tool to use in order to improve patient comfort,” says
Shannon Smith
, M.D., board-certified OB/GYN and What to Expect Medical Review Board member.
Unlike
pant extenders
(which help your jeans stay buttoned a little longer), belly bands are designed to wrap around your lower back and abdomen. Think of them as a gentle hug for your bump —
easing round ligament pain
, improving posture, and making it a little easier to stay on your feet all day.
How I Chose the Best Pregnancy Belly Bands
Finding the best belly band isn’t one-size-fits-all — and trust me, I tried. Here’s exactly how I narrowed down the most comfortable, supportive, and mom-approved picks:
I started with the research I did during my own pregnancy — comparing dozens of belly bands based on comfort, adjustability, materials, and effectiveness.
I spoke to three doctors to better understand how maternity bands work and the features you might want to look for when buying one. In addition to Dr. Dunmyre and Dr. Smith, I spoke to:
Jennifer Wu
, M.D., OB/GYN, and What to Expect Medical Review Board member
Katie Ruebush
, P.T., D.P.T., and What to Expect Medical Review Board member
These experts shared how belly bands can relieve round ligament pain, support the uterus, and even improve alignment.
I reviewed recommendations and guidelines from the
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
(ACOG) on how maternity support bands can help during pregnancy.
I spoke to four moms on the What to Expect staff who wore belly bands during their six pregnancies. They shared what symptoms they were trying to ease — and which bands actually helped.
I combed through What to Expect’s community forums and message boards for belly band reviews and recommendations, paying close attention to feedback on material, comfort, support, and pain relief.
Based on parent input, expert guidance, and research, every belly band on this list meets the following criteria:
Supportive:
Helps ease common aches like round ligament pain, lower back strain, and pelvic pressure
Comfortable:
Made with breathable, stretchy materials that move with you — not against you
User-friendly:
Easy to put on and take off (because struggling with Velcro at 30+ weeks isn’t the vibe)

Pregnancy belly bands are the most popular option, but some moms prefer to use
kinesiology tape
to gently lift and support their bumps. This method involves applying “K tape,” as it’s often called — flexible, water-resistant elastic bands — facing upward on your belly. (There are a number of tutorials on how to do this online, but always consult your practitioner for guidance.)
The benefit of using K tape instead of belly bands is that it offers endless adjustment options, it’s completely seamless under clothing and it’s blissfully lightweight (many moms-to-be note that K tape feels amazing in the summer, while even the most most minimalist belly bands can feel bulky and restricting under clothing on a hot day).
In a small 2017
study
, researchers applied K tape to pregnant women and found that low back pain decreased significantly compared to placebo. While K tape tends to be pretty similar from brand to brand, the researchers in that study used
Kinesio Taping Kinesiology Tape Tex Gold
on study participants.
But while kinesiology tape can help ensure a perfect fit, it’s definitely not as intuitive to use as belly bands and requires some trial and error to get the hang of. Some moms note that it can be a little painful to remove the tape, too. And while one box of tape is relatively affordable at $15, you’re likely to go through quite a lot of it, so it may become more expensive than a pregnancy belly band over time.

What to Look for in a Pregnancy Belly Band
Based on expert advice, as well my experience and feedback from moms in the What to Expect community, these are the most important features to consider when shopping for a pregnancy belly band:
Sizing:
Although some pregnancy belly bands are available in only one size, most come in sizes from small to extra large (and occasionally up to XXL). Look for maternity belts with a wide range of sizes or one-size bands with adjustable features to help ensure a comfortable fit. It’s also important to mention that many manufacturers recommend measuring yourself according to the brand’s size chart, as moms-to-be often aren’t their typical pre-pregnancy size when it comes to belly bands.
Material:
Ideally, you’ll want to look for a belly band that’s made of soft, easily adjustable fabric that can expand along with your growing bump. Make sure that the belt isn’t uncomfortable or too restrictive. “If you find them chafing or annoying, abandon them,” says Dr. Wu. And avoid awkward seams or tags that dig into already-sensitive skin!
Support:
Belly bands for pregnancy generally come in the same shape: a belt-shaped band of fabric that sits under your bump. Some also feature an additional strap that goes above your bump for extra support. Belly bands should be supportive enough to gently lift and cradle your bump without being overly tight or restricting. Dr. Smith prefers products that have Velcro straps. “[You can] adjust the tension to the level of support that feels adequate,” she says.
Care:
Because they’re often made from stretchy materials, most pregnancy belly bands need to be hand-washed, though some can go in the washing machine on a gentle cycle. It’s important to prioritize a comfortable, supportive fit over ease of care, but looking for a machine-washable band might be a top priority as well.
FAQs
When should I start wearing a pregnancy belly band?
Whether or not to use a pregnancy belly band is a personal decision, and there’s no right or wrong time to start. But most pregnant women choose to wear one once they develop round ligament pain. This symptom usually starts after week 14, so many women start considering belly bands during the second trimester when they’re looking for a little extra support and hoping to relieve these sharp, shooting pains.
Note that many pregnancy belly bands are eligible for reimbursement from health insurance companies and your FSA (Flexible Spending Account) or HSA (Health Savings Account).
How long can I wear a pregnancy belly band for?
In theory, you can wear most pregnancy belly bands 24/7. To be safe, however, doctors recommend removing the band every one to three hours for one hour to make sure you’re giving yourself a break. Some experts worry that overuse of belly bands might make your muscles too dependent on these support garments to function.
Some research
indicates that the pain-relieving benefits of belly bands apply only to pregnant women who wear the product regularly for short periods at a time. And a 2009 study from the
Journal of Clinical Nursing
found that support bands could potentially cause skin irritation and discomfort in some people.
To be safe, make sure the product you buy is supportive but doesn’t cut off circulation or restrict your movement. And if you have pelvic pain or back pain that worsens or isn’t improved by a pregnancy support belt, talk to your OB/GYN ASAP for help.
Are pregnancy belly bands safe during the third trimester?
Yes, belly bands can be worn throughout the entire pregnancy. If, however, your pelvic pain or back pain worsen, talk to your OB/GYN ASAP for help.
“Not only are pregnancy bands safe, but they are a wonderful tool to use in order to improve patient comfort,” says Dr. Smith.
To be on the safe side, some experts recommend removing the band every 1 to 3 hours for 1 hour. And look for a product that’s supportive but not too tight.
Do pregnancy belly bands work?
A small 2017 study in the
Journal of Clinical Nursing
found that women who wore pelvic belts for short periods of time had reduced pelvic girdle pain and could more easily do everyday tasks.
Pregnant women are most likely to feel round ligament pain when they change positions — for example, when sitting up and starting to walk or after engaging in physical activity, Dr. Dunmyre explains — so maternity belts can be especially helpful for on-the-go moms-to-be. Per the
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
(ACOG), pregnancy bands can also help make exercise more comfortable during the later stages of pregnancy. ACOG says that belly bands may also help support the back and prevent pregnancy-induced back pain.
Many pregnancy belly band manufacturers also claim that their products help prevent stretch marks. However, the
American Academy of Dermatology
(AAD) notes that many stretch mark prevention remedies don’t actually work. So be skeptical of these claims and remember that stretch marks are a normal, expected part of pregnancy — and nothing to be ashamed of!
Can I use a pregnancy belly band during postpartum recovery?
If your pregnancy belly band still feels comfortable on your stomach after you’ve given birth, there’s no reason why you can’t wear it for extra support. (If you’ve had a C-section, you’ll want to be mindful that it doesn’t irritate the incision area, however.)
Many moms also choose to invest in a
postpartum belly band
for this period. Like a pregnancy belly band, these products are meant to be worn around the waist to help support your body, but they tend to have a little more compression.
What’s the difference between under-belly vs over-belly bands?
In addition to where they’re placed on the belly, under-belly and over-belly maternity bands differ in the support they provide. Under-belly bands, which are typically wrapped around the hips, help to stabilize the hips, pelvis, and lower back. Over-the-bump bands provide extra, full-back support.
Can you exercise with a pregnancy support belt?
You can wear pregnancy belly bands when exercising, though you may want to look for a band designed to support you during your preferred workout.

I would have paid (almost!) anything for a pill to make me feel more like myself after childbirth. Although no magical postpartum pill exists, there are plenty of postnatal vitamins that promise to fortify your body with nutrients your diet may be missing after pregnancy. As a mom of four little ones, it feels like I’ve tried them all.
Yes, it’s technically possible to get all the essentials through a balanced diet rich in animal proteins, beans, and lentils. But
David Ilceski, M.D
., a board-certified OB/GYN at UnityPoint Health in Fort Dodge, says nothing beats the convenience of a postnatal vitamin — especially if you aren’t eating the most consistently balanced diet in the weeks following childbirth.
“I’m a fan of postnatals,” agrees new mom and dietitian
Jessica Cording, R.D
., also author of
The Little Book of Game-Changers
.
“Your nutritional needs are higher to support the healing process. There’s a lot of recovery that needs to happen.” And, if you’re breastfeeding, it’s crucial to do what you can to take care of things on the nutritional front for both you and your baby, points out
Christine Greves, M.D
., a board-certified OB/GYN at the Winnie Palmer Hospital for Women and Babies in Orlando, Florida.
While it’s just fine to finish up your
prenatal vitamins
, or return to vitamins you took pre-pregnancy, postnatals are designed to deliver specific nutrients new moms need to keep energy levels up and help ensure breast milk contains all the essential nutrients that exclusively breastfed newborns need.
How I Tested and Chose the Best Postnatal Vitamins
The best postnatal vitamin has to do it all: Provide the right nutrients (and the right amount of them) to support your body through the postpartum period, and be something you’ll willingly take daily. With so many options at the pharmacy, I narrowed down the eight best postnatal vitamins by:
Leaning heavily on my experience using postnatal vitamins after four pregnancies (I’m currently postpartum and using one of these supplements religiously, too.)
Consulting with Drs. Ilceski and Greves, as well as Cording and
Jill Purdie, M.D
., a board-certified OB/GYN in Atlanta, Georgia to learn what nutrients are needed in a good postnatal vitamin.
Reading through postnatal vitamin reviews in the What to Expect Community message board, paying close attention to ones that were recommended for their tolerability and cost.
Each vitamin that made the final list also needed to meet the following criteria:
Certified by governing bodies:
Since the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) doesn’t regulate supplements like postnatal vitamins, I only considered those that have been certified by the
National Sanitation Foundation (NSF)
and
United States Pharmacopeia (USP)
, indicating the vitamins are tested for quality and safety.
Easy to tolerate:
Pill size, flavor and aftertaste can impact your willingness to consume a postnatal vitamin, making these important factors.
Cause minimal side effects:
“Some people may tolerate certain vitamins better than others in regards to GI-related side effects, like nausea or constipation,” says Dr. Purdie.
Have a relatively affordable price tag:
Rarely are new parents flush with extra funds. To ensure your dollars are well-spent, we considered the cost per supplement serving.
A Doctor’s Note on Postnatal Vitamins
Doctors recommend keeping a few things in mind when it comes to taking a postnatal vitamin:
You don’t have to take one of these.
As we mentioned above, you can technically get all of your nutritional needs from your diet. But many new moms are busy, making good nutrition less of a priority during this time. A postnatal vitamin easily allows you to fill in those nutritional gaps.
You can finish up your prenatal vitamins.
Dr. Greves points out that you can technically take your prenatal vitamins in the postpartum period (I’ve done this, too). But these are designed for pregnancy, and you may not be filling all of your nutritional gaps as well if you take these supplements during the postpartum period.
Talk to your doctor if you’re unsure.
Many will recommend taking some kind of supplement during this period in your life, according to Dr. Greves. But they can help answer your questions about any individual needs you have, as well as suggest certain nutrients to focus on.

Essential Postnatal Vitamin Ingredients
When analyzing the ingredient label of postnatal vitamins, experts recommend looking out for the following.
Iron:
Iron is an essential nutrient that is an important component of hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that helps carry oxygen around your body. Blood loss and anemia (a condition where your body has lower-than-usual red blood cells) is common after childbirth, making it crucial to make sure you get enough iron, Dr. Greves says. Iron is also important for breastfeeding moms who don’t eat animal products to ensure their breast milk provides ample stores — especially after your period returns, since iron is lost through menstruation.
Vitamin D
:
This nutrient plays a lot of roles in the body, including supporting your immune system and brain health, according to the
National Institutes of Health (NIH)
. “It also may help with mood,” Dr. Greves says. One more thing to consider: Vitamin D helps your
body absorb calcium
, to promote strong bones and support your bone mineral density.
Choline:
Helpful for brain development, according
research
, choline is found in foods ranging from animal proteins to vegan favorites like nuts, seeds and beans. Because your body needs 550 milligrams daily while nursing, it’s best to pop a postnatal pill that fills in where food leaves off.
Omega-3 fatty acids
(DHA and EPA):
Supplementing with the docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) found in fish oil can help fortify your breastmilk with the healthy fats that support fetal brain development, according to a small
study
published in Current Research in Food Science. While some vegan formulas derive DHA from microalgae, others include fish oil.
Folic acid:
Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate, which
research
suggests supports cell accelerated growth during infancy. Breastfeeding women need 500 mcg (0.5mg) of folic acid daily to ensure there’s an ample amount in their breastmilk. That’s less than is needed during pregnancy, but more than a generic multivitamin typically provides.
Iodine:
Added to certain types of table salt, iodine is a trace mineral that supports both brain development and overall growth in breastfed infants, plus thyroid hormone production, according to the
NIH
. Nursing women need about 290 micrograms daily, with 150 micrograms of iodide, a form that’s easily absorbed, via supplementation.
Calcium:
Getting too little calcium could impact your own bone density, especially during a long breastfeeding journey:
Research
suggests lactating women lose up to 1000 mg of calcium a day to breastmilk. As such, the RDA for lactating women is 1,200mg/day, some of which you’ll find in certain postnatal supplements to pad a diet low in dairy.
And, if you don’t eat animal products,  you'll also need vitamins that are rich in:
Vitamin B12:
Found in animal products like meat, fish, eggs, poultry and dairy, plus fortified breakfast cereals and nutritional yeast, B12 can protect against the neurological delays that can result from this nutrient’s deficiency, according to a
review
in the Pan African Medical Journal.
Zinc:
Found in meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, legumes, seeds, and whole grains,
zinc
is a key nutrient for immune functioning as well as infant growth and weight gain. Because
research
shows that a nursing mother’s intake of zinc has no bearing on the zinc content of her milk, supplementing with the nutrient can help ward off low zinc levels to keep the immune system at the top of its game.
Freelance writer
Elizabeth Narins
originally contributed to this article.
FAQ
How long should you take postnatal vitamins?
Most doctors recommend taking postnatal vitamins for the first Six months postpartum right through your last breastfeeding session, says Dr. Ilceski.
What's the difference between prenatal and postnatal vitamins?
Because nutritional needs shift after pregnancy, postnatal vitamins look a bit different than prenatals. The biggest difference? “[Prenatal vitamins] have an increased amount of folic acid and iron necessary for fetal development, but typically exceed the requirements needed for postpartum mothers,” says Dr. Ilceski.
Postnatal vitamins designed to support lactating mothers usually contain iodine and choline, two nutrients you need more of when you’re nursing. So although many OB-GYNs do condone taking prenatal vitamins postpartum as a matter of practicality — and because there’s no great research that shows postnatal vitamins are superior to prenatal, according to Dr. Purdie — it’s best to choose and stick to a postnatal formula.
Are postnatal vitamins necessary?
Women who are vegetarian or vegan should take postnatal supplements with vitamin B12, since the nutrient is only found in animal-based foods, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Among nursing mothers,
maternal vitamin deficiencies
can impact quantities of both fat- and water-soluble vitamins in milk. In other words, if your diet comes up short on certain vitamins, your baby’s breastmilk will, too.
Are postnatal vitamins FSA-eligible?
Typically, only prenatal vitamins are FSA-eligible.
Do postnatal vitamins help with postpartum hair loss?
It’s a little complicated. Some
research
suggests that certain vitamins like biotin (which are often found in postnatal vitamins) may help with hair regrowth, but postpartum hair loss is different. Postpartum hair loss is typically due to the natural hormonal changes that happen after birth, and Dr. Greves says that vitamins will not change that. “However, postpartum vitamins could help with the replenishment of hair,” she says.
Are prenatal gummies, capsules, or powder better when breastfeeding?
One supplement form isn’t considered better than the other when it comes to breastfeeding, according to Cording. “Choose a supplement from a reputable brand,” she says. “But whatever form makes the most sense to you is best.” She suggests thinking about your lifestyle, as well as convenience, when choosing a type.

Your body needs a whole lot of nutrients when growing a baby. That’s where a daily prenatal vitamin comes in. Of course, no supplement can replace a balanced,
pregnancy-friendly diet
. But it's tough to meet the nutrient demands of pregnancy through food alone, and a supplement can help fill in any gaps, says
Nicole Rankins, M.D.
, an OB/GYN and site director of the OB Hospitalist Group in Norfolk, Virginia.
And no, your everyday multivitamin doesn’t quite cut it. “If comparing them side by side, you’d see that prenatal vitamins offer higher levels of many nutrients than a standard women’s multivitamin,” says
Olivia Small, R.D.N.
, a prenatal dietitian and certified lactation counselor at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. For example, prenatals typically contain more iron and folic acid — two must-haves to support pregnancy.
Editor’s Note:
Health experts, including the
U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
(CDC) and
American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
(ACOG), recommend that anyone who is pregnant or trying to conceive take at least 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid daily. Folic acid — the synthetic form of folate — is the only type of vitamin B9 proven in large studies to
reduce the risk of neural tube defects
, which affect the brain and spine early in pregnancy.
Some prenatal vitamins contain
folate instead of folic acid
. While folate is an important nutrient (typically found in dark leafy greens and other vegetables), it hasn’t been studied to prevent neural tube defects in the same way. For that reason, we’ve noted in the product reviews below any prenatal that does not contain folic acid, so you can discuss adding a separate folic acid supplement with your healthcare provider.
How I Chose the Best Prenatal Vitamins
The best prenatal vitamin should support your body (and your baby!) from the first trimester to the finish line. That’s why every prenatal vitamin on this list was selected based on nutrition guidelines set by the
ACOG
(which states you need folic acid, iron, vitamin D, choline, omega-3 fatty acids, B vitamins, and vitamin C). Here's what else I based my choices of off:
I spoke with experts, such as Small and Dr. Rankins, as well as a team of OB/GYNs:
Jill Purdie, M.D.
,
Christine Greves, M.D.
,
G. Thomas Ruiz, M.D.
,
Alexa Sassin, M.D.
, and
Meleen Chuang, M.D.
I had them break down what ACOG's list of important nutrients actually do — and why they matter (more on that below).
Additionally, per Small, all of the recommended prenatal vitamins have been certified by the
National Sanitation Foundation
(NSF) and
United States Pharmacopeia
(USP), which ensures they were tested for quality and safety.
I also included results from the
2024 What to Expect Mom Must-Have Awards
, where 200 community members voted on their favorites.
In addition to my own experience taking prenatal vitamins, I not only closely read online reviews of taste, smell, ease of swallowing, and side effects — and nixed any products that fellow moms couldn't stomach, because the best prenatal vitamin doesn't count if you can't swallow it — but asked What to Expect editors on staff what they used during their own pregnancies.
For additional insights, I also referenced standards set by the
CDC
, the

And remember: While the list below represents what we believe to be the best over-the-counter prenatal vitamins available,
always talk to your healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing your supplements

Ingredients to Look for in Prenatal Vitamins
Folic acid
(400 to 600 mcg): One of the B vitamins that's crucial to the formation of the neural tube, which becomes your baby's brain and spine. It's the only form of folate proven to reduce the risk of
neutral tube defects
(NTDs), according to the CDC.
Vitamin A
(750 to 770 mcg): "Vitamin A plays a role in the formation of the fetal eyes, ears, limbs, and heart," says Dr. Purdie.
Vitamin C
(80 to 85 mg) and
E
(15 mg): "These two play an important role in fetal collagen production and supporting the mother's immune system," says Dr. Purdie. Large doses of vitamin C a day (over 2,000 mg)
can cause symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting
, so don't take additional supplements outside of what's in your prenatal without consulting your doctor.
Vitamin D
(15 mcg or 600 IU): Vitamin D is important in developing fetal bones, as well as aiding maternal bone health. "There are also emerging studies that suggest it aids in immunity and improves mood for the mother," says Dr. Purdie. If your doctor suspects you may not be getting enough Vitamin D, she may recommend an extra supplement.
Calcium
(1,000 to 1,300 mg): All women ages 19 to 50
need at least
1,000 mg per day
of this crucial nutrient, which, in the case of pregnant women, helps build baby's bones and teeth.
Iron
(27 mg): During pregnancy, the amount of iron you need in a day greatly increases. This is because your body
needs more iron in order to make more blood to supply oxygen to your baby
. "Iron requirements in pregnancy increase, so supplementation is necessary to maintain adequate blood cell production," says Dr. Purdie. If, like many women, you become
anemic during pregnancy,
your doctor may recommend an iron supplement or a different prenatal vitamin with more iron.
Zinc
(11 to 12 mg): This mineral supports your immune system and healthy cell division.
DHA
: Regular prenatal vitamins may not contain DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid found in many types of fish that
aid in baby's brain development
, both before and after birth. If you're unable to get the recommended two to three servings (8 to 12 ounces) of
pregnancy-safe fatty fish
per week, ask your doctor if you should take a supplement.
Other nutrients
: You might also see several other additions on the label, such as copper,
choline
, thiamin, vitamin B12, magnesium, and ginger or vitamin B6 (both may help with morning sickness).
Thiamine
: Aka thiamin or vitamin B1, thiamine is important for the development of the baby's nervous system, Dr. Chuang says.
Vitamin B12 and B6
: Necessary for producing red blood cells, as well as the development of baby’s brain and nervous system, along with the placenta, Dr. Chuang says. "This is more of a common deficiency that's discussed," Dr. Greves says. "We check it in people who have less energy and bowel problems." B6 also aids in the metabolism of protein and may help with nausea. It should also give you an energy boost.
Magnesium
: Supports healthy muscle and nerve function, Dr. Chuang says. It also helps to regulate blood sugar levels. "Sometimes we recommend that women with migraines take magnesium to help prevent them," Dr. Greves says.
Probiotics
: "Probiotics can help support a healthy gut microbiome, which is beneficial for both the mother and baby's digestive health," Dr. Chuang says.
Choline
: Helpful in the fetus's brain development and preventing some birth defects, according to
research
, experts recommend 450 mg per day while pregnant.
FAQs
Why do I need to take a prenatal vitamin during pregnancy?
Health experts recommend taking prenatal vitamins before and during pregnancy because they help the body meet the increased need for certain nutrients to support a growing fetus. Prenatal vitamins also help fill in nutritional gaps, especially in those who are having trouble eating well due to pregnancy nausea and food aversions.
When should I start taking prenatal vitamins?
Start taking prenatal vitamins three months before you hope to conceive, suggests Dr. Rankins. Taking supplemental folic acid — a key component of good prenatal vitamins — before you get pregnant
can reduce the risk of neural tube defects
, which affect the brain and spine.
But if you didn't start taking prenatals until you learned that you're pregnant, don't beat yourself up. "Just take them as soon as possible," says Dr. Rankins.
Just like you can take prenatals before pregnancy, you can also take them after delivery. Prenatal vitamins can actually help fill gaps in your diet and provide essential nutrients when you're breastfeeding, says Dr. Greves. You can talk to your healthcare provider about continuing to take a prenatal after you give birth to see what is best for you and for how long you should take it.
When is the best time to take prenatal vitamins?
Ultimately, the best time to take a prenatal vitamin is whenever you will remember to take it (though experts recommend you take it with food). So if your mornings are particularly hectic, you may want to wait until nighttime to take your prenatal. If you’re experiencing nausea during your pregnancy, you’ll also want to factor in the time of day when you’re the least queasy.
Are there any side effects to prenatal vitamins?
Prenatal vitamins can cause mild side effects, including:
Constipation
: "The pregnancy hormone progesterone can cause
constipation
, and then if you add an iron supplement, it can be tough," says Dr. Rankins. Drink plenty of water and make sure you're getting enough fiber in your diet. You can also ask your doctor about a stool softener to help keep things moving.
Nausea and vomiting
: Iron can also make people feel queasy. To combat this, Dr. Rankins suggests taking prenatals with "easily digestible" foods such as crackers or applesauce. You may also need to take your vitamin at bedtime, switch brands or even experiment with different formulas to help relieve these symptoms.
Bright yellow urine
: Large doses of B vitamins, like riboflavin, may give your urine a more colorful hue that's typically harmless, but always check with your doctor if you're concerned.
If you struggle with side effects, ask your doctor about prescription prenatal vitamins. "Both prescription and over-the-counter vitamins will have all the necessary nutrients, however, the formulation may be different — the prescription vitamin may have iron that causes less constipation, or it may include a stool softener to help with constipation or vitamin B6 to help with nausea," says Dr. Purdie.
What is the most effective prenatal vitamin?
The most effective prenatal vitamin is one that will help meet the needs of you and your baby. However, we like the Nature Made Prenatal Multivitamin Folic Acid + DHA for its large spectrum of nutrients, gentle formulation and affordable price tag.
What is the most recommended pregnancy supplement?
Recommendations for pregnancy supplements can vary based on your needs. To find the right pregnancy supplement for you, it’s best to check in with your doctor. They should be able to assess your needs and make recommendations on key ingredients to look for in a supplement.

Of all the bothersome side effects that can happen during pregnancy, I was not expecting to deal with
itchy skin
. At best, my itchy pregnancy skin was annoying or distracting, at worst, it kept me awake all night long. It was an exercise in extreme patience as I tried — and often failed — to find relief from lotions, creams and other topical anti-itch treatments. (It didn’t help that some skincare products and even clothing can make this worse.) Thankfully, by the time I got pregnant for the second time, I had a solid anti-itch routine that kept my skin hydrated and moisturized from the start.
But to find the best treatment for
dry, itchy  skin during pregnancy
, it helps to understand why it happens. Essentially, changes in hormone levels, your immune system and the environment can sap the skin of its natural oils, leading to dryness and compromising your skin’s natural barrier, aggravating your already-stretched skin and nerve endings.
How I Chose the Best Products for Itchy Pregnancy Skin
To determine the most effective products for relieving itchy skin during pregnancy, I recalled more than 50 different lotions, creams, oils, washes and even humidifiers. I then spoke to
George Z. Han, M.D., Ph.D.,
a board-certified dermatologist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York, and researched recommendation from the
American Academy of Dermatology
(AAD) and the
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
(ACOG) on effective ways to treat itchy pregnancy skin.
Based on this guidance, I eliminated any products containing steroids, retinol and salicylic acid, as these can potentially be harmful to pregnant women. I avoided products containing fragrances and harsh chemicals like sulfates and parabens, as these tend to aggravate skin rather than retain moisture. I then
prioritized products that contain natural moisturizers, such as oats, shea butter, coconut oil, avocado oil or aloe, as well as ceramides
, which are lipids that restore the skin’s barrier.
But even if a product checks all the ingredient boxes, it also has to work. So I turned to the What to Expect staff and community to learn what other moms recommend to deal with itchy pregnancy skin.
Ready to scratch the itch (figuratively, of course)? Here are a few soothing and moisturizing products that are safe to use during pregnancy.
Why Trust Us?
What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. Our product recommendations are based on expert parent insight, advice from medical professionals and feedback from the millions of parents and parents-to-be in our community. Our editors adhere to the highest research and reporting standards and our team of vetted OB/GYNs, pediatricians and other health professionals ensure our recommended products are safe and effective for you and your baby.
