The Gadget That Saved My Sanity as a Busy Mom of Two
by
Stephanie Shore Fisher
| February 27, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Skylight
The Skylight Calendar promises a centralized system that keeps you organized. But does it deliver?
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
I found the
Skylight
the way many overwhelmed parents do: strategically served Instagram ads.
The mental load of parenting is no joke, and it’s become heavier as my kids have gotten older. Appointments. School schedules. Playdates. Meals. Errands. Plus, as a neurodivergent household, managing everyday tasks does not come easily to any of us. But, like most moms, I became the default keeper of all the information, and it was not sustainable. I needed help, and the Skylight seemed to offer that.
I tried cheaper solutions first. I streamed a calendar app to our smart TV, wrote out lists for everyone, and looked into an Echo Show. But I needed one place where scheduling, tasks, and meals could live together and be visible to everyone in the house.
The Skylight promised a centralized, visual system that did not rely on me remembering to check my phone. That’s what sold me.
Quick Summary
What it is:
The Skylight Calendar (15-inch touchscreen)
Who it’s for:
Busy families, multi-caregiver households, neurodivergent families
Why I love it:
It’s expensive, but the easy-to-use interface genuinely reduces mental load and keeps everyone organized
Price:
$149.99 to $599.99 (depending on size)
Where to buy:
Skylight
,
Amazon
,
Target
Exclusive promo:
Use code WTE20 for $20 off the 15-inch calendar from now through 3/9 at
Skylight
What It’s Like Using the Skylight Calendar
Part of Skylight’s appeal is its easy-to-use design. A large display screen and clearly labeled tabs make toggling between tasks simple — so much so, even younger family members can get in on the action. I, however, prefer to use the accompanying app so I can add and edit things on the go.
Pro tip: Put your Skylight in a highly trafficked area so no one misses out — ours lives on the kitchen wall, where the family frequently hangs.
On top of the intuitive display, Skylight has several features that add to its appeal.
Calendar and Scheduling
Leah Rocketto
Rather than being another calendar to maintain,  Skylight syncs with existing Google, Apple, and other major calendar platforms. This means everyone’s individual calendars come together in one place for easier scheduling. Plus, each family member has a color-coded profile, so it's clear who is busy and when.
Tasks and Routines
The Tasks feature was the real game-changer for our family.
Using the same color-coded system, you can designate one-time or recurring “chores” to a person. (You can even assign them a time of day to help develop routines.) Sounds simple, but some elements make it more appealing than a written checklist, especially for kids.
Leah Rocketto
To start, parents can award a star value to tasks and corresponding rewards. Skylight tracks the number of stars so kids know when they can cash them in. Additionally, tasks can be labeled with large emojis, so children who aren’t reading yet still have some autonomy over their to-do list. This has also taken a lot of pressure off me to manage everything verbally.
My 3-year-old is noticeably more motivated to complete her routine now that she can check them off herself and watch the celebration animation at the end when everything is complete.
Meal Planning
Meals appear directly on the calendar with their own label and color. I no longer have to remember what we planned or open another app to check.
Recipes can be attached to meals, and ingredients can be added to a grocery list if you want everything in one place.
Worth Noting
One downside of Skylight is having to toggle between the calendar and tasks tab. Since only one can be displayed, we sometimes miss tasks if the calendar is front and center.
Another minor annoyance: Tasks with due dates only appear on the day they are due, which can be limiting for things that require advance prep. Skylight releases frequent updates and is responsive to user feedback, so these feel like solvable issues rather than dealbreakers.
Skylight Calendar
$20 off w/code WTE20

See More
Is the Premium Subscription Worth It?
The Skylight works great without a subscription, providing you with calendar functionality and a streamlined version of the task feature. But the paid Calendar Plus plan unlocks its best features, like reward charts, meal planning, and photo albums.
The $79/year subscription also gives you access to Sidekick, which uses AI to turn emails, PDFs, photos, and voice notes into calendar events or task lists. I forward daycare emails, upload school supply lists, and dictate packing lists, and everything appears automatically on the screen.
For me, the subscription is worth it for Sidekick alone.
Is the Skylight Calendar Worth It?
The Skylight Calendar is an investment, but it’s one I would make again. It’s taken a significant amount of mental load off my plate, making household responsibilities visible to everyone. Our home feels calmer, and I no longer feel solely responsible for remembering everything.
If shared calendars and basic to-do lists work for your family, this may be more than you need. But if you are juggling too much information across too many places and need a centralized family command center, the Skylight Calendar is worth considering, especially with the limited-time

off the 15-inch model from now through 3/9 at

The first thing I noticed about the new
Hatch Baby
is the design. The original Hatch Rest is perfectly functional, but it definitely looks like baby gear. The new version, especially in the Putty color I chose, looks more like a tiny sculptural lamp.
It’s rounder, softer, and genuinely cuter than its more gadget-like predecessor, with the charming ability to blend in as nursery decor. Hatch also offers the device in Mint, Peach, and Greige, which makes it easier to match different nursery styles. If you, like me, care about how baby gear looks in your home, this upgrade alone is noticeable.
While the original Hatch Rest looks like baby gear, the Hatch Baby (above) looks like a tiny sculptural lamp.
Elizabeth Buxton
Hatch Baby vs. Hatch Rest: What’s Different
We’ve used the original Hatch Rest in Lou’s room since day one, so I noticed a few differences immediately when I swapped in the new model.
The design is a major upgrade:
The new version looks more like a modern nursery lamp than a sound machine, with softer curves and a more elevated finish.
The sound quality feels fuller:
White noise is the feature we use most, and the updated speaker sounds noticeably richer. The original worked well, but the new version makes the white noise feel deeper and less tinny.
The top button is easier to use:
A large “Big Button” on top lets you start baby’s routine or adjust volume with a quick tap. The original model used a flat ring that could be surprisingly finicky, so this update is much easier to use during middle-of-the-night wakeups.
6 months of Hatch+ sleep support is included:
The new Hatch Baby comes with six months of Hatch+, which unlocks predictive sleep schedules, milestone-based sleep guides, a library of premium stories and songs, and even a 1:1 chat with certified sleep consultants. The original Hatch Rest includes basic sounds and lights, but accessing the full content library requires a paid Hatch+ subscription.
A 30-night nursery trial:
Hatch is also offering a 30-night nursery trial, so you can test the sound machine in your baby’s room and return it within 30 days if it’s not the right fit.
The Hatch Rest (left) has a duller light than the Hatch Baby (right).
Elizabeth Buxton
The Hatch Baby Features We Already Loved
Importantly, the new model keeps the things that made the original Hatch Rest so useful in the first place.
You still get:
Continuous white noise
that runs all night (we’ve used this since Lou was a newborn)
A customizable nightlight
that’s soft enough for middle-of-the-night feedings and diaper changes
App-controlled routines and schedules
so you can adjust sound and light without walking into the room
Those core features are exactly why the Hatch Rest has stayed part of Lou’s bedtime routine for nearly two years.
Why Pink Noise and Other Sound Options Matter
White noise has long been a nursery staple, though lately it’s become a trending debate among parents and sleep experts about volume levels and long-term reliance. One thing I’ve always appreciated about Hatch is that it offers more than just traditional white noise. The original Hatch Rest includes brown noise and gentle nature sounds like ocean waves, while the new Hatch Baby adds pink noise, a softer, more balanced frequency often compared to steady rainfall. We’ve always kept the ocean setting running through the night, and it now signals bedtime almost instantly.
How the Price Compares
The new
Hatch Baby
is priced at
$99.99
, while the original Hatch Rest is still available through some retailers, like
Amazon, for around
$69.99
. The new version also includes six months of Hatch+ sleep support, which adds guided sleep tools and extra content compared with the original device.
Hatch has stopped selling the legacy Rest on its own website, replacing it with the new Hatch Baby model, though the original device can still be found through third-party retailers.
The Verdict
Bottom line:
Hatch Baby is a worthy upgrade to the Hatch Rest, with a softer sound profile, pink noise, and a design that looks much nicer in a nursery.
After a few nights of testing the new
Hatch Baby
in Lou’s room, I’m convinced it’s a worthy successor to the original Hatch Rest we’ve relied on since she was a newborn. It keeps everything we loved about the original, but looks nicer on the dresser and adds a few thoughtful upgrades.
Lou seems perfectly happy with the switch, which is about the best product review you can get from a toddler. And when baby #2 arrives in June, the new Hatch Baby will already be warmed up and ready to take over nursery duty from day one.

My Whole Family Slept in the Same Room Without Fighting: This Viral "Blackout Pod" Saved Our Vacation
by
Leah Rocketto
| April 16, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Leah Rocketto
Our first attempt at room-sharing was a disaster until we tried this viral sleep tent.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
Our first experience sharing a room as a family was a disaster. Olivia was four months old and technically a great sleeper, the kind of baby you have to wake to eat, so we assumed vacation sleep would be easy. It wasn’t. Every time we crept into the room, we woke her. A creaky floorboard or a flash of phone light was enough to set her off. And once she was back asleep, the problem flipped. Olivia is an “active sleeper,” so her midnight grunts and whimpers kept my husband up all night. By the second night, we were all exhausted and snapping at each other. I wasn’t looking forward to future trips, I was questioning them entirely.
Right on cue, my feed started serving me ads for the
SlumberPod
, a blackout “sleep tent” that mom influencers swear by. To me, it looked like a glorified tent, and I had questions. Would I hear her if she cried? Would it get too hot? Was this going to be a nightmare to set up?
Leah Rocketto
After nearly four years of using it, I can confidently say: yes, no, and only the first time.
I brought it on a trip to Vermont, still skeptical. The first night, I tiptoed around like usual. The second night, we stopped trying. We put Olivia down, left the lights on, and watched a movie at a normal volume. She didn’t stir. She was in her own dark, quiet bubble while we were three feet away, finally relaxing. We used the built-in monitor pouch to keep an eye on her, but the pod blocked just enough light and sound that my husband actually slept through her usual nighttime noises.
The real test came the next morning. The room was flooded with early sunlight, the kind that usually guarantees a 5 a.m. wake-up. I crawled inside the pod and had my husband zip it up. Total darkness. Even with the open bottom, it blocked nearly all the light.
Leah Rocketto
As for safety, it’s designed with airflow in mind. The fabric is breathable, and there’s a ventilation panel plus pockets for a small fan if you need it. I was worried about that going in, but it ended up being a non-issue.
The biggest drawback is setup. It’s not hard, but you do need space to bend the long poles into place. Do a test run at home and set it up as soon as you arrive; doing it while sleep-deprived is not the move. It’s also not cheap, usually around $180 to $200. But compared to booking a larger room or dealing with another trip like that first one, it paid for itself quickly.
Family vacations are rarely stress-free, but losing sleep doesn’t have to be part of it. The
SlumberPod
didn’t just help Olivia sleep, it gave us our evenings back.

The $6 ‘Instant’ Blackout Hack That Actually Keeps a Nursery Dark
by
Sarah Darby
| April 8, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Sarah Darby
Bright sunshine was waking my baby before dawn, so I tried a $6 DIY solution.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
After I stumbled into my crying baby’s room and blinked at the too-bright rays, I knew we had a problem. The summer sunlight was waking up my three-month-old at the actual crack of dawn, and I was over it messing up her sleep routine. But like most people, I didn’t have $100 to drop on premium blackout blinds or curtains. As I tried to rock my very awake baby back to sleep, I searched for dupes and found the perfect solution: $6 paper shades.
Sarah Darby
Available at Walmart,
RediShade blinds
are the perfect dupe to pricey blackout curtains. At $5.47 each, they can be cut to the exact size of your window using a box cutter. Plus, they have double-sided adhesive for quick installation. Want proof? I had these both cut and installed in less than 15 minutes.
But do RediShade blinds work as well as blackout curtains? As soon as I got the paper shades installed, I shut off the lights. To my relief, the room was pitch black. And it was almost time for the real test: nap time. My baby, who was firmly stuck on 32 minute naps, slept for over an hour! And the next day? She slept until almost 7 a.m.! I was officially sold.
Sarah Darby
For a paper product, these blinds are remarkably high-quality: a thick, strong, nearly indestructible material. (They haven’t torn even once since installation, despite opening and closing the window frequently and pulling the blinds up most mornings.) Nearly two years later, these are still on my now-toddler’s windows and they continue to do a fantastic job keeping the light out so she can sleep soundly during naps and bright early early mornings.
The only issue I had with these shades is that they don’t stay up when you actually want to let in some light. I solved this issue by placing
Velcro squares
on the bottom of the blinds and the window frame.
RediShade Blinds
Your New Nursery Dupe
$5.47
See More
See More
As a mom of two, I’ve bought a lot of stuff for my kids, but I have found very few life-changing products that cost this little money. I did get fancy blackout blinds for my first baby and in hindsight, I wish I had known that these RediShade paper blinds existed! Now, I tell all of my friends they should skip the pricey blackout curtains – and you should too.

The $7 Nursery Hack That Actually Shortened My Baby's Night Wakes and Saved My Sleep
by
Sarah Darby
| April 17, 2026
Latest update:
See more
Amazon / Sarah Darby
You don’t need a fancy color-changing lamp to protect your baby’s melatonin.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
As a sleep-deprived first time mom, I was willing to try anything to get a few more hours of rest. Expensive sleep courses? Sign me up. Wake windows? You know I followed them. Monitoring sleepy cues like a spy? Just call me James Bond. But I still couldn’t figure out why my baby was wide awake for hours in the middle of the night.
Determined to fix this, I embarked on a mini research project. Nearly all of the recommendations for handling middle of the night wakings included keeping the room dark and quiet to avoid waking your baby up more. I did my best, but I needed some form of light to change his diaper or nurse him without crashing into furniture.
Much to my delight, the online sleep experts had a solution: Red light, which is apparently less jarring to your eyes and internal clock than white lights. I wasn’t fully sold on the science of this, but I figured it couldn’t hurt to try.
I didn’t want to spend $50-plus on an actual red or color-changing light before knowing it would work, so I swapped my actual nursery light bulb for a
$7 red light bulb
I found on Amazon. My personal science experiment had begun – would this cancel our unplanned and undesirable middle of the night parties?
Sarah Darby
The first time my baby woke up overnight, I headed in and turned on the red light, eager to see if it would work. There was an instant difference. Usually my baby would be blinking from the bright light, and I too would feel jolted out of my slumber. The red light was warm and comforting, and I could feel both of us staying more calm. After we settled in the rocking chair, my baby drifted back to sleep fairly quickly. Better yet, I was able to fall right back to sleep after putting him back in his crib.
From that night on, our red light bulb stayed and our overnights got so much better. Of course, there were still some times when my baby would decide to party at 2 a.m., but I do feel like the red light dramatically decreased the frequency of these long wakes. Perhaps most important was how this red light kept me in a calm and peaceful state while I comforted my baby.
Sarah Darby
Now my kids are two and four, and we still utilize the red light. I never actually bought an official red light; rather I moved the bulb to my second child’s room when she was a baby. Even though they both sleep through the night (most nights), I turn on the red light to read books. The cozy glow has become a staple in our bedtime routine and I have no plans to ditch it anytime soon.

Like many first-time parents expecting a baby, I agonized over the decision of which stroller to buy. After all, finding the best stroller isn’t all that different from buying a new car. I found myself asking some of the same questions: How good is the suspension? What kind of terrain can it handle? What kind of storage does it have? With so many models available, choosing a stroller can feel as weighty as buying a car.
But shopping for strollers is also highly personal. Identifying the best stroller means considering your family’s lifestyle, taking into account how often you’ll be using it, where you’ll be using it and whether you’ll need it to grow with your family. That was something I didn’t consider enough when I was expecting my first son: At the time, I wanted an easy-use,
travel-friendly model
I could easily stash in a closet in my small apartment. While I loved the stroller I chose, two years later — pregnant with my second and parenting a toddler who was still too little to walk long distances — I found myself needing to shop for a
double stroller
, too.
Whether you need a sleek city stroller or a model that can fit up to three kids, read on for our complete guide to the best strollers on the market right now.
How I Chose the Best Strollers
In the end, the best stroller to buy is the one that safely gets your baby from point A to point B and works with your family’s lifestyle. (An umbrella stroller won’t exactly cut it for a family of three-under-3, for instance.) In order to help narrow down your choices, I first referenced stroller guidelines from the
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission
(CPSC) and the
American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP). Although every stroller on the market needs to adhere to the CPSC’s safety standards, there are some features that may add an extra level of security, according to the AAP. They recommend strollers:
Have easy-to-operate brakes that lock two wheels instead of just one
A wide base that can’t easily be tipped over
A five-point harness with straps over both shoulders, hips and between the legs
One footrest that extends across both sitting areas (for a side-by-side double stroller).
To ensure that we were featuring the absolute safest and best strollers on the market, I eliminated any that didn’t have these features.
Next, I spoke to three parents on the What to Expect editorial team who have tested and reviewed dozens of top-rated strollers. I asked about the stroller brands and models they’ve tested, features they liked (and disliked) and whether they’d recommend the stroller to other parents.
After that, I turned to our What to Expect community: I pored through countless community reviews to learn more about the strollers parents are loving right now. Finally, I analyzed results from the
2024 What to Expect Mom Must-Have Awards
, in which more than 770 parents in the What to Expect community voted for their favorite strollers and shared detailed feedback.
Based on this research, I identified the 12 best strollers as those that are easy to maneuver, versatile, built to last, and thoughtfully designed with ample storage space.

For parents on the go, you can’t beat the flexibility and convenience of the
Doona
, which is actually a hybrid car seat and stroller that weighs just 16.5 pounds.
Simply click a button, and the Doona goes from a stroller to a car seat. The wheels fold in for car rides, then fold back out again to stroll. Use it on planes, trains and automobiles — this system works no matter where the wind takes you.
Don’t expect it to perform quite as well as dedicated strollers, though. The wheels won’t take bumps quite as easily. So while it can be an incredibly convenient option, some parents dislike how short a lifespan it has, especially considering that for the price ($550) you could also buy a full-size stroller that would last for a number of years.

Why We Love It
If staying active with your little one is part of your post-baby game plan, the
Thule Urban Glide 3
just might be your new favorite running buddy. This high-performance jogging stroller glides like a dream — thanks to its rear suspension and air-filled tires — and looks sleek and sporty without feeling bulky. Whether you’re strolling sun-dappled sidewalks or jogging bumpy trails, this stroller keeps the ride smooth for both you and your tiny copilot.
What to Expect Community member and contributing creator Gabriella Barrera has been putting the Urban Glide 3 through its paces with her 14-month-old son, Louie. “I can push this stroller with just the tips of my fingers, even on bumpy terrain,” she says. “Louie always falls asleep during walks or runs, and I’ve been able to keep him comfortably in the stroller for much longer stretches of time.”
Her favorite features? The generously sized canopy (a must for mid-jog naps and shielding that sweet face from the Texas sun), the built-in hand brake for extra control, and the zippered undercarriage storage that actually fits more than just a diaper and a dream. The suspension is ultra-smooth, and the wheels pop off easily for storage. One note: While the fold isn’t exactly one-handed as advertised, Gabriella says the thoughtful design more than makes up for the extra step.
Any downsides? The price tag might give you pause — it’s definitely a splurge. And for a stroller in this higher range, Gabriella notes a couple of surprising misses: “There’s no cup holder, which feels like a big oversight for something built for movement. And no snack tray for Louie is kind of a bummer.”
Still, she says the performance and thoughtful design justify the investment: “Compared to my previous jogging stroller, this one feels like a major upgrade. It makes me feel more confident running on different terrain — which is probably more fun for Louie, too.”

The
Baby Jogger City Select 2 Double Stroller
is a popular choice among parents of multiples in the What to Expect community. This is a convertible double stroller, meaning it can be used as a single stroller initially then changed to a double by adding a second seat. You can also use the
City Select 2
with two seats and a back glider board, allowing you to push three children at once. (Just note that the
second seat
and
glider board
are sold separately, so if you intend to use this as a double stroller from day one, make sure to purchase the second seat, too.)
Reviewers appreciate how compatible this stroller is with a variety of car seats — an especially helpful feature for parents of multiples who drive often. It can be much easier to attach a car seat into a stroller as a travel system than unclip and re-clip two babies every time you make a stop. Baby Jogger, Britax, Chicco, Cybex, Graco, Maxi-Cosi, Nuna, Peg Perego and UPPAbaby infant car seats all work in this stroller (you’ll have to purchase adapters separately, however). And because it’s narrower than most side-by-side double strollers (and many convertible doubles, too), you’ll likely find it easier to maneuver in tight spaces, making it an equally good choice for families who live in cities.
Other nice features include reclining seats, a UV 50+ canopy with a peekaboo window (helpful to easily check on baby when she’s forward-facing), a telescoping handlebar and one-handed fold.

Why We Love It
Most strollers designed for multiples have just two infant or toddler seats with an optional rider board for an older child. But families with triplets or three under 5 have a much harder time finding a stroller that can fit their whole brood. One of the few options on the market that can accommodate larger families is the
Zoe The Triov2
, the updated version of the brand’s Trio+. (If you have four kids, the brand also has its
Tribe+ stroller
that starts as a quad and can be downsized to a double.)
The Triov2 would be an excellent stroller regardless of how many children it could seat. Although it’s not designed for newborns, it reclines 140 degrees (in twin mode) or 120 degrees (with the third add-on seat) and is safe for babies 3 months and older who have good head control. Strollers that accommodate multiple children are often on the bulky side, but this one manages to be as sleek as possible: It has a lightweight aluminum frame, a slim profile and can fold up easily. If you have twins and a toddler, you’ll also appreciate that it can convert down to a double when your older child outgrows the stroller years.
There are also a number of nice-to-have features included, such as a parent cup holder, two child cup holders, a snack cup and adjustable footrest (notable, since those are often add-ons you pay extra for with other strollers). Many families also appreciate that it’s
approved for use in Disney
.
More kids typically means less maneuverability, so it’s not very surprising that The Triov2 isn’t the easiest to push on tough terrain. But on pavement, parents say it works well. And you can’t beat the price and design for larger families.

Why We Love It
Once your toddler is toddling more than strolling, your stroller needs shift. You might no longer need a newborn bassinet or a full-on travel system — and you may not want to haul around a giant set of wheels for quick outings or airport adventures. What you
do
want? A compact stroller that folds like a dream, fits just about anywhere, and still has space for your little explorer’s must-haves (snacks, stuffies, and a sippy cup or two). Enter: the
Bugaboo Butterfly
.
The Butterfly is beloved by parents for its super simple one-second fold (yes, really), light weight (a smidge over 16 pounds), and carry-on-compatible size when folded. It’s easy to store in a closet, car trunk or even an airplane overhead bin — and just as easy to maneuver through tight spaces or busy sidewalks. Bonus: The roomy underseat basket fits all the essentials (and then some).
What to Expect staffer Steph Fisher put the Butterfly to the test during family trips — including a whirlwind week at Disney World. It quickly became her favorite travel companion. “It handles surprisingly well on uneven terrain for a travel stroller,” she says. “The fold and unfold was key — we had to break it down fast for buses, but could roll it right onto the Skyliner.”
She also raved about the storage: “The underseat basket gave us tons of space for all our gear and souvenirs on long park days.” Her toddler napped soundly thanks to the deep recline and extended canopy — and when her 6-year-old’s legs gave out, he climbed in too. “He’s tall but still under the 50-pound limit, and it was spacious enough for him.”
Yes, the Butterfly is on the pricier side — but for many parents (Steph included), the quality and long-term use are more than worth it. With one of the highest weight limits in its category and a tall backrest for growing kids, this stroller can go the distance. As Steph says, “If you can swing the price, every bit of it feels worth it.”

Why We Love It
For a stroller wagon that offers a few more bells and whistles without taking up more space, consider the
Larktale Caravan Coupe
. Though only slightly bigger than competitors, this luxe stroller wagon offers a slew of features that make it worth the more expensive price tag. To start, there are five — yes five! — storage units that help you bring everything you need in an organized fashion. This includes a rear- or front-attaching storage basket; an inner storage console and interior mesh pockets so riders have easy access to snacks, drinks and more; an exterior mesh pocket; and a removable handlebar console to keep your necessities within reach.
The stroller wagon features a large, foldable sun canopy with a mesh panel to ensure proper air flow, and comes with a rain cover to keep kids dry during drizzly adventures. Plus, it’s easy to fold flat for convenient storage in cars and closets.
The Larktale Caravan Coupe can comfortably fit up to two kids, with individually reclining seats to enhance comfort. The one downside is that it’s pretty heavy at 40 pounds, but Leah says that’s a small price to pay for what the Larktale provides.
“I was shocked that, despite being heavy, the Larktale stroller wagon is super easy to maneuver,” she says, adding that she recently used the wagon on a trip to the zoo and had no trouble weaving in and out of crowds or moving through doors. “My 2-year-old daughter and her 3-year-old friend were securely seated and had plenty of room to stretch their legs, and they were able to take in the views even with the canopy up. I especially loved and appreciated the console which held each of their water bottles and snack canisters. It gave them a sense of independence and gave me a break from constantly fetching food.”
Leah adds that the break can be a little difficult to operate when you first use the wagon, but after a few pushes it loosens for easy foot operation.
What to Look for in a Baby Stroller
There are a few additional factors to consider when buying a stroller to ensure it suits your family’s specific needs, beyond those we used to create our list. These include:
Family size
: Consider your current — and future — family size. If you only have one child or plan to space children several years apart, a single stroller may be all you need. But if you're expecting multiples or planning closely spaced siblings, you'll want to consider a convertible or double stroller. We selected a variety of strollers to suit different family sizes.
Location
: Families living in urban areas may appreciate a narrower stroller with strong maneuverability to help navigate small doorways and busy streets. Those in the suburbs who tend to drive more than walk might prefer a travel system that lets you click the infant car seat directly into the stroller frame. We selected strollers of varying sizes — both in use and when folded — to suit different living environments.
Cost
: Strollers can be incredibly expensive, but there are excellent budget-friendly options available. And if your timing is right, major retailers often offer significant discounts during shopping events like
Black Friday
,
Cyber Monday
and
Amazon Prime Day
. Just keep in mind: Investing upfront in a quality stroller may save you money long-term — especially if you plan to have more than one child.
Adaptable design
: The best strollers grow with your family and adapt to changing needs — whether that means accommodating an infant car seat or adding a bassinet attachment, second seat, or rider board.
FAQs
Which baby stroller brand is best?
There isn’t exactly a “best” stroller brand because the best stroller for one family might not be the same for another. That said, some of the most popular stroller brands include Graco, Chicco and Evenflo for all-around strollers, while brands like BOB Gear, Baby Jogger and Thule are common choices for parents looking for all-terrain or jogging strollers. Popular luxury stroller brands include Uppababy, Maxi-Cosi and Cybex. All of these brands are great options for your stroller depending on your preferences and price range.
Which stroller is best to buy?
For What to Expect editors, we say that the Mockingbird Single-To-Double Stroller 2.0 is the Best Stroller Overall due to its easy maneuverability, lightweight design and quick one-handed fold, but that doesn’t mean it’s the best stroller for every family. You may require a single-to-double stroller if you’re expecting your family to grow, a double stroller for twins or a jogging stroller to keep up with your active lifestyle. The best stroller is one that is big enough for your family, easy to use and fits within your budget.

When it comes to traveling with a baby — whether it's a big road trip or just a few quick errands around town — I quickly learned, like all new parents, that convenience is everything. And nothing is more convenient than a travel system. These car seat-stroller combos make getting from point A to point B with your little one so much easier.
A travel system is basically a
full-size stroller
and a compatible
infant car seat
that clips into the stroller when you're on foot or into the car when you're on (big) wheels. Car seat-stroller combos let you travel with your baby for years — I have been able to use mine from infancy right up through toddlerhood.
Most families need both a stroller and an infant car seat when they have a newborn. And in my experience as a mom of two, making sure the two products are compatible increases how much use you get out of both. Picture this: You’re driving with your baby in the backseat and need to stop to run a quick errand. Because you have a travel system stroller, you don’t have to unbuckle and lift your baby out of her car seat then re-buckle her into the stroller (possibly waking her up in the process). Instead, you simply unclip the entire car seat from its base and attach it to the stroller frame.
Not to mention, I’ve found that travel systems let you knock two big items off your baby checklist in one go and often allow you to save some money.
How We Chose the Best Travel Systems
To find the best travel systems, I compiled a list of around 50 car seat and stroller sets currently on the market. To whittle the list down, I referenced
stroller safety recommendations
from from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP): The group says strollers should have a five-point safety harness to keep your baby securely strapped in, easy-to-operate brakes and one footrest that extends across both sitting areas (for a side-by-side double stroller). I immediately eliminated any travel systems from the list with strollers that did not check all of these boxes.
I then considered car seats and strollers that I personally have tested and loved as a mom of two and parenting editor. I also noted the travel systems that parents in the What to Expect community have reviewed highly, and took into account feedback from parents on the What to Expect staff who have tested many of these strollers and car seats. Finally, I narrowed my list down to the best travel systems by showcasing those that have received top marks for:
Versatility
Maneuverability
Nice-to-have features (such as cup holders on the car seat, an adjustable stroller handlebar and washable fabrics)

What to Look for in a Travel System
The best travel system consists of a stroller and car seat that are not only compatible with each other, but with your family’s lifestyle, too. Because every family has different needs, here’s what you might keep in mind when shopping:
Size
:
This includes both a stroller’s dimensions as well as how many children it can accommodate. For example, some parents may prefer a larger stroller with a smoother ride, while others (particularly those who live in cities where they’re often navigating narrow streets) might appreciate a slimmer stroller frame.
Versatility
:
It’s often worth investing in a stroller that can adapt to changing situations. For example, if you have twins, you’ll need a travel system stroller that can handle more than one baby at a time in two infant car seats. You might also prefer for the travel system to include a convertible stroller that can become a double in the future should you have another baby. Some families might also like a travel system with a reversible stroller that lets them face baby forward or backwards.
Maneuverability
:
The easier it is to push and pull a stroller, the more likely you are to use it often. You’ll want a stroller that moves smoothly and turns without issue, even making tight corners.
Extra features
:
Some travel system strollers are basic, and focused on getting baby from point A to point B; others have additional features, like cup holders on the car seat, an adjustable stroller handlebar and washable fabrics. If you tend to tote a lot of gear with you, you’ll also want to look for a travel system stroller that can handle your stuff, too, such as one with parent storage or a large under-carriage basket.
FAQs
Should I get a car seat stroller combo?
This is a personal decision that really depends on your family’s needs. A travel system stroller allows you to switch your baby from car to stroller easily, but it might not be right for everyone.
A travel system can come in handy for families who are often out of the house. Because you already have the car seat installed, you only need to remember the stroller frame. A travel system can also help you save money: buying a car seat and stroller as a set may be cheaper than purchasing them separately. Still, there are some downsides to keep in mind before you invest:
The car seats that come in travel system strollers are for infants only, so you'll need to invest in a compatible toddler car seat later.
Even the lightest travel system stroller can be bulky, making it tough to load into and out of your trunk.
Infant stroller travel systems may not be good for dirt and gravel roads, since they're heavier than most strollers and tougher to push on uneven surfaces. They can also be tight squeezes through narrower grocery-store aisles.
You can only use the car seat that comes with the stroller (and not all companies sell extra car seat bases separately from the travel system). So if you have more than one car, you'll need to buy a second car seat if you don't want to unhook and reattach the one base the stroller comes with.
Is a car seat/stroller combo safe?
Car seat/stroller combos are very safe as long as they meet safety guidelines.
When buying any car seat (regardless of whether or not it’s part of a travel system), always make sure the product you’re considering:
Isn’t too old (you can check with the manufacturer or look for a label with the date it was made). Make sure, too, it has a label with the date of manufacture and model number.
Doesn’t have any visible cracks in it.
Comes with instructions so you can safely install the seat.
Isn’t missing any parts.
Wasn’t recalled (if you’re unsure, you can contact the NHTSA Vehicle Safety Hotline at 888/327-4236 or visit their
website
).
Hasn’t been in a car crash.
Strollers should have:
Easy-to-operate brakes that lock two wheels instead of just one to provide an extra measure of safety.
A wide base that can’t easily be tipped over.
A five-point harness with straps over both shoulders, hips and between the legs.
One footrest that extends footrest all the way across both sitting areas (for a side-by-side double stroller).
Once you’ve purchased a travel system, take these steps to ensure that your little one's secure:
As you put the system together, be sure to include all the pieces. There may be a lot of them, but every last one has a purpose.
Practice clipping the car seat into the stroller and unclipping it again before your baby's sitting in it (so you're a pro before you add a wee wiggler to the mix). Once your baby's in the car seat, gently shake the handle to make sure the seat's fully attached to the stroller before you hit the road.
Look for a label that reads "This restraint system conforms to all applicable federal motor vehicle safety standards. This restraint is certified for use in all motor vehicles and aircraft." This label means the seat has passed rigorous federal safety standards.
As always, remember that infant car seats should not be used for routine sleep, according to the AAP. The safest sleep position for a baby is flat on her back.
What are the different types of travel system strollers?
At their core, travel system strollers have a few things in common: They allow you to nestle baby’s car seat right inside and wheel away. But there are a few different types out there:
One-piece travel system strollers.
These convert the car seat into the stroller versus having a separate stroller.
Two-piece travel system strollers.
Most stroller systems are designed this way, with a separate car seat and stroller that work together.
Adjustable travel system strollers.
These stroller systems allow you to change the height for your comfort — and baby’s.
Two-seat travel system strollers.
While many travel stroller systems are designed for one car seat, some can fit two to accommodate twins.

After not one but two
C-sections
, I can tell you this: Recovery is no small feat. Whether your C-section was planned or totally unexpected, the days and weeks afterward can be a whirlwind. I remember vividly the mix of physical pain (those first few times getting out of bed — not to mention going to the bathroom — are no joke) and the mental exhaustion of learning
how to care for a baby
while my body was still recovering from major surgery.
The ups and downs of postpartum are completely normal, but the key to navigating it all is having the right tools on hand. My
C-section recovery essentials list
includes a mix of expert-recommended and mom-tested essentials — from the
best belly bands
to
successful scar treatments
to comforting must-haves worth packing
in your hospital bag
— that have proven to make things more manageable. It’s basically a survival kit I’d put together if I had to do it all over again.
How We Tested and Selected the Best C-Section Recovery Items
C-section healing and recovery is personal, and what works for one mom might not work for another. That’s why I approached this list from every angle — I factored in my own experience, medical advice from the experts, and the wisdom of other moms who’ve been through it, too. Here’s a detailed breakdown on how I started pulling products:
Personal experience:
I added what worked for me after two C-sections, from belly binders that made moving more bearable to the scar care products I wish I’d started using sooner.
Expert advice:
I consulted OB-GYNs,
Sheetal Dedania, M.D
., and
Matthew Carroll, M.D.
, about the healing process and asked for specific product recommendations for incision care, pain relief, mobility support, and more.
Community wisdom:
I gathered feedback from What to Expect community members and editors on staff who’ve been there, because everyone’s recovery journey is different.
Research:
I cross-checked expert advice with the
American College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians
(ACOG) guidelines to ensure each item is safe and truly helpful during recovery.
Based on the above, I then went on to make sure every recommendation met the following criteria:
Comfort and fit for post-C-section bodies:
From soft, breathable fabrics to adjustable sizing, every pick had to feel good on a healing belly.
What’s worth paying for vs. hospital freebies:
Some items you can stock up on from the maternity ward, while others are worth the splurge for better quality and long-term use.
FSA/HSA eligibility when possible:
Because products can add up fast, I prioritized products you might be able to pay for with pre-tax dollars.
Long-term usefulness:
The best recovery tools shouldn’t just collect dust after the newborn phase. I selected products that can support you well into your postpartum journey, not just the first six week.
Easy to use (even when you can’t bend, twist, or move much):
Everything here is simple to put on, take off, or apply — even when you’re sore, tired, and constantly carrying a newborn baby.
Supported by medical experts:
Last but tnot least, every product had to pass the “would an OB-GYN recommend this?” test, so you can feel confident it’s safe for recovery. Remember: Your doctor will tell you to take it easy and scale back any activity. Make sure to follow your doctor's advice so that you don’t put undue strain on your incision — which takes time to heal — and your energy levels.
A Doctor's Note on C-Sections
A
C-section,
or cesarean section, in case you’re not familiar, is the surgical delivery of a baby through incisions in the belly and uterus. As it is a surgical procedure, physical and emotional recovery typically takes longer than it does after a
vaginal birth
. You can expect to spend around three to four days in the hospital, and it will take at least four to six weeks at home before you’ll feel back to normal.
Roughly one in three babies (or about 32%) are born via C-section in the U.S. While any surgery warrants careful consideration, approaching it with some mental and emotional preparation can help you feel confident and empowered if a C-section becomes part of your birth plan. With that, scroll on to shop the best products for C-section recovery.

Korin Miller
originally contributed to this story.

Trust me, you’ll want to make sure you have pain relief like ibuprofen — which is considered safe if you’re

— within reach following a C-section delivery, and not just for your incision site. Even if you deliver by C-section, your uterus will continue to cramp until it shrinks back down to its pre-pregnancy size.
If your doctor gives you the go ahead to take ibuprofen, I'd stock up on
Advil Liqui-Gels
. It's the pain reliever of choice of plenty of What to Expect parents, aincuding me, and it's
FSA/HSA eligible
with most retailers. The coated liquid capsules are easy to swallow and work more quickly (typically within 30 minutes), absorbing faster than traditional tablets, reducing pain for four to six hours. Just remember to take any medication (even OTC painkillers like these) on schedule as prescribed by your doctor. It’s better to treat your pain ahead of time than to let it get so bad that you end up stuck in bed. And always be sure to take a pain reliever with food to reduce the risk of upsetting your stomach or dealing with ulcers.

What Doctors Want You to Know About C-Section Recovery
Recovery after a C-section isn’t one-size-fits-all experience, but there are common milestones. Here’s the general timeline of what to expect:
The first few days:
Pain, swelling, and limited mobility are normal. You’ll likely still be in the hospital for part of this period. Dr. Dedania says the first days are “quite challenging — navigating the pain, mobility, and caring for a newborn.”
Around two weeks:
Many moms notice a big improvement in mobility and energy. You may be able to do more activities independently, but still avoid heavy lifting or intense exercise.
Six to eight weeks:
Most people are cleared for normal activity by this point, provided there are no complications. Your provider will confirm whether your incision has healed and if you can resume exercise or sexual activity.
Beyond two months:
You may feel “close to normal,” but some soreness, swelling, or sensitivity can last up to three months.
Contact your provider right away if you notice any of the following:
Increased redness, swelling, or warmth around your incision.
Fever or chills.
Pus or foul-smelling discharge from your incision.
Severe pain that’s not relieved by medication.
Heavy vaginal bleeding or large clots.
These may be signs of infection or other complications that need immediate attention.
Aside from these physical cocerns, C-section recovery can take a toll emotionally, too. Some moms feel frustrated by the slower healing pace, but you can also feel sad or guilty if your birth didn’t go as planned — I definitely did, particularly after my first C-section. Dr. Dedania emphasizes that “everyone’s recovery pace is different, and patients should listen to their bodies.” This applies to your mental health as much as your physical recovery.
If you’re feeling down, anxious, or disconnected from your baby, reach out to your provider.
Postpartum mood changes
are common and treatable, and seeking support can make a huge difference.
C-section Recovery FAQs
How long does it take to recover from a C-section?
According to Dr. Dedania and Dr. Carroll, most people need about six to eight weeks before they’re ready to resume normal activity. The first few days are the toughest, but you’ll likely notice a big improvement around the two-week mark. (That’s when many moms are cleared to drive again.) Recovery speed varies, so listen to your body
and
your doctor.
When can I start walking or light movement safely?
Gentle movement, like short walks around your home, can usually start in the first few days after surgery — as long as you feel up to it, that is. Avoid anything strenuous until your provider clears you, although that's typically at your six-week postpartum check.
Should I use ice or heat on the incision area?
Ice can help reduce swelling and discomfort in the early days. Once your doctor confirms healing progress, gentle heat from a heating pad may help with stiffness or soreness, but always check before starting.
What kind of underwear is best when healing?
In the hospital, disposable mesh underwear is your absolute best friend. Once you’re home, Dr. Dedania recommends choosing underwear that sits either well above or below your incision to avoid irritation. High-waisted styles are a go-to for many moms (just like my favorite from Bodily).
How soon can I massage my scar safely?
Massaging your scar — especially if you’re considering a scar massage tool — should wait until your provider confirms your incision is fully healed, usually around six weeks postpartum. At that point, Dr. Dedania suggests options like cocoa butter, scar creams, or silicone scar sheets over massagers.
Do I still need a peri bottle after a C-section?
Yes! Even though it’s more often associated with vaginal births, you’ll still have
postpartum bleeding
and discharge (lochia) for several weeks.
A peri bottle (aka a perineal rinse bottle) is a small bottle that typically has a long neck that is designed to help you rinse off and keep your area clean. Using a peri bottle personally made bathroom trips much more comfortable for me.
What C-section recovery product factors should I consider before purchasing?
There are a few factors you may want to consider when searching for C-section recovery products. Those can include:
Type of relief provided:
There are a range of products that can help you feel better after a C-section, and each does something different. Some products (like ibuprofen) might help reduce pain and swelling, while others might help you address common postpartum complaints (like constipation or abdominal discomfort). Consider the kind of side effects the product addresses, and how it may be helpful.
Multiple purposes:
If you are short on space or budget, you may want to consider products that can be used for a variety of purposes, not explicitly just C-section recovery.
Fit:
The way items fit after a C-section is crucial. In general, you want things that are either loose or high-waisted to avoid putting direct pressure on your C-section scar, which takes time to heal.
Wound-specific items:
Some items are especially designed to help with your C-section scar by making it less painful or helping it heal faster.

We tried stickers, books, and straws — but this $20 find was the only thing that actually stopped our toddler from a mid-flight meltdown.
Just so you know, What to Expect may earn commissions from the shopping links included on this page. All sales and prices are accurate at the time of publishing.
Flying with a toddler is a completely different experience once they can walk. Lou was 16 months old on a recent trip; the first since she fully entered her “I want to move at all times” phase. And, of course, it was a longer-than-normal flight. Our previous flights had been just over an hour, so sitting in our seats wasn’t as much of a battle. This time, we had a three-plus hour flight from New York City to Florida, and I knew it was going to be harder. She’s more aware, less willing to sit still, and very set on doing what she wants in the moment. She also doesn’t nap easily outside of her crib, which is great at home but not ideal when your flight overlaps with naptime. Anytime we try to keep her contained, she’ll loudly protest, and once she’s tipped into overtired territory, nothing really works. We also don’t use screens, so a tablet isn’t an option.
I spent a lot of time researching screen-free travel ideas before the trip, and the one tip that kept coming up was snacks. Not just bringing snacks, but turning them into an activity. Lou has always been very into containers; opening them, taking things out, putting them back in. In short, she really locks into it. That’s what made the
GoBe snack spinner
stand out. It’s a snack container with separate compartments that you rotate through by pressing a button, making it much more engaging than a standard snack cup. I bought it a few weeks before the trip and hid it so it would feel new, then filled it with a mix of yogurt melts, peanut butter puffs, Once Upon a Farm puffs, cheese cubes, and little peanut butter sandwich bites.
Elizabeth Buxton
We pulled it out about 30 minutes into the flight after cycling through everything else we brought: lift-the-flap books, reusable stickers, bendy straws, and even plastic cups from the beverage cart. She was immediately interested, partly because it was new and partly because, well, snacks. It kept her occupied for a solid 30 minutes, which doesn’t sound like a lot but ended up being the longest stretch of calm we got. It outperformed every other activity we packed and had the added benefit of keeping her fed when a proper meal wasn’t really in the cards.
It didn’t eliminate meltdowns, but it reduced them enough to make the flight manageable. When she started to lose it again toward the end, and walking the aisles wasn’t cutting it, we brought it back out, and it worked like a charm as a quick reset.
We’ve used it constantly since then: car rides, park outings, and restaurants while waiting for food. It’s not the smallest thing to pack, and it took her a little time to figure out how to press the button herself, but that actually extended how long it held her attention. It’s simple, but it works, and for us, it made a noticeable difference in how the flight (and my stress levels) went.

When my kids were toddlers, their favorite toys were the musical ones: mini drum sets, ukuleles, and light-up xylophones dominated the playroom. The best musical toys for toddlers keep them entertained and help them expend energy, but in my experience, they also help build a foundational love of music. Now in their tween years, my children sing in a local choir and perform in musicals.
According to child development experts, playing with musical toys can encourage early cognitive development, helping toddlers develop coordination and laying the groundwork for future STEM skills. From simple shakers to toddler-friendly guitars and keyboards, there’s a wide variety of musical toys that can make your home come alive with sound (and sometimes sweet chaos!).
How I Chose the Best Musical Toys For Toddlers
Drawing from personal experience, I know anything that lets the kids shake, drum or dance is an instant hit. When choosing the best musical toys for toddlers, I kept safety top of mind, prioritizing options that are age-appropriate and designed to stand up to lots of play. To refine the list, I researched over 40 products and leaned on recommendations from the What to Expect community. I also sought insight from
Claire Goss
, Senior Manager of Family and Client Support at
Bright Horizons

Dr. Dana Suskind

American Academy of Pediatrics

What to Consider When Buying a Musical Toy
Age-appropriateness:
In addition to looking at the recommended age range, evaluate the toy as a whole. Look for easy-to-use features like large buttons or knobs that your child can use independently. For younger toddlers, consider more simple toys like shakers, tambourines or play mats that encourage movement and sensory exploration, while older toddlers may want something more advanced like a keyboard, microphone, or drum set to hone in on fine motor skills and creativity.
Open-ended play
:
Dr. Suskind suggests that the best musical toys allow toddlers to experiment. Instruments like xylophones, drums or toy pianos let them create rhythms and melodies of their own while building coordination and spatial awareness.
Safety and durability
:
Toddlers tend to play enthusiastically, so Goss stresses the importance of durable, non-toxic materials. Additionally, toys should have appropriate sound levels. Check that noise levels stay under 85 decibels to
protect your child’s hearing
. Musical toys with volume control are a great option.
Musical toy type:
Whether your toddler loves to dance, sing, or explore different sounds, there’s a musical toy to match their personality. Consider toy microphones for aspiring vocalists (aka your little chatterbox), drums for kids who love to hit and bang on things, or play mats with built-in tunes for energetic toddlers who never slow down.

As the weather gets warmer, I’m planning on getting outside with my two sons as often as possible. I mean, what better way to tire out two toddlers than letting them run wild in nature? But running around can get boring after a while, which is why I always make sure to have a few outdoor toddler toys at the ready.
During the toddler period, which is typically between 1 and 5 years of age, your child goes through a lot of exciting developments. “They become a lot more mobile as they learn to walk, run, and even climb, which leads to them actively exploring their surroundings,” says
Christina Johns
, M.D., MEd, FAAP, a pediatrician, pediatric emergency physician, and spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) based in Annapolis, Maryland. “The toddler stage is all about exploration, so the more new and interesting things they get to discover, the better.”
But outdoor play isn’t only great for exploration and fun: It can also help stimulate a toddler’s physical and emotional development, says
Katie Lockwood
, M.D., a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “Outdoor play offers more opportunities for
gross motor skills
like running, climbing, kicking and throwing that would [not] be feasible in most indoor environments,” she says.
Playing outside also allows toddlers more freedom to be in nature and use their imagination.“Children are innate scientists and love to experience the sights, scents, sounds, and textures of the outdoors,” adds Claire Goss, a childhood development expert and Senior Manager of Family and Client Support at
Bright Horizons
in Newton, Massachusetts. “Nature provides countless opportunities for discovery, creativity, and problem-solving.”
Although your child can experience all the benefits of outdoor play without a toy, the best outdoor toys for toddlers can help
encourage physical activity
and help get your kid’s energy out – away from the couch and screens.
How we chose the best outdoor toys for toddlers
Dr. Johns, Dr. Lockwood and Goss all agree that the best outdoor toddler toys are age appropriate and align with the milestones your child will reach during this two-year phase. Based on this guidance, I only selected toys in which the minimum age fell between 1 and 3 years old.
An outdoor toddler toy also has to be fun, and you really won’t know it’s fun until you open the box and play with it. I own plenty of outdoor toys for toddlers thanks to my two sons; I know which toys get played with daily and which ones collect dust in the closet. So I leaned heavily on my experience, but also relied on feedback and recommendations from What to Expect community members. All of the toys featured below received rave reviews for their ease of assembly (if it’s required), versatility and longevity — all of which contribute to a great outdoor toy for toddlers.

As the name suggests, these flexible buckets collapse into a flat circle that can be stored in any bag without taking up too much real estate. In addition to a bucket, you’ll get three shovels and a mesh bag to carry everything while getting rid of unwanted sand.
Bonus: The buckets and shovels are made of BPA-free material. So you don’t have to stress if your child decides they double as teething toys.

Part bean bag toss, part target game, Melissa & Doug’s Sunny Patch Dilly Dally is perfecting for helping kids reach various milestones. For toddlers, the tossing and the bean bag hones their gross motor skills and hand-eye coordination, while older kids can work on their counting and adding with an easy-to-follow scoring system.
It can also help kids, particularly toddlers, learn to share. “One social skill that toddlers are working hard on is learning how to take turns,” “This is a shaky skill through preschool, and toddlers can benefit from lots of practice,” says Goss. “You can play ‘stop and go’ games outside, which gives your child the opportunity to practice waiting and is great for boosting self-control.”
Aside from the toy’s many developmental benefits, Melissa & Doug’s bean bag toss is a quality toy. The turtle target has a durable, non-wobbly base to withstand the hardest throws. The bean bags are super lightweight, so even younger toddlers will be able to handle them.

Even if your child doesn’t show signs of being a soccer star, Dr. Johns says this type of toy can teach your child the crucial skill of playing with others. “Activities that involve taking turns or sharing, like kicking a soccer ball back and forth, can help children sharpen their consideration and communication skills,” she says.

Although it’s a bit of an investment, Avenlur’s 5-in-1 playset is loved by parents and kids alike. Made of sustainable, splinter-free material, the playset has multiple features to keep your child entertained (and wear them out): a ladder, a rock wall, a slide and a fabric tent for hiding.

ASTM International and the Consumer Product Safety Commission, meaning it meets all safety standards and is strong enough to withstand repeated use from children.

Why We Love It
I can personally vouch for Radio Flyer treetop tower, a well-made playhouse that will provide hours of fun. There are multiple features to encourage multiple types of play and help develop different skills: A climbing ladder to help with coordination and balance; a steering wheel to work on gross motor skills; a telescope and hidden alcove to encourage imaginative play. And, of course, a slide for fun. My 2-year-old has enjoyed learning to climb up its ladder and use the slide over and over (and over) again, while my 5-year-old loves playing hide-and-seek underneath.
As a parent, there is one feature I really appreciate: The playhouse is light and folds flat. This not only makes it easy to store, but makes it easy to bring inside during the colder months. Another plus is that it’s smaller than other playhouses, so you don’t need a giant playroom or sprawling yard to use it. The only downside to that is your kids will outgrow it within a few years.
How to Shop for Outdoor Toys
The right outdoor toys can encourage imaginative play, help kids develop important skills like hand-eye coordination and keep them active and moving. While they can be well worth it, you don't need to splurge on a fancy swing set or playhouse to keep your little ones entertained. “Outdoor toys do not need to be overly complex and instead should help kids focus on and engage with nature,” says Dr. Lockwood.
Here’s some guidance on what to keep in mind when you’re shopping for new outdoor toys:
Age recommendations
: Per the
AAP
, it’s always important to check the recommended age of any given toy to ensure it’s something your little one can safely use or is developmentally ready to enjoy.
Developmental appropriateness
: Two-year-olds are vastly different in their abilities from 3- and 4-year-olds, so tailor your purchases and your expectations accordingly. For example, “a younger toddler may need more supervision with gross motor activities, such as climbing up a slide or kicking a ball,” says Dr. Lockwood. “You can still use these toys, but you will need to play a more active role in assisting your toddler until they develop the motor skills to use them independently.”
Weight and capacity limits
: Toys where kids are sitting, riding or climbing on them (think: wagons, swings and slides) typically come with clear weight limits. Don’t ignore those for the sake of a cute toy — these limits ensure kids don’t injure themselves.
Choking risk
: Avoid toys with small or removable parts (or toys that can fit entirely in a child’s mouth) for babies and young children. Toddlers might be tempted to put them in their mouths, which is a
major choking hazard
.
Durability
: Outdoor toys are meant to be used outside, making the choice of material extra important. Many outdoor toys are made out of plastic, rubber or metal. Always choose toys made of sturdy, non-toxic materials. You will also need to maintain outdoor equipment to ensure there are no rusty nails, loose boards, splintering wood, etc.
Personal preference
: Dr. Lockwood recommends choosing toys that align with your child’s interests. Artsy kids might love sidewalk chalk, for example, while truck-obsessed tots might appreciate a sandbox or sturdier toy cars to use outside.
One last thing to keep in mind: The best toys are not meant to completely replace caregiver time, but enrich it. Solitary play is important, but using toys with caregivers helps further enhance the skills your little one learns from play. So consider things you’d like to do with your child when picking out outdoor toys — it’ll upgrade the experience for you both.

One day your baby is struggling to roll, and the next they're pulling themself up to stand at the coffee table. At least, that’s how fast it feels. When your little one starts showing interest in wanting to stand — usually
somewhere between 9 to 12 months
— you might want to look into buying one of the best standing toys to help them practice and develop important core and leg muscles.
How We Chose the Best Standing Toys
We spoke to a pediatrician and pediatric physical therapist to learn about the safety elements and entertainment features to look for in standing toys. Per their guidance, we evaluated toys based on the following factors:
Safety:
Your child will likely fall as they learn to stand, but the toy helping them master the skill shouldn’t pose fall risks. For this reason, you should
avoid seated baby walkers
, which have been found to pose fall risks and can delay baby’s motor development, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). Additionally, the standing component of your toy should be appropriate for children between 9 and 12 months old, the age when most children start to stand, and should be sturdy enough to hold your child's weight. Finally, the toy shouldn’t contain any removable small parts that could pose a choking hazard.
Versatility:
To get the most for your money, you’ll want a toy that provides multiple ways to play. A sit-to-stand walker, for example, may have a removable activity board that young babies can play with while sitting. Other toys, like activity tables, allow children to practice fine motor skills with buttons to press and levers to pull. Even a standing toy that teaches your child colors, letters and more is a worthwhile investment.
Interactivity:
A toy is useless if it doesn’t keep your child entertained. A good standing toy will have a variety of interactive elements, such as playing music and sounds or using lights to grab baby’s attention and engage with their senses. However, if your child gets overstimulated or is sensitive to sound, you may want to consider a non-electronic standing toy.
Each of the toys on this list meets or exceeds the safety standards, and has received overwhelmingly positive reviews from What to Expect community members for the other criteria.

FAQs
Are standing toys good for babies?
Standing toys are good for babies and a great way to help them practice standing. “Push toys, like a sturdy wagon or push cart, can also help kids cruise around and build confidence,” says Dr. Lockwood. “But [they] should only be used under supervision in a child-safe environment.”
You should also
avoid using seated baby walkers
, which have been found to pose fall risks and can delay baby’s motor development, per the AAP.
It’s important to note, however, that while standing toys are a great way to motivate baby, Dr. Rickerd says you don’t need one. As long as you’re giving them plenty of floor time, your baby will likely progress from crawling to standing to walking on their own. They may use the couch, the crib or even your body to start pulling to stand and practicing their balance.
What toys help babies stand up?
There are many types of toys to help baby stand up. You’ll want to look for elevated toys that encourage upright exploration, like a stationary activity table or a sit-to-stand walker. They should be sturdy and able to bear the weight of your child pulling without tipping over.
Some toys and objects you could use as baby learns to stand include:
Activity tables and stations:
An activity table is just what it sounds like — a child-sized table with an assortment of toys, buttons, levers, switches and more to explore attached to the top. These are designed to entice baby to stand and support him while he plays.
Push walker:
These are often wagons, carts with wheels or a sit-to-stand toy that comes with an activity board on the front. They include a bar for baby to grab onto to pull himself up. They’re also a great toy that grows with baby because when he’s able to take steps, he can use it to push it forward.
Wall-mounted toys:
If you want to save on floor space, wall-mounted toys are a great way to encourage baby to stand. These are often wooden activity boards that you can hang low on the wall for baby to play with while he practices standing. One thing to note is that they don’t typical offer a bar or surface for baby to use to pull himself up, so this might be a better option once he’s more comfortable on his feet.
Household objects:
A sofa, coffee table, laundry basket or diaper box can also work as a standing toy. Early walkers are known to find creative ways to use things in their environment to practice standing and even taking a few steps. So, you’ll also want to keep an extra eye on baby that he isn’t pulling on anything that can tip and fall over.
“With any toys, I recommend aiming for ones that children can get into and out of on their own,” Dr. Rickerd says. Ultimately, you want to avoid placing your child in a standing position, even if you’re using an activity table or the couch. Allowing them to figure it out on their own will go farther than simply placing them in the position.

Chances are that by 18 months, your toddler is always on the go. With their
constantly-developing motor skills
— such as independent walking and even running — the best toys for 18-month-olds will encourage this newfound mobility and burgeoning independence. They’ll also encourage your child’s cognitive and language skills, as your little one is getting better at problem-solving and trying out new words.
You can always make playtime out of just about anything — use household items to make up a game or turn a car ride into an educational opportunity to point out shapes and colors. But, you’ll likely want to have some toy options to further support their exciting new skills. Below, check out recommendations from What to Expect staff and community members, as well as child play experts.
How I Chose the Best Toys for 18-Month-Olds
Toys for 18-month-olds should be engaging but age-appropriate, so I spoke with three child development experts —
Sarah Lytle
, Ph.D., Executive Director of the Playful Learning Landscapes Action Network (PLLAN);
Natasha Burgert, M.D., F.A.A.P.
, a pediatrician in Overland Park, Kansas; Lori Caplan-Colon, a leading speech language pathologist and founder of
Montclair Speech Therapy
; and
Sanam Hafeez, Psy.D
, a neuropsychologist in New York City — to learn more about what parents should consider when shopping for toys for 18-month-olds.
I also included recommendations from users in the What to Expect community as well as parents on the What to Expect staff, who’ve road-tested many of these toys with their little ones at home.
Based on this feedback, I made sure that each toy was:
Developmentally-appropriate:
If a toy’s too easy, your child will get bored; too difficult and they’ll get frustrated. I prioritized toys that encourage toddlers’ growth in at least one of the following areas: fine and gross motor skills, cognitive skills and language skills.
Versatile:
For the most value — and to provide the most interest for your child — I prioritized toys that can be played with in multiple ways. For instance, many of the toys on our list can be used for counting as well as sorting, or can be used for educational play as well as imaginative play.
Safe:
At 18 months, you still need to keep an eye out for toys with loose or small parts that could potentially become a choking hazard, so we took time to ensure that each of our picks is safe for your little one to hold and put in their mouth. All toys on this list are free from these hazards.

Our Research
To determine what to look for in toys for 18-month-olds, we reviewed the
AAP recommendations for toys
and spoke to the following experts:
Sarah Lytle, Ph.D., director of the Outreach and Education division at the
Institute for Learning and Brain Sciences (I-LABS)
at the University of Washington.
Natasha Burgert, M.D., F.A.A.P.
, a pediatrician in Overland Park, Kansas.
Lori Caplan-Colon, a leading speech language pathologist and founder of
Montclair Speech Therapy
.
Sanam Hafeez, Psy.D
, a neuropsychologist in New York City.
We also spoke with Shelley Gingrich, Executive Director of Brand Solutions and mom of a 1- and 5-year-old, as well as Leah Rocketto, Associate Director of Commerce and mom of a 3-year-old, who has experience with several toys on this list.
Additionally, as a mom of two and a parenting writer, I’ve included my personal experience with many of the toddler toys on this list.
Finally, we canvassed the What to Expect community boards to see which toys parents of 18-month-olds gave high praise.
FAQ
What are the best toys for 18-month-olds?
Toys that encourage your child to move with their whole body, like music they can dance to or a ball they can kick, roll or chase, are developmentally on-target for this age group’s gross motor skills. Toys that develop fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination, like sorting toys, stacking toys and even car and doll toys, are also great options. Many of these types of toys also help your tot’s cognitive development as it requires them to problem-solve fitting items into certain shapes or solving a puzzle. Art toys also help encourage their creativity and imaginative play while helping them hone fine motor skills, too (through grasping and using art supplies).
Books are always a great choice for your little one when working on their language skills. Reading with your child every day
is recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics
(AAP), as it will help encourage their vocabulary development. Toys that play music or sound and encourage repetition, such as teaching numbers, colors, letters and nursery rhymes, are also great for this area.
